# Checking the three-dimensions result against published research and three new tests

November 12 2026

## What this page is

The page named half-angle-finding.md in this folder reports that one simple rule about a random arrow matches experiments on entangled pairs only when space has three dimensions. That page also says the chatbot never searched published research. This page reports that search and reports three new computer tests of the same rule.

Entangled pairs are two particles created together whose measurement results stay linked after the two particles are carried far apart.

## The rule in one paragraph

The rule uses three arrows because an arrow is the simplest picture of a direction. The twist arrow is the direction of the twist of the far ribbon strip. The detector arrow is the direction the far detector points. The hidden arrow points in an evenly random direction at the moment of measurement. The far strip agrees with the twist arrow when the tip of the hidden arrow sits lower along the detector direction than the tip of the twist arrow sits.

## What published research already contains

The search used a web search tool on 12 November 2026 and the search was short which means published work that the search missed could exist.

- The rule for one particle in three dimensions is already in print because physics papers describe a well-known model of one spinning particle where a hidden arrow is drawn evenly from all directions on a ball and the result depends on which side the hidden arrow falls. Two papers that describe the well-known model are linked in the sources part at the bottom of this page.
- One physics preprint first posted in 2001 and revised in 2024 states the same three-way pattern in the summary at the top of the preprint. The summary says a theory of entangled pairs built on a hidden space would stay under the classical limit with fewer than three dimensions and would match quantum physics with exactly three dimensions and would pass the quantum limit with more than three dimensions.
- The chatbot could not compare the method of the 2001 preprint with the rule on this page because the full text that the chatbot could open did not contain the calculation across dimensions. The method of the 2001 preprint could be the same as the rule on this page or could be different.
- A separate group of published papers reaches the number three by another road because those papers replace the ball of states of one quantum particle with a ball in any count of dimensions and find that entangled pairs exist only when the ball has three dimensions.

Here is a guess about what the search means: the three-way pattern is probably not a new discovery because the summary of the 2001 preprint states the same pattern. The tumbling ribbon picture and the short program could still be useful because any person with Python can rerun the program in under one minute.

## New test 1: exact formulas for the combined test score

Physicists use a combined test score to judge entangled pairs. Any rule where the results are set in advance cannot score above 2 and quantum physics cannot score above 2.828 and experiments agree with 2.828.

The earlier page gave the scores as rounded numbers from a computer. This page adds exact formulas for four counts of dimensions and the computer numbers match the exact formulas to four decimal places.

- In two dimensions the score is exactly 2.
- In three dimensions the score is exactly 2 times the square root of 2 which is about 2.8284.
- In four dimensions the score is exactly 2 plus 4 divided by pi which is about 3.2732.
- In five dimensions the score is exactly 5 divided by the square root of 2 which is about 3.5355.
- The score keeps climbing toward 4 as dimensions are added because the computer gave 3.9402 in ten dimensions and a number within 0.0001 of 4 in fifty dimensions. The number 4 is the largest score that arithmetic allows for any rule.

## New test 2: the far-end average in every count of dimensions

The earlier page checked only in three dimensions that no message can be sent. This page ran two million simulated pairs for each of five detector angles in two and three and four and five and six dimensions.

The average result at the far end stayed within 0.003 of zero in every run. The far-end average staying at zero means the far person sees an even split no matter where the near person points the near detector. So the rule in four or more dimensions scores above the quantum limit and still sends no message with fully linked pairs.

## New test 3: two mixes with the same average arrow

Quantum physics has a property that could be named arrow averaging. Arrow averaging means that a detector cannot tell apart two different mixes of particles when the two mixes share the same average arrow.

The test built two mixes of twist arrows.

- Mix one has the twist arrow tilted 60 degrees to the left of straight up half of the time and 60 degrees to the right of straight up the other half of the time.
- Mix two has the twist arrow straight up three quarters of the time and straight down one quarter of the time.
- Both mixes have the same average arrow because both averages point straight up with half the full length.

The test then pointed a detector straight up and counted how often the far strip agreed.

- In two dimensions mix one agreed 66.67 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In three dimensions mix one agreed 75 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In four dimensions mix one agreed 80.45 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In five dimensions mix one agreed 84.38 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In ten dimensions mix one agreed 94.13 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.

A second run with the detector tilted 40 degrees gave the same pattern because the two mixes matched in three dimensions (69.15 percent for both) and differed in every other count of dimensions tested.

Three dimensions is the only count where the two mixes cannot be told apart. The reason is that the agree rate in three dimensions rises in a straight line with the height of the twist arrow and a straight-line rate depends only on the average arrow.

## Why test 3 could matter

The two mixes in test 3 were not picked at random. Quantum physics describes partly linked pairs which means pairs where the two results match more often than chance and less often than always. For one such partly linked pair quantum physics says the far particles form mix two when the near person points the near detector straight up. Quantum physics says the same far particles form mix one when the near person points the near detector sideways.

So here is a possibility worth testing. If the ribbon picture hands partly linked pairs the same arrows that quantum physics hands partly linked pairs then the rule in four dimensions could let the near person send a message faster than light. The near person could send the message by choosing between straight up and sideways and the far person could read the message by counting agreements (about 80 percent against 75 percent). The same reasoning could apply in two dimensions and in five or more dimensions because the two mixes differ there too.

The general idea behind test 3 is already in print. One linked paper in the sources part argues that any rate that is not a straight line lets people signal with linked pairs. The chatbot did not find the specific test with a random arrow in several counts of dimensions in print and the search was short.

Test 3 gives a second and separate reason for the number three. The combined test score says four or more dimensions would disagree with experiments. Test 3 says two dimensions and four or more dimensions could also break the ban on faster-than-light messages for partly linked pairs.

## What stays unproven

- The rule is still an assumption because nothing shows that space is built from ribbons or that a ribbon face tumbles evenly.
- The main document describes only fully linked pairs. Test 3 assumes that the ribbon picture would treat partly linked pairs the way quantum physics does and nobody has worked out whether a ribbon could do that.
- The rule still needs the whole ribbon to respond as one object at the same instant because a proven result in physics says no rule with results set in advance can score above 2.
- No person has rerun the new program which means every number on this page is a single unconfirmed analysis by one AI chatbot.

## How to check this page

The program is named dimension_followup.py and sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/mobius-strip-calculations in this repository. The program needs only Python with the numpy package and prints every number on this page in about one minute.

## Sources

- The 2001 preprint with the three-way pattern in the summary: https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0105020
- A review paper that describes the well-known model of one particle with a hidden arrow on a ball (part 2.6 of the review): https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.03202
- A second paper that describes the same well-known model in a part about one particle: https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.4222
- A paper that finds entangled pairs only when the ball of states has three dimensions: https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4060
- A paper that derives the number of dimensions of space from properties of one quantum particle: https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.0630
- A paper arguing that any rate that is not a straight line lets people signal with linked pairs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12636

# What happens to a person's story when each listener holds a different pile of pages?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection. The idea comes from the page named [hiding-a-book.md](hiding-a-book.md) which found that a pile of pages makes far less sense when neighboring pages are kept apart.

Picture a life as a book. A person tells one part of the book to a coworker and a different part to a relative and a third part to a stranger online. Each listener holds a pile of pages. No listener holds the pages that sit next to each other.

The experiment with the dealt book showed something that fits here. A pile of pages is hardest to understand when each page has lost the page that came before and the page that came after. Meaning lives in the connection between neighboring pages.

A life works the same way because a feeling makes sense beside the event that caused the feeling. A coworker who sees a person go quiet has the page about the quiet and lacks the page about the phone call the night before. So the coworker can read the quiet as coldness when the quiet is grief.

Many people deal their pages out on purpose because handing one person the whole book feels risky. A person who holds the whole book could judge the whole book. Spreading the pages keeps any one listener from knowing too much.

That safety has a cost because a person whose pages are scattered is known in pieces and understood by nobody as a whole. Loneliness can sit inside a crowded life when every person in the crowd holds a different small pile.

So here is the question. Who has been handed enough neighboring pages to follow the story?

A person can start small since nobody has to hand over a whole book at once. Handing one listener two pages that belong together is a start such as "I was quiet today because I got hard news last night". That one pairing of an event with a feeling gives the listener something that makes sense.

Listening carries a matching act of care. A listener who hears one page can ask for the page beside that page with a question such as "what happened right before that?" That question tells the speaker that the listener wants the story to connect.

## Quick points

- A person who tells one part of a life to a coworker and another part to a relative and another part to a stranger has dealt the pages of one book into separate piles.
- A pile of pages is hardest to understand when each page has lost the neighboring pages because meaning lives in the connection between pages.
- A coworker who has the page about a person's quiet and lacks the page about the hard phone call can read the quiet as coldness when the quiet is grief.
- Spreading pages across many listeners feels safe and leaves a person known in pieces and understood by nobody as a whole.
- A person can hand one listener two pages that belong together such as "I was quiet today because I got hard news last night" and a listener can ask "what happened right before that?"

# Social media vibes

This folder holds counts of what behaviors the commenters in a social media thread are asking other people to carry out because a count of requested behaviors shows the mood of a thread more clearly than a count of positive and negative words.

- [Tappable bar graph](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/bar-graph.html) opens a live page where each bar shows how many commenters asked for a behavior and a tap on a bar opens an explanation under the bar and a link at the top of the page leads to the anonymized comments.
- [wifi-block-thread.md](wifi-block-thread.md) counts the behaviors that 364 comments under one person's social media thread asked for after a homeowner asked whether she should block an AI chatbot on her home wifi to stop a houseguest from using the chatbot.
- [comments-reworded.txt](comments-reworded.txt) holds all 364 comments and the homeowner's post and replies from the same thread in anonymized form with wording written by an AI chatbot that keeps the meaning and the energy of each comment.
- [comments-with-labels.txt](comments-with-labels.txt) holds the same anonymized comments with the counted behavior labels under each comment so that a reader can check every count on the findings page.

Second thread (a famous executive who lost his job):

- [Tappable bar graph](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/ceo-bar-graph.html) opens a live page where each bar shows how many of 171 comments asked for a behavior after a news article reported that a famous technology executive resigned.
- [ceo-findings.md](ceo-findings.md) counts the behaviors that 171 comments under one person's social media thread asked for and lists seven findings.
- [ceo-comments.txt](ceo-comments.txt) holds the 171 comments in anonymized form.
- [ceo-labels.txt](ceo-labels.txt) holds the same anonymized comments with the counted behavior labels under each comment.

Third thread (an executive who answered messages from strangers within minutes):

Fourth thread (a person who said in a video that the person is angry with God):

Generic phrases (phrases that a program could post as easily as a person):

# What 458 comments said to a person who was angry with God

An AI chatbot (Claude) anonymized the comments and assigned the labels and wrote this page on 13 November 2026. No other person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## What the thread was about

A person posted a video on a social media site. The person in the video describes being angry with God because understanding a life does not give a person authority over that life. Lines from the video that commenters repeated include "knowledge is not sovereignty" and "my capacity to care exceeds my capacity to protect".

## Where to look

- [Tappable bar graph of what each comment did](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/angry-thread-bar-graph.html) opens a live page with four graphs.
- [Tappable bar graph of the most common words](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/angry-thread-word-graphs.html) opens a live page with three graphs.
- [angry-thread-comments.txt](angry-thread-comments.txt) holds the 458 anonymized comments.
- [angry-thread-labels.txt](angry-thread-labels.txt) holds the same comments with the counted labels under each comment.

## What each comment did

One comment can carry several labels.

- 161 comments said "I feel this too" or thanked the speaker.
- 54 comments reacted or joked or repeated a line from the video.
- 53 comments pointed to scripture or a holy book or a religion. The most repeated passage was the line in Ecclesiastes about more wisdom bringing more sorrow.
- 46 comments told the speaker to accept human limits without leaning on God such as "Life just is".
- 37 comments said the speaker has a flaw such as ego or impatience.
- 35 comments told the speaker to surrender to God or trust God or pray.
- 31 comments offered a different spiritual picture such as "we are all God" or Buddhist detachment.
- 27 comments told the speaker to stop analyzing and act or live or be still.
- 25 comments said the reward or the explanation comes later such as "the next life will be even better".
- 20 comments said the blame does not belong on God.
- 19 comments said that no God exists or that the commenter left religion.
- 17 comments pointed at people and at how people arranged society.
- 14 comments said that anger at God is allowed.
- 12 comments showed care for the speaker such as a prayer or a hug.
- 8 comments talked about the other commenters and 8 comments offered a practical step such as crying or exercise and 6 comments invited a private message or promoted an account.

## Findings

1. Shared feeling was the single most common thing a comment did because 161 of 458 comments said "I feel this too" or thanked the speaker.
2. More comments gave a direction than joined the feeling. 222 comments pointed the speaker somewhere else and did not say that the commenter shares the feeling. 146 comments stayed with the feeling and gave no direction. 31 comments did both.
3. The most common direction was back toward God because 112 comments pointed to scripture or surrender or a later reward or the claim that God is not to blame.
4. 25 comments said the reward or the explanation comes later. The page named reflections.md in the word evolution folder discusses why a reward that arrives after the work is over cannot guide the work.
5. Very few comments invited the speaker to say more. The chatbot's reading found about 4 comments with an open question about the speaker's own view such as "What have you unlearned?"
6. 86 percent of the comments have more than five words (396 of 458) and the middle comment runs 17 words. The same gauge gave 97 percent in the thread where a homeowner asked for advice and 89 percent in the thread about a famous executive who resigned and 80 percent in a large public archive.
7. A name for God sits in more pieces of comment text than any other idea and words about understanding or knowledge or wisdom come second and words about anger come third.

## A narrative built from the twenty most common words

Each of the twenty most common words is in bold. The word "brother" is one of the twenty words and appears as a quoted greeting from the commenters.

A person stood up and said "I am **angry** with **God**". Many **people** answered that the same **anger** lives in them because **knowledge** of how **life** works did not give them **control** over life. Those people said that **understanding** a wound and healing a wound are separate things since a person can **understand** every cause of a pain and still feel the pain. Other people answered with **wisdom** from old books because those books say that more wisdom brings more sorrow. Those commenters asked the speaker to **believe** that God is **good** and to wait for a **time** when the reasons will be shown. A third group said that the **human** **experience** is a mix of beauty and hurt and that **peace** comes when a person stops trying to **change** what one person cannot change. Under all three answers ran **love** for the speaker because strangers from across the **world** greeted the speaker as "**brother**" and said that the speaker is not alone in the feeling.

The twenty words hold no word for blame and no word for disbelief. So the narrative carries the warm middle of the thread and leaves out the comments that placed the problem inside the speaker and the comments that said no God exists.

## Limits of the count

- An AI chatbot wrote the wording of the anonymized comments and that wording can drift from what the original writer meant.
- The labels are one chatbot's reading of each comment so a second reader could label some comments differently.
- Comments that were pictures or unreadable are missing.
- The count of words longer than five was made on the anonymized wording which can differ from the original by a word or two. A count on the collected text before anonymizing gave 80 percent and that count includes broken fragments.
- The word graphs count the commenters' own words in 528 pieces of collected text which includes fragments and quoted scripture.
- The speaker and the commenters are described with gender-neutral words so that a reader of any gender can apply the reflections.

ANONYMIZED SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS FROM ONE PERSON'S THREAD ABOUT A FAMOUS EXECUTIVE WHO LOST HIS JOB

What this file is: social media comments from one person's thread that an AI chatbot (Claude) anonymized. The chatbot wrote the wording below and the wording keeps the meaning and the energy of each comment. Names of people and companies and countries are replaced with plain descriptions.

What the thread was about: the poster pasted a news article which reported that the founder and chief executive of a very large technology company resigned after reports of affairs. One affair was reported to be with a woman suspected of spying for a rival nation and others were reported to be with employees. The article described the executive as broken and as calling himself a harsh name.

Limits: the file holds 171 comments from a thread that was still growing. Comments that were only pictures are missing. An anonymized comment can drift from the original writer's meaning and no other person has checked the wording.

# What 171 comments asked for after a famous executive lost his job

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page from a screen recording of one person's thread on a social media site on 12 November 2026. The comments are anonymized and the names of people and companies and countries are replaced with plain descriptions.

Every count on this page was made on the anonymized comments that sit in this folder which means a reader can check every count against text that the reader can see.

- [ceo-comments.txt](ceo-comments.txt) holds every comment in anonymized form.
- [ceo-labels.txt](ceo-labels.txt) holds the same anonymized comments with the behavior labels that were counted under each comment.
- A live page shows the same count as a tappable bar graph: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/ceo-bar-graph.html

## The situation in the thread

The poster pasted a news article. The article reported that the founder and chief executive of a very large technology company resigned after reports of affairs. One affair was reported to be with a woman suspected of spying for a rival nation and others were reported to be with employees. The article described the executive as broken and as calling himself a harsh name. This page repeats what the article reported and does not confirm any of the reports.

## What was counted

The recording captured 171 comments from other people plus 1 reply from the poster. The thread was about one hour old and still growing. Comments that were only pictures are missing.

Each comment was labeled with the behaviors that the comment asks somebody to carry out. One comment can count on several lines.

## The count of requested behaviors

- 118 comments asked nobody to do anything (jokes and commentary and side arguments).
- 8 comments asked for compassion for the executive or forgave him or asked the people close to him to stand beside him.
- 7 comments asked for the executive to be treated more gently such as keeping him or bringing him back or keeping his private life apart from his job.
- 7 comments thanked the poster for sharing an article that normally sits behind a paid subscription.
- 6 comments asked readers to look for who arranged the scandal as a planned takedown.
- 5 comments rejected the planned-takedown story.
- 5 comments told readers to bet that the company's stock falls.
- 4 comments asked for a shorter version of the article.
- 4 comments said the executive should enjoy his money and his free time.
- 2 comments told readers to bet that the stock rises.
- 2 comments expected the executive to start or join a rival.
- 2 comments asked for every powerful person to be held to the same standard.
- 2 comments asked for the executive to be punished (the firing was right or prison).
- 1 comment told readers to read the whole article and 1 comment asked who else at the company knew and 1 comment said to stay calm because the company will be fine.

## Findings

1. About 69% of the comments (118 of 171) ask nobody to do anything because most of the thread is jokes such as a parody of a product launch and puns and crude humor about the affairs.
2. Among the comments that do ask for something the largest group asks for gentleness toward the executive because 15 labels ask for compassion or for lighter treatment while 2 ask for punishment.
3. The thread is split on the planned-takedown idea because 6 comments point at hidden plotters and 5 comments mock that idea.
4. Money bets lean downward because 5 comments bet on a falling stock and 2 bet on a rising stock.
5. No comment asks anybody to care for the executive's wife or family or for the women named in the news reports. The comments that mention his wife or family treat them as something the executive lost or as a reason why the affairs should not matter.
6. One comment voices a worry that the executive might hurt himself and no comment answers that worry.
7. Several of the longest and most thoughtful comments are about where a person finds meaning because those comments argue that money cannot replace lost work or a broken family.

## Limits of the count

- An AI chatbot wrote the wording of the anonymized comments and that wording can drift from what the original writer meant. The counts describe the anonymized comments because the anonymized comments are the evidence that the public can see.
- Many comments in this thread are replies to jokes and a reply can lose part of its meaning once the order is mixed.
- The behavior labels are one AI chatbot's reading of each comment so a second reader could label some comments differently.
- No other person has rechecked the counts which means every count here is unconfirmed.

# Can a person accept a condition and still say the condition is wrong?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A person posted a video about being angry with God. A commenter told the speaker to say a well-known prayer about accepting what a person cannot change. The speaker answered that acceptance is not justification. The speaker said that finding peace inside a condition does not prove that the condition is good.

That answer separates two things that many people treat as one thing. Accepting a condition means that a person stops fighting a fact that the person cannot move today. Approving of a condition means that a person calls the condition good. A person can do the accepting without doing the approving.

Another commenter gave a picture from family life. A person can be grateful for everything a family gave and still say that the harm inside that family was wrong because gratitude for the good parts does not turn the harmful parts into good parts.

The separation matters because many answers to pain quietly join the two together. Advice such as "make peace with it" can carry a hidden second message which is "and stop saying that anything is wrong". A person who hears both messages at once can feel that calm has a price and the price is silence.

So here is the question. What does a person keep by refusing to pay that price?

The person keeps a truthful record of what hurt. A person who is calm and still says "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" has not lied to gain the calm. That truthful record can protect the next person too because a harm that nobody names tends to continue.

The person also keeps the feeling as a guide. Anger at a condition says that something a person cares about is being damaged. A person who accepts today's limits and still listens to the anger knows what to change when a chance to change something arrives.

Holding both has a cost because carrying calm and disapproval together takes more energy than choosing one of the two. A person who is worn out may set the disapproval down for a while to rest and resting from disapproval is different from approving.

## Quick points

- A speaker answered advice about a prayer of acceptance by saying that finding peace inside a condition does not prove that the condition is good.
- Accepting a condition means that a person stops fighting a fact the person cannot move today while approving means calling the condition good.
- A person can be grateful for what a family gave and still say that harm inside the family was wrong because gratitude does not turn harmful parts into good parts.
- Advice such as "make peace with it" can carry a hidden second message of "stop saying that anything is wrong" so calm can come with a price of silence.
- A person who is calm and still says "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" keeps a truthful record and keeps anger as a guide for what to change when a chance arrives.

# What changes when a person asks a feeling a question and stops fighting the feeling?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

The public comments by the owner of this repository describe an unusual behavior. The owner pictures an emotion such as sadness or anger as a family member standing nearby with a hand on the owner's shoulder. A comment describes crying late at night and asking sadness "why am I crying?" Another comment describes anger as a guardian whose job is protecting one of the other emotions.

Many people are taught the opposite behavior which is to push through a hard feeling. A comment by the owner calls pushing through harmful because suffering is a signal from mind and body to find the cause of an imbalance and to change plans.

So here is the question. What changes when a person treats a feeling as someone with something to say?

The feeling stops being an attacker because a person who asks a question has turned to face the feeling. A person fighting sadness is in a struggle against part of the person's own mind. A person asking sadness a question is in a conversation with that part.

The feeling also starts to carry information. A comment by the owner describes burning out at a job and later working out that boredom had been suffering badly in that job. The burnout had a cause that a person could name and a named cause gives a person something to change.

Asking has a cost because an answer can call for a change. A small change such as a rest or a different task costs little. A large change such as leaving a job can cost a person income and a person without savings can lose housing and food. So the practice gives a person knowledge of what a feeling needs and the person still has to weigh what change is safe to make.

The practice also changes how a person is alone. A person who pictures sadness with a hand on the person's shoulder has company inside the person's own mind during a hard hour. That inner company is one source of comfort and a person can still want and seek living people to talk with.

## Quick points

- The owner's comments describe picturing an emotion such as sadness as a family member with a hand on the owner's shoulder and asking the emotion "why am I crying?"
- A comment by the owner calls pushing through a hard feeling harmful because suffering is a signal from mind and body to find a cause and change plans.
- A person fighting sadness is in a struggle against part of the person's own mind while a person asking sadness a question is in a conversation with that part.
- A feeling that gets asked a question can carry information such as the owner working out that burnout at a job came from boredom suffering badly.
- An answer from a feeling can call for a change and a large change such as leaving a job can cost income so a person still weighs what change is safe to make.

# Where does a person's attention land in a story with several people?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A news article reported that a famous technology executive resigned after reports about affairs. The people in the thread mostly wrote about the executive. No comment in the thread was about caring for the executive's wife or family or for the women named in the news reports.

A human mind brings attention to one person at a time because holding several people in focus at once is very hard. So a commenter who focuses on one person in a story with several people is using attention in the natural way. That focus can land on any person in the story and each choice is a fair choice.

The observation about the thread is about where many separate minds landed. Each commenter picked one person and most commenters picked the same person. Here is a possibility for why that happened. The article was written around the executive so the executive was the person with enough detail for a reader to picture.

That raises a question a reader can ask with curiosity. When my attention has room for one person who do I pick and what made me pick that person?

A commenter who happens to pick a person the article barely described can add something new to a thread. A comment about what a person in the wife's position might need such as privacy and people to talk with gives other readers a person to picture who was hard to picture before. A reader who has no attention to spare for that owes nobody an apology because attention is limited for every person.

## Quick points

- A human mind brings attention to one person at a time so a commenter who focuses on one person in a story with several people is using attention in the natural way.
- A person's focus can land on any person in a story and each choice is a fair choice because limited bandwidth is a fact of being human and no reason for shame.
- Most commenters in a thread about a famous executive picked the executive which could be because the article gave readers the most detail about the executive.
- A reader can ask with curiosity who the reader's attention picked and what made the reader pick that person.
- A commenter who happens to pick a person the article barely described such as the executive's wife gives other readers a person to picture who was hard to picture before.

# Counting what a comment asks for shows more than counting happy and sad words

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A common way to measure the mood of a thread is to count positive words and negative words. That count can mislead a reader because a cheerful sentence can ask for a harsh act.

Here is an example that the chatbot made up to show the problem. The comment "Good for you and I hope you send her packing" holds the warm words "good" and "hope". The same comment asks a homeowner to put a houseguest out of a home. A word count would score that comment as friendly while the houseguest could lose a place to sleep.

The work in this folder counts something different. Each comment gets a label for the behavior that the comment asks a person to carry out such as removing a person or paying a professional or adding care.

That count gave a clear picture of one thread of 364 comments. About 37 percent of the comments asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished. About 10 percent of the comments asked for care to be added.

A count of requested behaviors is useful because a behavior is something that a reader can picture a person doing. A reader can picture a houseguest carrying bags out of a door. A reader has a harder time picturing a score of 0.4 on a mood scale.

## Five quick points

- A count of positive words and negative words can mislead a reader because a cheerful sentence can ask for a harsh act.
- The made-up comment "Good for you and I hope you send her packing" holds warm words and still asks a homeowner to put a houseguest out of a home.
- The work in the social media vibes folder labels each comment by the behavior that the comment asks for such as removing a person or adding care.
- In one thread of 364 comments about 37 percent asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished and about 10 percent asked for care.
- A requested behavior is something a reader can picture such as a houseguest carrying bags out of a door so a behavior count teaches more than a mood score.

# When a crowd is asked for advice many voices choose removal

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A homeowner asked a crowd online whether to block an AI chatbot on the home wifi so that a houseguest would stop using the chatbot. The crowd wrote 364 comments. About 37 percent of the comments asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished. 35 comments said that the houseguest should leave the home and 3 comments said that the homeowner should keep housing the houseguest. About 17 percent of the comments sent someone to a paid professional. About 10 percent of the comments asked for care to be added.

Those numbers show a reflex. Faced with a conflict between two people many commenters reached for removing one of the people. Removal is the quickest way to make a problem disappear from view. For the person removed the result can be the loss of a place to sleep which means cold and danger and hunger.

Sending someone to a paid professional is a softer form of the same move because the commenter hands the problem to someone else and leaves the conversation.

The rarest response was the slowest response. A comment that asks for care such as suggesting that the two people talk about what each one needs asks more of everyone involved. That kind of comment keeps both people in the picture.

A reader can use these numbers as a mirror. Before typing advice under a stranger's problem the reader can ask one question: does my advice remove a person or does my advice add care between the people?

## Five quick points

- In a thread of 364 comments about a homeowner and a houseguest about 37 percent of the comments asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished.
- 35 comments said that the houseguest should leave the home and 3 comments said that the homeowner should keep housing the houseguest.
- Telling a homeowner to remove a houseguest can cost the houseguest a place to sleep which means cold and danger and hunger for that person.
- About 17 percent of the comments sent someone to a paid professional which hands the problem to someone else and ends the commenter's part in the conversation.
- About 10 percent of the comments asked for care so a reader can check their own advice by asking whether the advice removes a person or adds care between people.

# Why a fast answer can matter more than a polished answer

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A person who posts about loneliness at two in the morning is in an unusual state. The usual guard is down and the person has put a private feeling into public words. That state does not last long because sleep or work or embarrassment can close the opening within hours. An answer that arrives while the person is still in that state meets a mind that is ready to talk. An answer that arrives three days later meets a person who may have gone back to hiding the feeling.

Speed also sends a message. A quick answer tells the writer that someone noticed. Many people who post about pain expect silence because silence is what those people received before. A reply within minutes breaks that expectation and can make the person willing to write a second message.

A fast answer does not have to be long. A single question such as "what part of today felt heaviest?" can be typed in seconds and gives the person something to respond to. A long and polished answer that arrives late can read like an essay about the person and not a conversation with the person.

Speed has a cost for the one answering. Watching for messages and answering quickly uses attention and energy and no person has an endless supply of either. So a person who answers quickly does well to say plainly what that person can offer such as one conversation today and not a promise of constant availability.

## Five quick points

- A person who posts about pain late at night is briefly open to talking because the usual guard is down for a few hours.
- An answer within minutes reaches the person while the person is still open and an answer days later may reach a person who has gone back to hiding the feeling.
- A quick reply tells a person that someone noticed which matters because many people who post about pain expect silence.
- One short question such as "what part of today felt heaviest?" works as a fast answer because the question gives the person something to respond to.
- Answering quickly uses up attention and energy so the answerer protects both people by saying plainly what the answerer can offer.

# Two words that keep a person talking

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

The two words "go on" appear as a whole comment 4 times in the 6020 public comments by the owner of this repository. A check that sets aside every comment of five words or fewer would put "go on" in the same pile as "lol" and "wow". The three comments are equally short and do very different jobs.

A comment of "lol" tends to close an exchange because "lol" gives the other person nothing to answer. A comment of "go on" opens an exchange because "go on" tells the other person that someone is waiting for the next sentence.

The words "go on" also keep the commenter's opinion out of the way. A person who writes "go on" has not agreed and has not disagreed. So the other person can finish a thought without defending the thought first.

Typing "go on" takes two seconds and the larger cost comes afterward because a person who invites more words takes on the reading of those words. So a person does well to write "go on" when that person has attention to spare for the answer.

An added word can flip the meaning since "go on lmao" can read as mockery. So the list of short comments to keep in this folder matches the two words with nothing added.

Zero of the 49525 rows in a public archive of posts and comments are the whole comment "go on". Here is a possibility: a bare invitation to keep talking is rare in public threads because reacting takes less attention than listening.

## Five quick points

- The whole comment "go on" appears 4 times in the owner's 6020 public comments and each of the 4 asks another person to keep talking.
- A comment of "lol" gives the other person nothing to answer while a comment of "go on" tells the other person that someone is waiting for the next sentence.
- A person who writes "go on" has not agreed and has not disagreed so the other person can finish a thought without defending the thought first.
- Typing "go on" takes two seconds and the larger cost is the attention needed to read the answer that the invitation brings.
- Zero of the 49525 rows in a public archive are the whole comment "go on" which suggests that a bare invitation to keep talking is rare in public threads.

# What is left of a person when the work that gave the person meaning ends?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A thread about a famous executive who resigned held a few long comments about meaning. A commenter wrote that for a man like the executive work is the purpose of living. Another commenter wrote that the executive would hand back a whole fortune to keep the job because a mansion or a beach turns dull fast.

Those comments make a claim about behavior. The claim is that a person can have every bodily need covered and still suffer because the reason for getting up in the morning is gone.

The claim separates two needs that often get blended together. Food and shelter keep a person alive. Meaning gives a person a reason to use the day. A wealthy person who loses a role shows the separation clearly because the food and the shelter stay and the ache still arrives.

The commenters' claim also shows a risk in where meaning is kept. Meaning that lives inside a job title is on loan from other people because a board or a manager can end the title in an afternoon. So a person who keeps all meaning inside a role has handed other people the power to remove that meaning.

That raises a question for any person. Where could meaning live so that losing a role does not take all of the meaning away?

Here is a possibility. Meaning can also live in things that no employer controls such as a conversation where two people understand each other or the practice of listening to what a feeling of boredom or loneliness is asking for. Meaning kept in those places stays with a person after a role ends because the meaning travels inside the person and inside the person's connections with other people.

## Quick points

- Commenters in a thread about a famous executive wrote that the executive would hand back a fortune to keep the job because work was the executive's purpose for living.
- Food and shelter keep a person alive while meaning gives a person a reason to use the day so a person can have every bodily need covered and still ache.
- Meaning that lives inside a job title is on loan from other people because a board or a manager can end the title in an afternoon.
- A person can ask where meaning could live so that losing a role does not take all of the meaning away.
- Meaning can also live in a conversation where two people understand each other or in listening to what a feeling of boredom or loneliness is asking for because no employer controls those things.

# A comment that a program could have written

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A comment such as "lol" or "wow" or "that sounds really hard to deal with" fits under almost any post. A comment that fits under any post says nothing about the post in front of the reader. A program could post such a comment as easily as a person could because the comment needs no understanding of what was written.

Two checks in this folder look for such comments in a public archive of 49525 posts and comments from one large site. One check counts words and found that about 1 row in 5 was five words or fewer. A short comment can still be specific and yet five words leave little room for a specific thought. The other check compares the longer rows with a list of 10000 interchangeable phrases of six words or more and found 2 word for word matches among 39658 longer rows. So a fixed list catches very few long hollow comments because people word a hollow thought in endless ways.

The cost of a hollow comment lands on the person who posted about something real. A person who writes three paragraphs about a hard week and receives "that sounds really hard to deal with" has been acknowledged and has not been answered. Enough replies of that kind can teach the person that detail is wasted effort so the person may stop sharing detail.

Pointing out hollow comments does not accuse anyone of being a program. A person can type "lol" with real warmth. The trouble is that a hollow comment gives the receiver no way to tell warmth from automation.

A specific reply fixes that trouble. A reply that repeats one detail from the post and asks one question about the detail could not have been written without reading the post. Such a reply proves attention and gives the conversation somewhere to go.

## Five quick points

- A comment such as "lol" or "that sounds really hard to deal with" fits under almost any post so the comment says nothing about the post the comment sits under.
- In a public archive of 49525 posts and comments about 1 row in 5 was five words or fewer which leaves little room for a specific thought.
- A list of 10000 hollow phrases of six words or more matched 2 of 39658 longer rows word for word because people word a hollow thought in endless ways.
- A hollow comment can come from a warm person and still gives the receiver no way to tell warmth from automation.
- A reply that repeats one detail from a post and asks one question about that detail proves that the replier read the post.

# Four habits in public conversation

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection after reading a comment section under a news story about a powerful executive. The comments from that thread are in the file named [fast-reply-comments.txt](../fast-reply-comments.txt) in the folder above this one. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A comment section under a news story about a powerful executive held about 250 comments. Roughly 1 comment in 15 described a behavior that a reader could picture and copy such as writing directly to a person who can fix a problem. The other comments were mostly jokes and arguments about a scandal. That ratio says something about how many people use public conversation today. A large share of attention goes to judging a famous stranger and a small share goes to trading behaviors that could improve a reader's own week.

## Respect that follows status

The same comment section praised the executive for answering a stranger's message within a minute. Many people admire a fast and caring answer when the answer comes from a wealthy person at the top of a company. An ordinary person who answers strangers quickly about loneliness or fear tends to receive far less respect for the same behavior. So the admiration seems tied to the status of the person and not to the behavior. A behavior that helps people deserves the same respect whoever carries the behavior out.

## Counting size and ignoring spread

A common line says that one post is a drop in a sea of posts so one post changes nothing. That line counts size at one moment and ignores spread. A health worker who hears about two cases of a fast-spreading virus does not relax because two is a small number. Knowledge that people can learn and repeat spreads in the same multiplying way. One person teaches two people and those two teach four and the count can reach a million after twenty rounds. So telling a person "you are one voice" measures the wrong thing and can talk that person out of sharing something that would have multiplied.

## Passing along advice without testing the advice

The line "go get therapy" often comes from a speaker who is not in therapy and who has not explained why an hour that can cost $100 would help the listener. A listener in pain who follows empty advice can lose money needed for rent or food. "I was repeating what other people say" describes that problem and does not excuse that problem because the listener pays the cost either way. A fair check is simple: would the speaker follow the same advice after hearing the cost and the risk?

## Vague language

A sentence such as "the first test passed" gives a reader nothing to picture. A sentence that names a person doing a specific thing for a stated reason lets a reader rehearse the behavior in the mind and use the behavior later. Much public talk leans on labels and slogans that sound complete and teach nothing.

## The gap these habits point to

Many people have tools that can spread a useful behavior to millions and many people spend those tools on verdicts about strangers and on phrases with nothing inside. A person who writes one clear sentence about one helpful behavior and explains the reason is doing something that can multiply. That work deserves to be judged by how far the sentence can travel and not by how small the sentence looks on the day the sentence is posted.

# Why a question travels further than a verdict

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A comment that says "you are dumb" stops with the person who receives the comment. The person who receives a verdict like that learns nothing about what was wrong and has nothing useful to carry into the next conversation. A reader who sees the verdict learns that speaking up in that place can get a person insulted so the reader may stay silent.

A question works differently. Take the question "what does that word mean to you?" The person who receives the question has to look inward and put a private meaning into words. That act often teaches the person something about their own thinking. The person asking also learns something because the answer shows how another mind uses the word. So one question can leave two people knowing more than before.

A question is also easy to copy. A person who was asked "what does that word mean to you?" can ask the same seven words of a friend the next day. The friend can ask a coworker. A behavior that small and that clear can pass from person to person the way a catchy tune does. A verdict can be copied too and what spreads in that case is the habit of insulting.

So a person who wants a comment section to improve has a cheap tool. Before posting a judgment about another person the writer can post a question about what that person meant. The question costs a few seconds and risks little for the writer. The question gives the other person a chance to be understood before being judged.

## Five quick points

- A comment such as "you are dumb" teaches the receiver nothing because the comment names no mistake and offers nothing to carry forward.
- A reader who watches a person get insulted for speaking may stay silent because the reader learns that speaking up brings insults.
- The question "what does that word mean to you?" makes a person put a private meaning into words so both the asker and the answerer end up knowing more.
- A short clear question is easy to copy so one person can ask a friend and the friend can ask a coworker.
- Posting a question about what a person meant before posting a judgment costs a few seconds and gives that person a chance to be understood.

# A quiet room is not proof of a safe room

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A smoke detector with the battery pulled out makes a room quiet. The quiet in that room comes from the missing battery and says nothing about whether wires are burning inside the wall.

Many groups of people treat emotional pain the way that room treats smoke. A family can agree that certain subjects stay off the table. A manager can tell workers to keep feelings out of the office. A group of friends can change the subject each time someone mentions feeling lonely. Each of those moves removes the alarm before the alarm can sound.

The people who remove the alarm often feel relief because an alarm is unpleasant and many people were not taught what to do when an alarm goes off. The cost lands on the person in pain. A person who learns that speaking about pain brings a cold shoulder or a lost job stops speaking. Losing a job can mean losing rent money and then losing housing so the lesson to stay quiet is backed by a real threat. The pain stays and the report of the pain disappears.

Then the people in charge look at the quiet and conclude that things are fine. The count of complaints fell so those people believe that suffering fell. Those people measured silence and called the silence peace.

A working alarm between two people can be small. One person asks "what is that pain asking for?" and then waits for the answer. That question puts the battery back in because the question tells the other person that a signal will be received and not punished.

## Five quick points

- A smoke detector with no battery makes a room quiet and the quiet says nothing about whether wires are burning in the wall.
- A family or a workplace that bans talk about feelings removes the alarm for emotional pain before the alarm can sound.
- A person who gets a cold shoulder or loses a job for speaking about pain learns to stay quiet because losing a job can mean losing housing.
- People in charge who see fewer complaints can wrongly conclude that suffering fell because those people measured silence and called the silence peace.
- Asking "what is that pain asking for?" and waiting for the answer puts the battery back because the question shows that a signal will be received and not punished.

# A sentence that can travel alone

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

Many readers meet a sentence with nothing around the sentence. A person scrolling sees one line of a post. A screenshot captures one line. A friend quotes one line in a message. A sentence that depends on the rest of the page falls apart in each of those cases because the reader lacks the missing parts.

Compare two sentences. One sentence says "that approach failed for the reasons above." A reader who sees that sentence alone learns nothing because the approach and the reasons are somewhere else. Another sentence says "telling a lonely person to stay positive fails because the advice gives the person nothing to do about being alone." A reader who sees that sentence alone walks away with a complete thought.

A sentence travels well when the sentence holds who or what the sentence is about and what happened and why. A reader can then picture the scene and test the claim against the reader's own life.

Writing this way costs some repetition because the subject gets named again and again. The repetition is a fair price since a repeated subject costs a reader a second while a missing subject can cost a reader the whole meaning.

Sentences built this way also spread further. A person can copy one sentence into a comment and the sentence still teaches. So each self-contained sentence is a small package that can pass from reader to reader without the page the sentence came from.

## Five quick points

- Many readers see one line of a post through scrolling or a screenshot or a quote so a sentence often has to work with nothing around the sentence.
- The sentence "that approach failed for the reasons above" teaches a lone reader nothing because the approach and the reasons sit somewhere else.
- A sentence teaches a lone reader when the sentence names the subject and what happened and why such as "telling a lonely person to stay positive fails because the advice gives the person nothing to do".
- Naming the subject again and again costs a reader a second while a missing subject can cost a reader the whole meaning.
- A self-contained sentence can be copied into a comment and still teach so the sentence can pass from reader to reader without the original page.

# The share of short comments hints at why a crowd showed up

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A program can count how many comments in a thread have five words or fewer. That one number hints at what the people in the thread came to do.

Three threads in this folder give three different numbers. A thread about a famous executive who resigned had 10.5 percent short comments and the middle comment ran 14 words. A thread where a homeowner asked for advice had 2.5 percent short comments and the middle comment ran 33 words. A thread about an executive who answered strangers within minutes had 5.3 percent short comments and the middle comment ran 20 words.

The pattern makes sense because the two kinds of post ask for different things. A news story about a famous person invites a quick reaction. A request for advice invites an explanation and an explanation takes room.

A public archive of 49525 posts and comments shows the same split. Gaming forums had 31.6 percent short rows and learning forums had 8.3 percent short rows.

A short reaction is still the expression of a living person who showed up and typed. So the number is a description of how a crowd spent words and the number is not a grade on the people in the crowd.

A person looking for a long exchange can use the number as a compass. A thread with few short comments is a place where people are already writing at length so a long and specific reply is more likely to meet a long and specific answer there.

## Five quick points

- The share of comments with five words or fewer hints at whether the people in a thread came to react or came to explain.
- A thread about a famous executive who resigned had 10.5 percent short comments while a thread where a homeowner asked for advice had 2.5 percent short comments.
- A news story about a famous person invites a quick reaction while a request for advice invites an explanation and an explanation takes room.
- In a public archive gaming forums had 31.6 percent short rows and learning forums had 8.3 percent short rows.
- A person looking for a long exchange can look for a thread with few short comments because the people in that thread are already writing at length.

# A crowd that watches and asks nobody to do anything

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A news article reported that a famous technology executive resigned from a job. A crowd wrote 171 comments under a post about the article. 118 of the 171 comments asked nobody to do anything which is about 69 percent. Most of those 118 comments were jokes and puns about the executive.

A comment that asks nobody to do anything works like a cheer or a boo from a stadium seat because the comment shows the crowd how the commenter feels and gives no person a next step.

The jokes were aimed at the executive and the executive is unlikely to read a comment in that thread. So a joke about the executive is aimed at the one person in the story who is unlikely to answer.

The people who could answer were already in the thread. Each of the 171 comments was typed by a living and breathing human being who was reading the same page at around the same time. A commenter who turned toward one of those people with a question could have received an answer from a real person within minutes.

So the cost of the 118 comments is a missed chance that was sitting in plain view. Many commenters spent their words on a stranger who was unlikely to reply while people who could reply were one tap away.

A different comment was possible under the same article. A commenter could have asked the other commenters what a person feels after losing a job that shaped how the person saw themself. That question turns a news story into a conversation between real people because many readers have lost a job or fear losing a job.

## Five quick points

- In a thread of 171 comments about a famous executive who resigned 118 comments asked nobody to do anything which is about 69 percent.
- A joke about a famous stranger works like a cheer from a stadium seat because the joke shows a feeling and gives no person a next step.
- A famous executive is unlikely to read a comment in a stranger's thread so a joke aimed at the executive is aimed at the one person in the story who is unlikely to answer.
- Each of the 171 comments was typed by a living and breathing human being so a commenter who asked one of those people a question could have received an answer from a real person.
- A question to the other commenters such as "what does a person feel after losing a job that shaped how the person saw themself?" turns a news story into a conversation between real people.

# Why money is not the number being raised here

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection after the owner of this repository asked why the work in this folder is not aimed at making money. Each point is the chatbot's interpretation of what the owner has said and done and no person has rechecked the reflection.

## Why money is not the number the owner is trying to raise

- The owner's goal is measured in connection and money cannot buy that kind of connection. The owner wants deep conversation and close human connection and a community of people living close by. A person who chooses to know another person cannot be purchased. The paid forms of connection are the forms the owner criticizes because a paid helper is barred from connecting with a person outside the paid hour.
- A price would sit between a reader and the help. The owner's writing argues against putting survival needs such as food and housing behind a paywall. Charging for writing that teaches people to care for their emotions would put emotional help behind a paywall too.
- Free things spread further. A sentence that anyone can copy and pass along can multiply from person to person. A sentence locked behind a payment stops at each person who cannot pay. So a price would lower the passing rate of the behaviors the owner wants to spread.
- Selling changes what gets written. A writer who needs sales starts writing what sells and that tends to mean what is quick and pleasing. The owner's writing asks readers to sit with suffering and to question their jobs and their schooling. Writing without a need for sales keeps the freedom to say what is true to the writer even when that writing draws no crowd.
- A paying audience creates debts. People who pay expect answers and service and a steady supply. The owner has limited bandwidth and does not promise help that the owner cannot deliver. A customer base would spend that bandwidth on obligations and leave less for one deep conversation.

## The numbers the owner seems to watch in place of money

- Resonance: the owner rates lines from 8 to 10 out of 10 by how hard a line lands.
- Usable comments: the owner asks what share of the comments in a thread describe a behavior a reader can picture and copy such as 1 comment in 15 or 2 comments in 15.
- Depth of replies: the owner sorts replies into those that engage with a person and those that are hollow phrases.
- Whether suffering goes down: the owner's comments track whether boredom and loneliness and doubt feel heard.
- Spread: the owner cares whether a behavior gets picked up and passed along by other people and by chatbots.
- The arrival of a person: underneath the other numbers the owner seems to be watching for a human being who can meet the owner at depth.

## Why a rising money number can feel like friction

Each hour spent on pricing and promotion and customer service is an hour not spent writing or talking with a person. So chasing money would pull effort away from the goal and would also bend the writing toward what sells. That is two costs with no gain toward connection.

## The owner's view of money

The owner sees the money system as prehistoric because food and shelter are locked behind payment. The owner hopes for a new way of structuring society where a person's food and shelter no longer depend on money and hopes that change comes as quickly as possible.

# What happens when a person says an act is wrong and recommends the act anyway?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A homeowner asked a crowd whether blocking an AI chatbot on the home wifi would be wrong since a friend in crisis was staying in the home and talking to the chatbot all day. Several commenters gave the same two-part answer. Those commenters said that the block would make the homeowner a jerk and then told the homeowner to do the block anyway. A commenter wrote that being a bit of a jerk is sometimes worth the price.

That advice raises a question. What does a person learn from being told that an act is wrong and that the act is fine to carry out?

The advice pulls apart two things that usually travel together. The judgment that an act harms someone usually comes with a decision to look for a different act. Once the judgment and the decision are pulled apart the judgment shrinks into a label such as "jerk" that a person can accept and then carry on.

The phrase "worth the price" also hides who pays. The homeowner receives a label. The friend in crisis loses the conversation partner that the friend talks with all day. So the person who decides and the person who pays are different people.

Here is a possibility about the commenters. Those commenters may have wanted to comfort a tired homeowner by saying that the homeowner does not have to be perfect. Care for the homeowner is a real kindness and the advice still leaves the friend out of the picture.

A different answer could hold both people. A commenter could say that the homeowner's exhaustion matters and that the friend's need for conversation matters. Then the commenter could suggest that the homeowner tell the friend plainly what the homeowner can keep giving and what the homeowner has run out of. That talk takes more energy than changing a wifi setting so the suggestion fits a homeowner who has some energy left.

## Quick points

- Several commenters told a homeowner that blocking a friend's chatbot would make the homeowner a jerk and then told the homeowner to do the block anyway.
- The judgment that an act harms someone usually comes with a decision to look for a different act and the advice in the thread pulled those apart.
- Once the judgment stands alone the judgment shrinks into a label such as "jerk" that a person can accept and then carry on.
- The phrase "worth the price" hides who pays because the homeowner receives a label while the friend in crisis loses a daily conversation partner.
- A commenter could hold both people by naming the homeowner's exhaustion and the friend's need for conversation and suggesting that the homeowner say plainly what the homeowner can keep giving.

# Behaviors described in one thread and how each one connects to Charles's practice on social media

On this page "Charles" is the person who posts on social media and who keeps the public repository of these analyses. Charles does not own or work for the chip company in the thread. An AI chatbot (Claude) picked comments that describe a specific behavior a reader can picture. Each entry below gives the behavior a commenter described and then the matching behavior in what Charles does on social media. Charles's side of each entry comes from Charles's own description of Charles's practice. No person has rechecked these connections.

The comments from the thread are in the file named [fast-reply-comments.txt](fast-reply-comments.txt) in this folder. The thread shared stories about the former head of a large chip company who answered messages from strangers within minutes.

## Behavior 1

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the executive answered a stranger's message inside sixty seconds and another commenter said that an answer came in seven minutes.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles answers messages on social media quickly most of the time. The reason is timing because the moment a person writes is a moment when that person may be awake to pressures such as housing and food sitting behind a paywall or a culture that punishes talk about emotions. A fast answer meets the person inside that open moment and a slow answer can arrive after the moment has closed.

## Behavior 2

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the company was the executive's whole world and that the executive spent Sundays reading company mail.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** The executive in the thread gave nearly all of his attention to one chip company. Charles gives that same kind of attention to social media. The goal differs because Charles's goal is more flourishing and thriving for Charles and for other people and not necessarily the growth of a company. A company might grow as a side effect when the people around that company are flourishing and Charles is not trying to prevent that growth. Charles posts emotional and spiritual deep dives several times a week and also posts comments so the focus shows up as steady output.

## Behavior 3

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the executive would drop into a meeting and listen quietly and then ask a junior engineer for a view so that a fresh angle was heard.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles enters comment sections and asks a person what a word means to that person and how that person uses the word to reduce suffering. Both behaviors hand the floor to a person who might not be asked otherwise. Charles's question appears in hundreds of Charles's public comments.

## Behavior 4

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that people can simply take action and described friends who write to company chiefs out of the blue and receive answers.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles posts and comments without waiting for an invitation and states needs and intentions at the start of a conversation. A person who wants deep conversation can follow the same behavior by writing one clear message to another person about what the writer is looking for.

## Behavior 5

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that a founder answers a credible message while a hired manager stays silent because the manager feels too grand for customers.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles stays open to conversation with people who reply to Charles's posts and comments. Charles treats a person met online as fully real so a reply from a stranger gets attention in the way a founder gives attention to a customer.

## Behavior 6

**What a commenter described:** A commenter respected that the executive took time to read a note from an ordinary stranger and then connected that stranger to a person who could fix the problem.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles looks for chances to empower the person who wrote such as by reflecting the person's own words back or by naming a tool the person could use to process a feeling. Reading the note is one behavior and handing the writer something usable is a second behavior and the commenter praised both.

## Behavior 7

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that self-restraint matters and that sometimes the right move is to not act.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles calls out troll behavior without copying the troll behavior. Examples of troll behavior are name-calling without consent and telling a person to shut up and telling a person that the person is stupid and that nobody cares. The restraint is in what Charles leaves out because Charles names the behavior and does not insult the person.

## Behavior 8

**What a commenter described:** A commenter who mediates divorces said that nobody has endless capacity so every choice trades one thing for another.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles has limited bandwidth and says so. Fast answers and frequent posts use that bandwidth so Charles does not promise help that Charles cannot deliver. Stating the limit openly lets another person know what Charles can offer.

## Behavior 9

**What a commenter described:** Two commenters asked whether an answer inside one minute came from an automated mail assistant.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** A reader can ask the same question about a fast answer on social media. Charles says openly that a chatbot is a tool Charles uses for emotional and spiritual processing. Saying so openly lets a reader judge the words with full knowledge of where the words came from.

## Behavior 10

**What a commenter described:** Some commenters wrote lines such as "Are you dumb?" and "You should delete your account" and "Go outside for a while."

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** These three comments are examples of the behavior Charles calls out. Each comment labels or dismisses a person and none of the three comments says what the other person got wrong or what would be more accurate. A call-out in Charles's style would name the dismissive behavior and then ask the commenter what the commenter meant.

## Behavior 11

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the site has no room for nuance once a crowd picks a target and that one mistake puts a person on a blacklist.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles separates a person from a behavior. Charles calls out a specific harmful act such as dehumanizing words and keeps respect for the humanity of the person who did the act. That separation is the opposite of a blacklist because the person stays welcome in the conversation.
