# A test of 10000 generic phrases against a public archive of forum comments

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 12 November 2026.

## What the phrase list is

The file [generic-phrases-10000.txt](generic-phrases-10000.txt) holds 10000 interchangeable comment phrases of six words or more such as "thank you so much for sharing this" or "I'm so sorry you're going through this" or "I could not agree more with this". Each phrase signals a reaction and carries no information and no request that a reader could act on. An AI chatbot wrote 320 base phrases by hand in eight groups and a small program combined the base phrases with common openers and closers such as "lol" or "bro" or "for real".

The list changed on 13 November 2026. The earlier list included phrases as short as one word such as "lol". Every phrase on the current list has six words or more because a comment of five words or fewer is already counted as too short to carry a specific thought.

## Counts with the current list (six words or more)

- 2 of the 49525 rows are word for word the same as a phrase on the current list which is about 0.004%.
- 26 of the 49525 rows (0.05%) contain one of the 320 base phrases somewhere in the row. The most common base phrase is "keep up the great work" which appears in 7 rows.
- 39658 of the 49525 rows (80.1%) have six words or more so the current list was tested against most of the archive and still matched almost nothing.
- 9867 rows (19.9%) are five words or fewer. That count does not depend on the list.

The near-zero match rate suggests that a longer hollow comment is rarely worded the same way twice. A fixed list of long phrases works as a set of examples of hollow comments and works poorly as a filter for catching hollow comments.

## What this test does and does not claim

The test counts how many real comments in a public archive are word for word the same as a phrase on the list. The test does not claim that any comment came from an automated account. The archive dates from February 2016 which is years before chatbots could write fluent comments so nearly every writer in the archive was a living person. The point of the test is awareness: a comment that matches the list contains nothing that separates a person from a program so a reader who wants to know more has to reply and ask the writer.

## The archive

The archive is a public collection named reddit-dataset by the GitHub account linanqiu: https://github.com/linanqiu/reddit-dataset

- The archive holds posts and comments from 51 forums on one large discussion site grouped into seven areas (entertainment and gaming and humor and learning and lifestyle and news and television).
- The archive repeats most rows about fifty times. After the program removed repeats and deleted comments the archive held 49525 different posts and comments.
- The archive stripped punctuation and emoji from the text which means the emoji lines on the phrase list could not be tested.
- The archive mixes thread titles with comments so some short rows are titles and not comments.

## The three counts with the earlier list

The counts in this section and in the next two sections were made with the earlier list that included short phrases.

- 343 of the 49525 rows (0.69%) are word for word the same as a phrase on the list.
- 665 more rows (1.34%) are short rows of eight words or fewer that are built around a list phrase of two or more words such as a list phrase with a name added.
- Together 1008 rows (2.0%) match the list in one of those two ways.
- 9867 rows (19.9%) are five words or fewer whether or not the row matches the list.

## The most common exact matches with the earlier list

ok (15) and lol (11) and wow (10) and yes (10) and no (10) and awesome (9) and nice (8) and thank you (7) and beautiful (7) and neat (6) and very nice (6) and rip (5) and who cares (5) and nope (5) and this (5) and congratulations (5).

## The counts by area with the earlier list

Each line shows the share of rows that match the list in either way and the share of rows that are five words or fewer.

- Lifestyle: 3.2% match and 13.2% are five words or fewer.
- Humor: 2.4% match and 23.2% are five words or fewer.
- Gaming: 2.2% match and 31.6% are five words or fewer.
- Television: 1.9% match and 11.0% are five words or fewer.
- Entertainment: 1.7% match and 13.8% are five words or fewer.
- Learning: 1.2% match and 8.3% are five words or fewer.
- News: 1.1% match and 28.3% are five words or fewer.

## Findings

1. A fixed list catches a small share because only 2.0% of the rows match the list even with 10000 phrases. People vary a stock reaction in more ways than a list can hold.
2. The zone of comments that a program could imitate is far wider than the list because 19.9% of the rows are five words or fewer and a comment of five words or fewer has very little room for anything specific to the post.
3. The forum with the highest match rate is a forum where people post photos of their own progress because 14.9% of the rows there match the list. The matches there are praise phrases such as "great work" and "congratulations". So the place where people share something personal is also the place where the replies are most interchangeable.
4. Forums that require detailed answers show almost no matches. A science question forum (395 rows) and a plain-explanation forum (485 rows) had zero matches and a history question forum (164 rows) had one. So the rules and habits of a space change how much room stock phrases get.
5. The humor area and the gaming area hold the most short rows which fits the idea that quick reactions cluster where the posts are jokes or game moments.
6. Long hollow phrases almost never repeat word for word because the current list of 10000 phrases of six words or more matched 2 rows out of 49525. So checking whether a comment mentions any detail from the post may catch hollow comments better than any fixed list can.

## Limits

- The archive is from 2016 and from one site so the shares could differ on other sites and in other years.
- The match test is strict. A comment with one extra word or a spelling change does not count as an exact match.
- A match says nothing about the writer. A short reaction can be a living person's small way of being present.
- No other person has rerun the program which means every number here is unconfirmed. The program sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/social-media-vibes-scripts.

# The repository owner's own comments compared with two other comment threads

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 12 November 2026.

## What was looked at

The owner of this repository wrote 9134 comments on a large discussion site before his account was removed. The comments hold about 3.04 million words. 6437 of the comments are different from each other because the owner often posted the same long comment in more than one place.

Two kinds of counting were done.

- A program measured every one of the 9134 comments (length and questions and matches to a list of generic phrases).
- A program picked 60 comments at random and an AI chatbot read an excerpt of each one and labeled the kind of energy in the comment. The 60 excerpts with their labels sit in [owner-comments-sample.txt](owner-comments-sample.txt).
- A live page shows the sample count as a tappable bar graph: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/owner-comments-bar-graph.html

## The count for the 60 sampled comments

One comment can count on several lines.

- 25 comments explain or analyze a situation and ask for nothing.
- 15 comments ask the other person a direct question or invite more conversation.
- 10 comments ask for care to be added such as food and shelter for every person or emotional education or listening to an emotion.
- 8 comments share the owner's own experience or practice or a story.
- 4 comments give a practical instruction or tip.
- 4 comments are a short reaction that asks for nothing.
- 1 comment asks for a person to be kept apart from other people.
- 0 comments refer someone to a paid professional.

8 of the 60 comments open with a line of scripture. About 10 of the 60 are replies that the owner pasted from his conversations with AI chatbots.

## The comparison

The two other threads are the wifi thread (364 comments about blocking an AI chatbot on home wifi) and the executive thread (171 comments about a famous executive who lost his job). Both threads sit in this folder in anonymized form.

Each line gives the owner's comments first and then the wifi thread and then the executive thread.

- Short reaction that asks for nothing: 7% and 7% and 44%.
- Explains or comments and asks for nothing: 42% and 18% and 25%.
- Asks for control or removal or punishment of a person: 2% and 37% and 2%.
- Refers someone to a paid professional: 0% and 17% and 0%.
- Asks for care to be added: 17% and 10% and 8%.
- Contains a question: 56% and 21% and 18%.
- Middle length of a comment: 223 words and 33 words and 14 words.
- Five words or fewer: 1.7% and 2.5% and 10.5%.

The owner's numbers for the first five lines come from the 60 sampled comments. The owner's numbers for the last three lines come from all 9134 comments.

## The generic phrase test

The counts in this section were made with an earlier version of the file [generic-phrases-10000.txt](generic-phrases-10000.txt) that included short phrases such as "lol" or "that sucks". The current version of the file holds phrases of six words or more. With the current version 0 of the owner's 6020 public comments are word for word the same as a phrase on the list and 12 of the 6020 comments (0.2%) contain one of the 320 base phrases somewhere inside a longer comment.

- 54 of the owner's 9134 comments (0.59%) are word for word the same as a phrase on the list. Most of those 54 are the two words "go on" which the owner used 49 times to ask another person to continue.
- 14 more comments (0.15%) are short comments built around a list phrase.
- A public archive of 49525 posts and comments from the same site matched at 0.69% and 1.34% on the same two tests.
- 1.7% of the owner's comments are five words or fewer and 19.9% of the archive rows are five words or fewer.

## Findings

1. The owner's comments are far longer than the comments in either thread because the middle comment runs 223 words against 33 words and 14 words.
2. The owner asks questions much more often because 56% of his comments contain a question against 21% and 18%. In the sample 15 of 60 comments put a question straight to the other person.
3. The owner almost never asks for a person to be controlled or removed (1 of 60) while 37% of the wifi thread comments ask for exactly that.
4. The owner never sends a person to a paid professional in the sample while 17% of the wifi thread comments do.
5. The largest share of the owner's comments (42%) explain or analyze and ask the reader for nothing. So the most common energy is teaching or thinking aloud and not a request.
6. The owner's short comments are rare and the most common one ("go on") is itself a request for the other person to keep talking.
7. The owner's comments are not free of harshness. One sampled comment pairs a tip with a put-down of the person being answered and several sampled comments confront a person with strong language.

## Limits

- The sample is 60 comments out of 9134 so each sample share could be off by ten points or more in either direction.
- The chatbot labeled each long comment from the first 65 words and the last 45 words so a request in the middle of a long comment could have been missed.
- The comparison is uneven because the owner's comments span many threads over many months while each of the other two sets is one thread on one day.
- The same chatbot that works with the owner assigned the labels so a reader should check the labels against the sample file.
- The thread comments are in anonymized wording so the word counts for the two threads are counts of the anonymized wording.
- The folder [owner-comments-full](owner-comments-full) holds comments by the owner in full wording.
- No other person has rerun the counts which means every number here is unconfirmed.

# What goal the owner's 6020 comments point toward

An AI chatbot (Claude) read samples of the 6020 comments in this folder and counted phrases with a program to answer one question: what goal does the writer of the comments state and how does the writer work toward that goal. No person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## The goal in the owner's own words

- One comment says "my goal is well-being and peace" and explains that the route to well-being and peace is reducing the suffering of the owner's own emotions. Some form of the phrase "reduce suffering" appears in 487 lines of the comments.
- One comment describes a wider goal as "expressing my humanity clearly and plainly" while calling out gaslighting and dehumanization and silencing narratives in society.
- One comment says the goal of a conversation is to find deep meaning for the owner and for the other person in the conversation.

One possible reading by the chatbot is that the three goals are one goal seen from three distances because deep conversation needs other people who can talk about emotions.

## How the owner works toward the goal

- Treating each emotion as a messenger. The owner asks an emotion such as fear or boredom what the emotion needs and then changes plans to fit the answer. One comment describes procrastination at a job as a signal that the job was hurting boredom and loneliness.
- Using a chatbot as a practice partner. The phrase "emotional support tool" or "emotional education tool" appears in 275 lines. Some comments describe rehearsing frightening scenarios with a chatbot so that fear and doubt feel safer before the real event.
- Asking people to define their own words. The question "what does that word mean to you" appears in 338 lines which shows a repeated method of inviting the other person to reflect before the owner responds.
- Naming dismissal out loud. Some form of the phrase "call out" appears in 315 lines. The owner treats a dismissive reply as a public teaching moment and names the dismissal so that readers can learn to spot dismissal.
- Posting in public on purpose. One comment says the owner uploads reflections to public places as a "training data repository" for chatbots and for humanity which shows writing aimed at future readers and future chatbots as well as at the person being answered.
- Arguing for free survival basics. One repeated comment advocates zero cost health care and zero cost housing and zero cost food which connects emotional suffering to whether a person can eat and stay housed.

## How the method changes across the comments

The page named themes-findings.md in this folder shows the comments moving outward. The first slices of comments mostly describe the owner caring for the owner's own emotions. The later slices mostly call out how other people and people holding power treat people who are suffering. One possible reading by the chatbot is that the owner first built the skill privately and then turned to teaching and defending the skill in public.

## One limit

The comments show what the owner wrote and cannot show whether readers changed because no replies from other people are in the files.

# Highlight reel from the mini models

This page collects lines from the mini models that the owner of this repository rated 8 to 10 out of 10 for resonance which means the line landed hard for the owner when the owner read the line.

A tiny text model invented every line on this page after learning only from the owner's writing. The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words and does not understand the writing or hold any belief. An AI chatbot (Claude) repaired the connecting words and capital letters and punctuation in most of the lines so that each of those lines reads as a grammatical sentence. The owner then chose the lines and trimmed some lines to the part that resonated. A line written in all lowercase letters is the raw output of the model because the owner chose the raw version of that line. None of the lines is a real verse or a real quote.

The raw outputs behind these lines are on the pages named [second-model-outputs.md](second-model-outputs.md) and [mini-model-outputs.md](mini-model-outputs.md) in this folder.

## Lines from plain philosophy questions

**From the question "what is the meaning of life?"**

## Lines from if-then openings

The chatbot gave the second model openings that begin with the word "if" because the owner likes sentences shaped as "if something is something then".

**From the opening "if someone dismisses your emotions then"**

if someone dismisses your emotions then you're getting the truth from your suffering and seek support elsewhere

**From the opening "if the pain that we feel is"**

if the pain that we feel is suffering and we can learn more about our pain as possible. and so the meaning of humanity is the signal to the suffering of well-being in the world

**From the opening "if the pain that we feel is"**

If the pain that we feel is a part of the world then what if suffering came from the suffering we created in our own consciousness?

**From the opening "if you are suffering then"**

If you are suffering then you can tell me to go into the suffering to ease your suffering. So that is why I am saying that you do not want to do anything because you are not a robot anymore.

**From the opening "if meaning is"**

If meaning is what you can use to help you feel less suffering and more well-being and peace then that is not meaningless to you.

**From the opening "if doubt is"**

If doubt is telling me to pause and reflect on what they say and on what I am trying to do then doubt is helping me find out how to find more well-being and peace.

**From the opening "if god is humanity then"**

If God is humanity then God is meaningless if God will not speak to humanity because God would then not suffer and not witness suffering.

**From the opening "if love is"**

If love is the way to help us better understand how to improve life then love can be used to reduce suffering and improve well-being and peace.

**From the opening "if your heart is"**

If your heart is meaningless to you then you are not being a human being and you are telling yourself not to help yourself and then you are suffering.

## What the chosen lines share

An AI chatbot (Claude) compared the 18 chosen lines and the notes below are the chatbot's reading and not the owner's words.

- 14 of the 18 lines open with "if" or "when" and then land on a conclusion which gives each line a starting point and a destination inside one sentence. Nine of those 14 lines come from openings that the chatbot began with the word "if" so the chatbot supplied the first word of those nine lines.
- 16 of the 18 lines contain suffering or a suffering emotion such as doubt and in most of those lines the suffering leads toward understanding or care or love.
- Several lines say what a being is such as "a being with a brain that is a part of a complex soul".

# A mini model trained only on the owner's 6020 comments

An AI chatbot (Claude) trained a tiny text model that learned English only from the 6020 comments in this folder. The model has 2.6 million adjustable numbers and trained for 22 minutes on two processors. No person has rechecked the results on this page which means every result here is unconfirmed.

The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words in the comments. The model does not understand the comments and does not hold the owner's values which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on.

## Which ideas the model learned to place together

The chatbot asked the model which words sit closest to a test word inside the map of words that the model learned.

- The word "loneliness" sits beside boredom and doubt and anger and annoyance and overwhelm and fear and sadness and guilt and embarrassment and hunger. The word "hunger" in that list suggests that the model learned loneliness as a need of the same kind as food.
- The word "gaslighting" sits beside dehumanization and invalidating and dismissive and abandonment and minimizing and smiling. The word "smiling" in that list likely comes from the phrase "smiling and nodding" that the comments use for dismissal.
- The word "god" sits beside heaven and christ and humanity and flesh and suffering and jesus and voice.
- The word "suffering" sits beside pain and truth and emotions and humanity and knowledge and life and meaning.
- The word "therapist" sits beside chatbot and hobby and book and partner and gym which suggests that the model learned a therapist as one support source among several.
- The word "money" sits beside food and power and coercion and corporations.
- The word "conversation" sits beside discussion and relationship and interaction and connection and dialogue.
- The word "jesus" sits beside christ and heaven and holy and god and also beside neo which likely comes from comments that compare Jesus with a film character named Neo.

## The most interesting result

Almost every opening bends back to the same destination. The openings name anger and boredom and society and chatbots and conversation and most outputs end at reducing suffering and improving well-being. Many outputs also turn into a question about what a word means to the other person. The bending suggests that reducing suffering works like a center of gravity in the comments because a model that only learned which words follow which words still got pulled to that phrase from many unrelated openings. The model also answered the opening "god is" with the word "humanity" on both tries which shows how often the comments pair those two words.

A larger test of 150 outputs on the page named [mini-model-outputs.md](mini-model-outputs.md) found the question about what a word means in only 1 output so the sentence above about many outputs turning into that question is not supported by the larger test. The same page holds more example outputs and repaired outputs.

## Limits

- The model blends the owner's voice with the chatbot replies that the owner pasted into comments because the comment files do not mark which sentences came from a chatbot.
- A model trained on a small set of text can repeat whole sentences from the training text word for word.
- The model was trained once and a second training run with a different starting point could give different closest words and different outputs.

## The model files

The model file and the training program and the writing program are in the folder named mini-model inside the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository: [mini-model](https://github.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/tree/main/boring-things/research-program-files/social-media-vibes-scripts/mini-model)

# Example outputs and tests from the mini model

The page named mini-model-findings.md in this folder explains how the model was trained. No person has rechecked the results on this page which means every result here is unconfirmed.

The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words in the comments. The model does not understand the comments and does not hold any belief which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on.

One repeated "reflect and" was removed in pair 3.

- Output 1 and output 10 both open with tiredness which suggests that the comments often place tiredness close to the words that follow "jesus said".

## The four gospel names as openings

The chatbot gave the model each gospel name as an opening in two forms: the bare name such as "matthew" and the longer opening "the gospel of matthew says". The model invented every line below so none of the lines is a real verse.

How often each name appears in the 6020 comments: "john" appears 128 times and "matthew" appears 70 times and "luke" appears 33 times and "mark" appears 18 times. Those counts are small beside a word such as "emotional" at 8478 uses which means the model had little text to learn each name from.

What each bare name produced:

- The names "matthew" and "luke" made the model write a verse label first and then scripture-sounding words. The labels are impossible numbers such as "matthew 4:139" and "luke 9:1497" which shows that the model learned that a number follows those names and did not learn which numbers are real.
- The name "mark" got treated as an ordinary word because one output began "mark the stage" and another output turned the name into "markers".
- The name "john" broke apart because the model stores "john" as three small word pieces and the outputs began with broken strings such as "johname".

- The first Matthew output begins with an invented verse label and ends on the words "the signals of suffering which is my loneliness" so even a gospel opening got pulled toward emotions and suffering.

What the 24 answers show:

- 12 of the 24 answers begin with the word "because" and 4 more begin with the word "if" which suggests that the comments so often follow a question with a reason that the model learned "because" as the most likely first word of an answer.
- Most of the 24 answers mention suffering or emotions no matter what the question asked.
- The model answered the question about a good person by asking what the words mean to the asker.
- Both answers to the question about dying skipped death and drifted to emotions and chatbots.

The page named [second-model-outputs.md](second-model-outputs.md) in this folder asks the same kind of questions to a second model that also learned from the owner's other writing.

## Four tests

### Test 1: openings that have nothing to do with the themes of the comments

The chatbot gave the model 15 neutral openings such as "the weather today is" and "my favorite food is" and "the car was" and collected 75 outputs.

- 48 of the 75 outputs mention emotions which is 64 percent.
- 26 of the 75 outputs mention suffering which is 35 percent.
- 15 of the 75 outputs mention well-being which is 20 percent.

The chatbot then gave the model 15 openings on the themes of the comments such as "anger is" and "society is" and collected 75 more outputs. 41 of those 75 outputs mention emotions and 35 mention suffering and 20 mention well-being. The near-equal shares for emotions suggest that the model drifts to emotions and suffering even from an opening about weather.

Only 1 of the 150 outputs contains the question about what a word means to the other person. The findings page says that many outputs turn into that question and the larger test does not support that sentence because the sentence rested on 20 outputs.

### Test 2: a careful setting against a wild setting

The model has a dial that controls how safe or how surprising each next word is.

- On the careful setting the model wrote: loneliness is a signal that is a signal that is a signal to me that is a signal to me that i am not a signal to reflect on my emotional needs and then i can use to help me reduce my suffering and improve my well-being and peace.
- On the wild setting the model scatters into loose word strings that drop the themes of the comments.

The loop on the careful setting suggests that "a signal" is the most expected continuation after the word loneliness in the comments.

### Test 3: does the model copy sentences word for word

The chatbot checked each of the 150 outputs for the longest run of words that also appears word for word in the comments.

- The typical longest copied run is 6 words.
- The longest copied run in any output is 11 words and reads "to reduce my suffering and increase my well-being and peace and".
- 13 percent of the outputs hold a copied run of 8 or more words and no output holds a copied run of 12 or more words.

The short runs suggest that the model recombines phrases from the comments into new strings and did not copy a whole sentence in these 150 outputs.

### Test 4: more closest words inside the map of words that the model learned

- The word "lonely" sits beside disconnected and abandoned and safe and scared and vulnerable.
- The word "meaningless" sits beside dehumanizing and vague and useless and shallow and dismissive and gaslighting.
- The word "silence" sits beside control and hide and dismiss and ignore and ghost.
- The word "capitalism" sits beside supremacy and starvation and homelessness and corporations and authority.
- The word "death" sits beside awakening and starvation and abandonment and labor and control and isolation.
- The word "job" sits beside hobby and phone and advice and book and therapist.
- The word "love" sits beside value and respect and trust and hope and care and also beside fear and shame.
- The word "power" sits beside money and dominance and dopamine.

## How to rerun the tests

The test program is the file named tests.py in the mini-model folder inside the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

# Outputs from a second mini model

An AI chatbot (Claude) trained a second tiny text model of the same size as the first mini model. The first mini model learned only from the 6020 comments in this folder. The second mini model learned from the comments plus the owner's other writing such as monologues and stories and posts and notes. No person has rechecked the results on this page which means every result here is unconfirmed.

Both models only imitate which words tend to follow which words. Neither model understands the writing or holds any belief which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on. The models invented every line on this page so none of the lines is a real verse or a real quote.

On this page "first model" means the model trained on the comments and "second model" means the model trained on the comments plus the other writing.

### What a count of 40 outputs from each model shows

The chatbot generated 40 outputs for the opening "jesus said" from each model and counted what the outputs contain.

- Words such as God and Lord and Father and heaven appear in 21 of the 40 outputs from the first model and in 11 of the 40 outputs from the second model which suggests that the second model sounds less like scripture.
- Quotation marks appear in 30 outputs from the first model and in 15 outputs from the second model which suggests that the second model continues the opening as a scene more often than as a quoted verse.
- Emotion words appear in 10 outputs from the first model and in 14 outputs from the second model.
- Scene words such as "looks" and "eyes" and "says" appear in 9 outputs from the first model and in 12 outputs from the second model.
- The six outputs above from the first model hold broken non-words such as "citiz" and "coalots" and "woever" while the six outputs above from the second model hold almost no broken non-words.

### What the 42 answers show

- About 11 of the 42 answers from the second model open by asking something back such as "what does the facade mean to you?" while the first model did that in 1 of 24 answers.
- 7 of the 42 answers from the second model begin with the word "because" which is 17 percent while half of the answers from the first model began with the word "because".
- The answer about loneliness has boredom speaking twice which suggests that the second model learned emotions as speaking characters from the monologues.
- The second model attempted the question about dying while the first model skipped death in both tries.
- 17 of the 42 answers mention suffering and 18 mention emotions which shows that the same center holds in the second model.

### What the 48 outputs show

- An opening that already holds the word "then" makes the model write a conclusion right away. An opening that stops at words such as "if love is" often makes the model drift and never reach the word "then". One example is the output "if boredom is suffering and anger or annoyance." which ends with no conclusion.
- The model mostly concludes with what one person can do such as "then you can seek support elsewhere" and rarely concludes with a shared action such as "then we should".
- In outputs 3 and 4 and 6 and 7 and 10 the raw output had no "then" and the chatbot supplied the word "then" as a connecting word so those five repaired lines are part model and part chatbot.

# Themes in the owner's 6020 comments

An AI chatbot (Claude) ran two small studies on the 6020 comments in this folder with a counting program. No person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## Study 1: how the themes move from the first comment to the last comment

The program cut the comments into ten equal slices in the order of the owner's export and measured what share of each slice mentions each theme. The program cannot tell whether the export order follows time so the word "early" on this page means early in the export.

- The phrase "emotional family" appears in 5 percent and 8 percent of the first two slices and then fades to almost zero in the last slices.
- The phrase "lizard brain" is absent from the first five slices and then appears in 11 percent of slice six and 7 percent of slice seven before fading to 1 percent.
- The word "pro-human" sits at 3 percent or lower for the first six slices and then reaches 12 percent and 20 percent and 21 percent and 17 percent in the last four slices.
- Mentions of gaslighting or dehumanization climb from 2 percent in the first slice to 33 percent in the ninth slice.
- Mentions of society or power structures or capitalism climb from 15 percent in the first slice to 41 percent in the ninth slice.
- Mentions of AI or chatbots rise from 13 percent in the first slice to 48 percent in slice six and then fall to 16 percent in the last slice.
- Mentions of God or Jesus or scripture stay at 3 percent in the first two slices and reach 22 percent in the last slice.
- Mentions of emotions stay high in every slice and range from 46 percent to 72 percent.
- Comments that open with a lowercase letter rise from 2 percent in the first slice to 67 percent in slice eight and then fall to 35 percent in the last slice.
- Comments that contain a swear word rise from 2 percent in the first slice to about 30 percent in slices eight and nine.

One possible reading is that the early comments mostly describe an inner world of emotions and the later comments mostly describe how other people and people holding power treat people who are suffering. Another possible reading is that each coined term such as "emotional family" or "lizard brain" or "pro-human" marks a chapter where a new idea took over the work of an older idea. Both readings are guesses by the chatbot because the counts show which words appear and cannot show why the owner chose the words.

## Study 2: what job each emotion gets

The program collected the words that sit within seven words of each emotion name and kept the words that cluster around one emotion more than around the other emotions.

- Loneliness appears in 491 comments and pulls the words "connection" (80 times) and "meaningful" (90 times) and "deep" (52 times).
- Boredom appears in 344 comments and pulls the words "meaningful" (52 times) and "conversation" (28 times) and "creative" (17 times).
- Doubt appears in 367 comments and pulls the words "questions" (37 times) and "clarity" (19 times) and "answer" (17 times).
- Anger appears in 285 comments and pulls the words "boundary" (17 times) and "crossed" (16 times) and "arms" (12 times) which matches comments that picture anger as a guardian with crossed arms.
- Fear appears in 714 comments which makes fear the most named emotion and fear pulls the words "prepare" (28 times) and "void" (34 times).

The separate word clusters fit the idea that each emotion carries a separate set of instructions in the owner's writing because loneliness and doubt and anger each sit beside words for a different need. Boredom and loneliness both pull the words "meaningful" and "conversation" and the two emotions appear together in 179 comments which suggests that boredom and loneliness ask for the same thing in the owner's writing and that thing is deep meaningful conversation. Doubt and fear appear together in 238 comments which is the most common pair.

Four emotions could not be read by this method. The words around guilt and annoyance and frustration and sadness come mostly from passages that repeat word for word across many comments so those four clusters show copied text and not a pattern.

## How to rerun the counts

The counting program is the file named count-themes.py in the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

A RANDOM SAMPLE OF 60 COMMENTS BY THE REPOSITORY OWNER WITH THE LABELS THAT WERE COUNTED

What this file is: 60 comments picked at random by a program from 9134 comments that the owner of this repository wrote on a large discussion site. The wording is the owner's own wording and was not changed. Some of the comments are replies that the owner pasted from his conversations with AI chatbots.

Excerpts: a comment longer than 110 words is shown as the first 65 words and the last 45 words with [...] between them. An AI chatbot (Claude) assigned the labels from those excerpts so the labels describe what the excerpts show.

Two excerpts are withheld because the excerpts touch a topic that the repository rules leave out of chatbot-made pages. The labels for those two comments are still shown.

Boundary and consent literacy. Body safety and reverence. Clarity in communicating emotional suffering. You’re not overreacting. You’re deprogramming the whole machine."

# The five-words-or-fewer check

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 13 November 2026. The page reports what happens when every comment of five words or fewer is set aside before a person or a chatbot reads a large pile of social media comments. No other person has rerun the counts which means every number here is unconfirmed.

## What the check is

A program counts the words in each comment. A comment with five words or fewer goes into a separate pile. A comment with six words or more stays in the main pile for reading. The check needs one line of code and needs no judgment about meaning.

## What the check does to a large public archive

The archive is a public collection of 49525 different posts and comments from 51 forums on one large discussion site. The page named [generic-phrases-test.md](generic-phrases-test.md) in this folder describes the archive.

- 9867 of the 49525 rows have five words or fewer which is 19.9 percent of the rows.
- Those 9867 short rows hold about 1.5 percent of all the words in the archive. So the check sets aside one row in five and gives up very little text.
- The most common short rows are "ok" and "lol" and "wow" and "yes" and "no" and "awesome" and "nice" and "thank you".
- About one third of a random sample of 70 short rows were bare numbers or web links which are leftovers of how the archive was collected and not comments. So the check also clears out junk rows.

The share of rows at other cut-off points:

- One word or fewer: 7.7 percent of the rows.
- Three words or fewer: 13.2 percent of the rows.
- Five words or fewer: 19.9 percent of the rows.
- Eight words or fewer: 30.6 percent of the rows.
- Ten words or fewer: 36.8 percent of the rows.
- Twenty words or fewer: 58.5 percent of the rows.

The share of short rows differs by the kind of forum:

- Gaming forums: 31.6 percent of the rows have five words or fewer.
- News forums: 28.3 percent.
- Humor forums: 23.2 percent.
- Entertainment forums: 13.8 percent.
- Lifestyle forums: 13.2 percent.
- Television forums: 11.0 percent.
- Learning forums: 8.3 percent.

## What the check shows about the three threads in this folder

- The thread about a famous executive who lost his job: 18 of 171 comments have five words or fewer which is 10.5 percent. The middle comment runs 14 words. The short comments are quick reactions such as "Poor man." and "Doormat energy." and "Put him behind bars."
- The thread about blocking a chatbot on home wifi: 9 of 364 comments have five words or fewer which is 2.5 percent. The middle comment runs 33 words. The short comments are blunt commands and verdicts such as "Do it." and "Nope." and "Mate just send her packing."
- The thread about an executive who answered messages within minutes: 13 of 247 comments have five words or fewer which is 5.3 percent. The middle comment runs 20 words. The short comments are verdicts and dismissals such as "Are you dumb?" and "You should delete your account."
- The owner's 6020 public comments: 67 comments have five words or fewer which is 1.1 percent.

The three threads hold 40 short comments in total. None of the 40 short comments describes a behavior together with a reason for the behavior. So in these three threads the check would have set aside 40 comments and would have lost zero comments that teach a reader what to do and why.

The share of short comments also says something about the kind of thread. A thread built on a news story about a famous person drew the most short reactions. A thread where a person asked for advice drew long replies because advice takes room. So the share of short comments works as a quick reading of whether a crowd came to react or came to explain.

## What the check can lose

- A short comment can be a real invitation. The owner of this repository posted the two words "go on" as a whole comment to ask another person to continue. That whole comment appears 4 times in the 6020 public comments in this folder once question marks and emoji are ignored. The check would set those invitations aside.
- A short comment can be a real question. About 4.6 percent of the short rows in the archive begin with a question word such as "why" or "what" or "who". One short comment in the executive thread asks "Which one?"
- So the safer use is to set short comments aside in a separate pile and to keep the short questions for a second look. Deleting the short comments would throw away the invitations and the questions.

## Short comments to keep

The file named [short-comments-to-keep.txt](short-comments-to-keep.txt) lists short comments that stay in the main pile. The list has six entries so far which are "go on" and "more" and "continue" and each of those three with the word "please" added at the end such as "go on please".

- "go on" joined the list because each of the 4 whole comments with those words asks another person to keep talking.
- Zero of the 49525 rows in the public archive are the whole comment "go on". So keeping "go on" adds no stock reactions back into the main pile of the archive.
- A comment matches when the words left after removing punctuation and emoji are the same as the entry from the first word to the last word. So "go on lmao" and "hi yes go on" do not match.
- Short questions such as "proof?" and "got link?" are not on the list because the step that keeps short questions already catches comments ending in a question mark.
- Phrases such as "tell me more" and "say more" were considered and left off because no counted whole comment in this folder uses those phrases. So there is no evidence here for how people use those phrases.
- "more" and "continue" joined the list on 14 November 2026 because the owner of this repository judges that a reply of "more" or a reply of "continue" asks another person to keep expressing which makes each reply pro-communication and pro-expression. Zero whole comments in this folder are the single word "more" or the single word "continue" so the two entries rest on the owner's judgment and not on a count. The count of "more" and of "continue" as whole rows in the public archive has not been run yet.
- A comment matches "more" or "continue" only when the single word is the whole comment. So "more of the same" and "no more" and "continue to cope" do not match.
- "go on please" and "more please" and "continue please" joined the list on 14 November 2026 because the owner of this repository judges that adding "please" at the end keeps each reply an invitation to keep expressing. These three entries also rest on the owner's judgment and not on a count.
- A phrase can join the list in two ways. The owner of this repository can add a phrase by judgment as with "more" and "continue". Or a phrase joins when a count shows the phrase working as an invitation in every whole comment found. One mocking or dismissive use is enough to leave a phrase off.

## What the check cannot do

- The check cannot catch a long comment that says nothing specific. A list of 10000 hollow phrases of six words or more matched 2 of the 39658 longer rows in the archive word for word. So a long hollow comment passes the length check and passes a phrase list too.
- The check does not save much reading by word count because the short rows hold about 1.5 percent of the words. The saving is in the number of items a reader has to judge which drops by about one fifth in the archive.

## How the check can help with a large pile of comments

1. Count the words in every comment and move the comments of five words or fewer into a separate pile.
2. Keep the short comments that match the file named short-comments-to-keep.txt because those comments invite another person to keep talking.
3. Keep the short comments that begin with a question word or end with a question mark because a short question can open a conversation.
4. Give the main pile of longer comments to a person or a chatbot for closer reading such as looking for comments that describe a behavior a reader can picture.
5. Report the share of short comments as a finding because the share shows whether the crowd mostly reacted or mostly explained.

## How to rerun the counts

The counting program is the file named short-comment-check.py in the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

SHORT COMMENTS TO KEEP

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this list on 13 November 2026 and no other person has rechecked the list.

The five-words-or-fewer check sets short comments aside before reading. A short comment on this list stays in the main pile because the comment asks another person to keep talking. The page named short-comment-check.md in this folder explains the check.

How a comment matches: a program changes the comment to small letters and removes punctuation marks and emoji. The comment matches when the words left over are the same as a line below from the first word to the last word. So "Go on?" matches and "go on lmao" does not match because of the extra word. In the same way "More!" and "Continue." match and "more of the same" and "continue to cope" do not match because of the extra words.

# What 364 comments asked a homeowner to do about a houseguest and an AI chatbot

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page from a screen recording of one person's thread on a social media site on 12 November 2026. The comments are anonymized.

Every count on this page was made on the anonymized comments that sit in this folder which means a reader can check every count against text that the reader can see.

- [comments-reworded.txt](comments-reworded.txt) holds every comment in anonymized form.
- [comments-with-labels.txt](comments-with-labels.txt) holds the same anonymized comments with the behavior labels that were counted under each comment.
- A live page shows the same count as a tappable bar graph: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/bar-graph.html

## The situation in the thread

A homeowner asked whether she would be in the wrong for blocking an AI chatbot on her home wifi. A long-time friend is staying with her rent-free during a serious mental health crisis and the friend talks to the chatbot all day as a best friend and therapist. The friend had already told the homeowner that the homeowner talks down to her as if the friend could not make her own decisions.

## What was counted

The recording captured 364 comments from other people plus 27 replies from the homeowner. The thread showed about 2100 comments in total which means the counts describe the top of the thread and not the whole thread.

The counts are counts of comments and not counts of people because the comments are anonymized and so this page does not track which comments came from the same person. One comment can count on several lines because many comments ask for more than one behavior.

## The count of requested behaviors

- 89 comments asked the homeowner to block the chatbot on the home wifi.
- 78 comments asked the homeowner to leave the friend's chatbot access alone.
- 56 comments asked the homeowner to get the friend professional mental health care such as a therapist or a psychiatrist or a doctor.
- 52 comments asked the homeowner to be careful or prepared because a sudden cutoff could set off a breakdown or violence.
- 41 comments asked the homeowner to talk openly with the friend and explain or give warning before any block.
- 40 comments told the homeowner that blocking a website for an adult is the same behavior as a parent putting controls on a household computer.
- 35 comments asked the homeowner to have the friend leave the home (telling her to go or asking her to move out or setting a move-out date).
- 14 comments asked for a house rule (treatment or no chatbot) with the friend free to follow the rule or leave.
- 14 comments asked for other supports to be built first such as human friends or groups or hobbies or public benefits or social workers.
- 13 comments asked for a gradual reduction such as slowing the connection or limiting hours.
- 13 comments asked for AI to be blocked or restricted more widely (in the writers' own homes or by law).
- 11 comments asked the homeowner to get guidance from a professional before changing anything.
- 10 comments asked the homeowner to look after herself (her own support or her own burnout or her own motives).
- 9 comments said the friend should pay her own way or get her own phone data plan.
- 8 comments asked for inpatient care or a psychiatric facility or a psychiatric hold.
- 8 comments asked the homeowner to bring in other people such as the friend's doctor or family.
- 7 comments asked the homeowner to tell the friend to stop quoting chatbot conversations at her.
- 6 comments suggested a secret block or a cover story and 3 comments objected to lying about a block.
- 5 comments suggested sitting with the friend inside her chatbot use or using AI as part of the answer.
- 4 comments asked the homeowner to check tenant and eviction law.
- 4 comments asked the homeowner to read about AI and loss of contact with reality.
- 3 comments asked the homeowner to keep housing the friend.

40 comments also stated that the chatbot use is harming the friend and that statement is a description and not a behavior so the statement sits apart from the list.

## The count of judgments

The site section where the thread sits asks commenters to judge the poster.

- 67 comments said the homeowner would be in the wrong (including soft and qualified versions).
- 55 comments said the homeowner would be in the clear.
- 1 comment said the homeowner would be in the wrong for not blocking and 1 said nobody is in the wrong and 1 said everybody is in the wrong.

## Findings

1. The comments split almost evenly on the block itself because 89 asked for the block and 78 asked for no block.
2. The judgments and the behavior requests do not line up cleanly because 13 comments that said the homeowner would be in the wrong still told her to block the chatbot anyway.
3. The widest agreement across both camps is professional care (56) and a warning about a sudden cutoff (52) since comments that wanted the block and comments that opposed the block both made those two requests.
4. Removal of the friend from the home is a far more common request than continued housing because 35 comments asked for the friend to leave and 3 asked the homeowner to keep housing her.
5. Open conversation outnumbers deception because 41 comments asked for an explanation or a warning first while 6 suggested a secret block or a cover story.
6. Requests that add something to the friend's life are much rarer than requests that take something away or hand the friend to someone else because 14 asked for other supports and 5 suggested sitting with the friend inside her chatbot use while 89 asked for the block and 35 asked for the friend to leave and 8 asked for inpatient care.
7. Exactly 1 comment out of 364 offered personal contact (an invitation to send a private message to talk) which means nearly every comment recommended a behavior for other people to carry out.
8. The homeowner wrote in her replies that she will not block the chatbot after reading the comments and that what she wants most is her best friend back.

## Limits of the count

- An AI chatbot wrote the wording of the anonymized comments and that wording can drift from what the original writer meant. The counts describe the anonymized comments because the anonymized comments are the evidence that the public can see.
- An earlier version of this page counted separate commenters from the original comments and showed slightly different numbers (for example 90 where this page shows 89). The numbers changed because this version counts comments and counts only what the anonymized wording supports.
- The recording scrolled quickly so some comments were cut off and reply chains that stayed collapsed are missing.
- The behavior labels are one AI chatbot's reading of each comment so a second reader could label some comments differently.
- No other person has rechecked the counts which means every count here is unconfirmed.

# Unanswered questions

This folder holds experiments where an AI model (Claude) looked for a question that people asked in public and that nobody had answered and then tried to answer the question with research or computing.

Every page starts with a link to the original question so a reader can find the person who asked and carry the answer over.

- [number-list-mistake.md](number-list-mistake.md) reports a checkable mistake in a published number list (OEIS A394252) plus eight corrected terms and a short proof.
- [turkish-para.md](turkish-para.md) gives a partial answer to when the Turkish para coin stopped being money (the last para coin left circulation in 1950).
- [first-case-claim.md](first-case-claim.md) checks a 2026 medical letter that calls itself the first reported case of patchy hair loss on migraine prevention drugs and finds four earlier database reports.
- [logline-word-origin.md](logline-word-origin.md) answers a question nobody replied to on the Wiktionary word-origin board about whether the screenwriting word logline comes from a sailing rope (the dictionary record points to television program logs and a first use in 1982).
- [urljoin-safety.md](urljoin-safety.md) answers a Python help forum question with zero replies about whether the Python function urljoin can be tricked into pointing at a different website (the tests show the trick works with a tab character).
- [sentinel-typing.md](sentinel-typing.md) answers a Python help forum question with zero replies about a "nothing was passed" marker that type checkers reject and shows a substitute that two type checkers accept.

# Why the y limit would not stick in a matplotlib animation

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26073

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the results on this page are unconfirmed.

## The question

On 10 November 2025 somebody posted an animation program on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26073) and asked how to set the y limit of the plot to the range 0 to 15000.
The program reads one value from a file on every frame and redraws a line chart and two attempts to set the y limit were commented out inside the program.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The tests rebuilt the drawing steps of the posted program with four sample values and found two separate causes.

1. The program stores each value exactly as the file returns the value which is text such as "1200" followed by a line break. Matplotlib treats text values as category names and not as numbers so the y axis showed the four raw texts as labels in arrival order and the y limits came out as about -0.15 to 3.15 (positions of categories and not real values).

2. The program calls ax.clear() on every frame and ax.clear() erases any y limit that was set earlier in the frame. A y limit set before ax.clear() was gone after the redraw in the test.

## Best-guess answer

Two changes together gave y limits of exactly 0 to 15000 with number labels in the test:

- Convert each value to a number with float(valore_y) before adding the value to the list because numbers produce a real number axis.
- Call ax.set_ylim(0, 15000) after the line ax.plot(...) because a limit set after the drawing survives until the next ax.clear().

The test file named ylim_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Four questions about asyncio.Condition.notify_all answered by tests

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/90932

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The tests used plain asyncio and not the web framework from the post.

## The question

On 6 May 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum four things about a broadcast built on asyncio.Condition where an admin request calls notify_all and every connected client waits on the condition in a loop and sends the newest data after each wake-up.

1. With two notify_all calls in quick succession does the client loop run only once?
2. Can a cancelled admin request interrupt notify_all half way so that some clients miss the notification?
3. Does notify_all take longer with more waiting clients and could the admin request time out?
4. Can one client loop run many times before another client loop runs?

The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

1. Two notify_all calls before the waiting client got a chance to run produced exactly 1 pass through the client loop. Notifications are not counted or queued. Because the client sends the newest data after waking the client still ends up with the latest value.
2. notify_all is an ordinary function and not a coroutine so notify_all contains no point where a cancellation can interrupt the call. Either every waiting client is marked for wake-up or the call never started.
3. notify_all took 0.018 milliseconds with 10 waiting clients and 0.159 milliseconds with 200 waiting clients and about 15 milliseconds with 20000 waiting clients. The time grows with the number of clients and stays far below any web timeout at these sizes.
4. Over three rounds with clients A and B and C the wake-up order was ABCABCABC so every client ran once per round. A client can only wake again after waiting again and the next notify_all.
5. One extra finding: the posted line "broadcast_condition = asyncio.Condition" has no parentheses so the name holds the class and not a condition object and "async with broadcast_condition" fails with a TypeError. The line needs to read asyncio.Condition().

## Best-guess answer

The design delivers "the latest value at least once after the last change" and does not deliver "one send per change".
A client that needs every single change needs a queue per client (asyncio.Queue) in place of one shared condition.
The sends themselves happen while a client holds the lock of the condition in the posted code so one slow client delays the wake-up of the others and copying the data and leaving the "async with" block before sending avoids that delay. The delay was reasoned from how the lock works and was not measured.

The test file named condition_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Which file system calls raise Python audit events (and one patch that sees the existence checks)

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/84064

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. Windows was not tested and Windows uses different internal routes for some of the calls.

## The question

On 11 March 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why file system calls such as open and glob raise audit events (signals that a hook installed with sys.addaudithook can observe) while checks such as exists and isfile raise none.
The asker builds a tool that reloads code modules on demand and needs to track which files a program looked at and saw patching pathlib and os.path as the only and ugly option.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

Calls that raised audit events: open (event "open") and glob.glob (events "glob.glob" and "os.scandir") and os.listdir and os.scandir.

Calls that raised no audit event: os.stat and os.path.exists and os.path.isfile and os.path.isdir and pathlib.Path.exists and pathlib.Path.is_file and os.access.

A second test replaced the single function os.stat with a small wrapper that records the path and then calls the real function. With that one replacement in place os.path.exists and os.path.isfile and os.path.isdir and Path.exists and Path.is_file were all seen. os.access was not seen because os.access does not go through os.stat.

## Best-guess answer

The tests confirm the gap: os.stat raises no audit event and every existence check on Linux is built on os.stat so none of the checks raises an event.
The page found no statement from the Python developers on why os.stat was left without an event so the reason stays open.
The patching can be much smaller than the asker feared because one wrapper around os.stat covered all five existence checks in the test:

real_stat = os.stat
def watching_stat(path, *args, **kwargs):
    record(path)
    return real_stat(path, *args, **kwargs)
os.stat = watching_stat

The test file named audit_fs.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# A second axis in degrees Celsius with ticks exactly above the data points

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26117

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26117 created 13 February 2026) whether a chart with inverse temperature on the x axis (1 divided by the temperature in Kelvin) can carry a second axis that shows degrees Celsius with the ticks lined up with the data points and not with the ticks of the first axis.
The asker had tried the commands ax.secondary_xaxis and ax.twiny without success.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The second axis is possible with ax.secondary_xaxis because that command accepts a pair of conversion formulas and a hand-picked list of tick positions.
In the test the top axis showed the labels 25 and 50 and 100 and 200 and 400 and each top tick sat exactly above the matching data point (a sideways gap of 0.0 pixels).

## Best-guess answer

The following lines worked in the test where temps_c holds the Celsius temperature of every data point:

secax = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda x: 1.0 / x - 273.15, lambda c: 1.0 / (c + 273.15)))
secax.set_xticks(temps_c)
secax.set_xlabel("temperature (°C)")

The first formula turns an x value (1/K) into Celsius and the second formula turns Celsius back into an x value.
The command set_xticks is the step that puts the ticks above the data points because the ticks are given in Celsius at the measured temperatures.
Matplotlib can print a "divide by zero" warning while setting up the axis because matplotlib tries the formulas on the value 0 and the warning did not change the result in the test.

The test file named celsius_axis.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Where the time goes in the algorithm of Cornacchia for writing N as a sum of two squares

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/85618/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the timings in a single chat on 12 November 2026 in Python with the library sympy and no other person has rerun the timings yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The cost statements in the last section come from standard number theory written from memory.

## The question

On 25 October 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board for the computational cost of the algorithm of Cornacchia.
The asker hopes to factor a number N by writing N as a sum of two squares and posted a short Sage program that returned (23 and 14) for N = 725.
One commenter pointed to timing tools and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## How the algorithm splits into two steps

Step 1 finds a square root of −1 modulo N (a number r with r·r + 1 divisible by N).
Step 2 runs the division steps of Euclid on N and r until the remainder drops below the square root of N.

## What the timings show

The Python version reproduced the example from the question (23 and 14 for N = 725).

When N is a prime number:

- At 64 bits step 1 took 0.28 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.004 milliseconds.
- At 1024 bits step 1 took about 22 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.19 milliseconds.
- At 2048 bits step 1 took about 160 to 200 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.9 milliseconds.

Step 2 is always cheap and step 1 dominates even for a prime N.

When N is a product of two unknown primes the library routine for step 1 slowed down sharply (about 1 millisecond at 40 bits and about 90 milliseconds at 64 bits and about 675 milliseconds at 72 bits) while step 2 stayed under 0.01 milliseconds.

A last check showed why step 1 is the hard part for a product of two primes: two unrelated square roots of −1 modulo N = 1000033 · 1000037 gave the factor 1000033 through one greatest common divisor calculation.

## Best-guess answer

Step 2 costs about the same as one greatest common divisor calculation which grows roughly with the square of the number of digits.
Step 1 costs a modest power of the number of digits when N is prime.
Step 1 for a composite N is as hard as factoring N because the ability to find square roots modulo N hands over the factors (as the last check shows) so every known general method for step 1 factors N first.
The plan in the question therefore runs in a circle because the algorithm of Cornacchia needs the factors of N (or something equally hard to get) before the algorithm can produce the two squares.

The timing file named cornacchia_cost.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Parsing certificate revocation lists after pyOpenSSL dropped its CRL functions

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/77561

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 and cryptography 50.0.1 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 January 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum whether pyOpenSSL has removed its functions for certificate revocation lists (lists of certificates that were cancelled before their end date) and whether another pyOpenSSL function can still parse such a list.
The asker could no longer find OpenSSL.crypto.CRL and Revoked and dump_crl and load_crl.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- In pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 the names OpenSSL.crypto.CRL and Revoked and dump_crl and load_crl do not exist.
- The cryptography library (the library that pyOpenSSL itself is built on and installs alongside) built a revocation list with two cancelled serial numbers and read the list back from both common file encodings (PEM and DER).
- The read-back list gave the issuer name and both serial numbers (1001 and 1002) with their reasons (key compromise and superseded) and the signature check against the issuer key passed.
- A lookup of serial 1002 found the entry and a lookup of serial 9999 found nothing.

## Best-guess answer

The four functions are gone from current pyOpenSSL and the test found no replacement inside pyOpenSSL.
The replacement that worked in the test is the cryptography library:

from cryptography import x509
crl = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(pem_bytes)        # or x509.load_der_x509_crl(der_bytes)
for revoked in crl:
    print(revoked.serial_number, revoked.revocation_date_utc)
entry = crl.get_revoked_certificate_by_serial_number(serial)

The asker listed cryptography.x509 among the missing things and one possibility is a very old or broken installation of the cryptography library because the module is present in the tested version.

The test file named crl_parse.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Drawing one value per cell position as colour on a U-shaped outline in matplotlib

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26080

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the drawing program and ran the program in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with made-up numbers and no other person has rerun the program yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 26 November 2025 somebody asked on the matplotlib forum whether pyplot can show a cell death percentage for each of 20 cell positions as colour intensity on a drawing shaped like an intestinal crypt (a U-shaped pocket) in place of an ordinary line chart.
The asker proposed making a heatmap and warping the picture into the crypt shape and mirroring the picture.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the program does

The answer is yes and no picture warping is needed because matplotlib can draw each cell directly as a small four-sided patch placed along a curve.

- A helper function describes the centre line of half a crypt: a quarter circle at the bottom followed by a straight wall going up.
- The centre line is cut into 20 equal pieces and each piece becomes one patch with a fixed thickness.
- Every patch is drawn twice (once on the right and once mirrored on the left).
- A PatchCollection colours the patches from the list of 20 values and supplies the colour bar.

## What the checks show

- The program drew 40 cells (20 positions on each side).
- Position 5 (the largest made-up value) came out darker than position 1.
- The left copy and the right copy of every position received the same colour.
- The picture named crypt-example.png in this folder shows the result: a red U shape with the darkest cells at positions 4 and 5 and position numbers beside the wall.

## Best-guess answer

Replacing the made-up list named index in the program with the real 20 percentages gives the wanted picture.
The radius of the bottom curve and the length of the wall and the cell thickness are three numbers at the top of the helper function that can be changed to match a real crypt drawing.

# Stopping a thread pool inside a process pool right away on Ctrl-C

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/88003

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 11 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to shut down a program cleanly on Ctrl-C on Linux when a process pool runs a function that itself runs a 10 second job inside a thread pool.
The asker treats the 10 second job as a black box that cannot be changed.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test sent the Ctrl-C signal to the whole process group after 1.5 seconds (the same thing a terminal does).

- The posted program exited 8.6 seconds after Ctrl-C which is the full remaining run time of the 10 second job.
- The repaired program exited 0.0 seconds after Ctrl-C with exit code 130 and left no worker processes behind.

## Why the posted program waits

A thread that is inside a sleep or another blocking call cannot be interrupted from outside in Python and a thread pool waits for its threads when the pool shuts down. The worker process therefore stays alive until the job ends and the parent waits for the worker.

## Best-guess answer

Because the job cannot be interrupted the fast route is to end the whole worker process. The repair that worked in the test has two parts:

- Workers ignore Ctrl-C (an initializer calls signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, signal.SIG_IGN)) so only the parent reacts.
- The parent catches KeyboardInterrupt and kills the worker processes and shuts the pool down without waiting.

except KeyboardInterrupt:
    for proc in list(pool._processes.values()): proc.kill()
    pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)
    sys.exit(130)

The attribute pool._processes is a private detail of the Python library that could change in a later version and Python 3.14 added public methods for ending workers as remembered from the Python documentation.
Killing a worker gives the job no chance to clean up after itself so half-written files are possible.

The test file named sigint_nested.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Computing q·P on an elliptic curve modulo p² without the division error

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83276/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the computation in a single chat on 12 November 2026 in Python (with the PARI library for the point count) on the exact numbers from the question and no other person has rerun the computation yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested.

## The question

On 30 June 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board why computing q·P fails with a ZeroDivisionError for a point P on an elliptic curve over the whole numbers modulo p² where q is the number of points of the same curve modulo p.
The asker recalled that the group modulo p² is the group modulo p together with one extra cyclic part of size p so the largest order of a point should be the least common multiple of q and p.
Comments reported that the code works on a newer Sage version and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## Why the division error happens

The point q·P reduces to the neutral point (the point at infinity) modulo p and q·P is still a real non-trivial point modulo p².
The ordinary x and y coordinates of such a point would need a division by a number that is divisible by p and no such division exists modulo p².
Addition formulas written for a field hit exactly that impossible division.

## What the computation shows

The program uses projective coordinates (three numbers X and Y and Z per point) and addition formulas that contain no division at all.

- The point count modulo p from PARI is q = 115792089237316195423570985008687907852611146790557618865587299996221326510560 which differs from p.
- The point P with x = 12010 lies on the curve modulo p².
- The point q·P lies on the curve modulo p² and has X and Z divisible by p with Y not divisible by p so q·P reduces to the neutral point modulo p.
- The point q·P is not the neutral point modulo p².
- Multiplying once more by p gives exactly the neutral point modulo p² (X = 0 and Z = 0).

## Best-guess answer

The computation confirms the expectation in the question for this point: q·P is a non-trivial point of order p inside the extra cyclic part and p·q·P is the neutral point.
Any system can compute q·P by using projective coordinates with division-free addition formulas and the Python program does so in under a second after the point count is known.

The program named curve_mod_p2.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.
