# Why a dollar format on spreadsheet columns is ignored with pandas and xlsxwriter

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/79453

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with pandas 3.0.5 and xlsxwriter 3.2.9 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The asker used older versions on Windows.

## The question

On 4 February 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why the dollar format set with set_column is not applied to the money columns of a spreadsheet written with pandas and xlsxwriter.
The posted script builds every row by joining values into one text line and splitting the line again and then calls set_column("E:F", 12, dlrformat).
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test rebuilt the data of the post and read the finished file back.

- With the posted approach cell D2 (Proforma amt) held the text "130.8" with the format General and cell E2 (Cost) held the text "99.88" with the dollar format attached. The date cell held the text "12/1/24".
- After converting the two money columns to numbers and the date column to dates and setting the format on columns D to E both money cells were stored as numbers with the format $0.00 and the date cell was stored as a real date.

## Two causes

1. Every value in the posted table is text because the rows are built from text lines. A number format changes how numbers are shown and does nothing to text so "99.88" stays as typed even with the dollar format attached.
2. The column letters are shifted by one. The header order is Sales rep (A) and Proforma date (B) and Job id (C) and Proforma amt (D) and Cost (E) and Reason (F) so "E:F" formats Cost and Reason and leaves Proforma amt out.

## Best-guess answer

The repair that worked in the test:

for col in ("Proforma amt", "Cost"):
    df[col] = pandas.to_numeric(df[col])
df["Proforma date"] = pandas.to_datetime(df["Proforma date"], format="%m/%d/%y")
...
worksheet.set_column("D:E", 12, dlrformat)

Keeping the numbers as numbers from the start (a list of lists in place of joined text lines) avoids the conversion step.

The test file named dollar_columns.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Cloning with dulwich and then switching to one chosen older revision

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/94414

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library dulwich version 1.2.21 on a small repository made on the spot and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The test used a local repository and not a GitHub address.

## The question

On 4 June 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to fetch a repository with the pure-Python git library dulwich and then check out one specific revision.
The asker knew that porcelain.clone with refspecs=None brings the latest commit and could not work out the checkout step.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test repository had three commits. Commit 2 holds "version 2" in one file and has an extra file that commit 3 removes again.

- After porcelain.clone the working files showed commit 3 (one file with "version 3").
- After porcelain.reset(target, "hard", sha_of_commit_2) the working files showed exactly commit 2 (two files with "version 2") and the branch pointed at commit 2.
- After porcelain.checkout(target, sha_of_commit_2) in a second clone the working files also showed exactly commit 2 while the branch name still pointed at commit 3 (the state that git calls a detached head).

## Best-guess answer

Two lines worked in the test:

porcelain.clone("https://github.com/mystuff/repo", target)
porcelain.reset(target, "hard", "full 40 character hash of the wanted revision")

The reset route moves the branch itself to the wanted revision. The checkout route (porcelain.checkout(target, hash)) leaves the branch alone and only switches the working files which fits a temporary look at an old state.
One practical note from the test machine: a commit signing setting in the global git configuration made dulwich commits fail until the test ran with an empty configuration and reading or switching revisions was not affected.

The test file named dulwich_checkout.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Row-reducing a matrix so the identity appears on any chosen columns

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83654/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 1 August 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to get an echelon form of a matrix G with k rows and n columns (k smaller than n and rank k) where the k by k identity matrix sits on any chosen set of k columns such as the last k columns.
The built-in command G.echelon_form() puts the identity on the first columns.
The question had zero answers and zero comments when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The method

Take the k by k block B made of the chosen columns of G and multiply G from the left by the inverse of B.
The product has the identity on the chosen columns because the inverse of B times B is the identity and the product has the same row space as G because multiplying from the left by an invertible matrix only recombines rows.
The method works exactly when the chosen columns are linearly independent.

## What the checks show

- For a random 3 by 7 whole-number matrix the method put the identity on the columns (4 and 5 and 6) and on (1 and 3 and 6) and on (6 and 0 and 2) and the row space stayed the same in all three cases. The order of the chosen columns decides which row gets which 1.
- The same method with arithmetic modulo 2 worked for a 4 by 8 matrix over the field with two elements (the setting of binary codes).
- Choosing two linearly dependent columns raised a clear error because no such form exists then.

## Best-guess answer

In Python with sympy:

block = G.extract(list(range(k)), list(cols))
E = block.inv() * G

Over a field with p elements the line becomes (block.inv_mod(p) * G) with every entry reduced modulo p.
In Sage the matching line worth trying is G.matrix_from_columns(cols).inverse() * G and that line was not tested for this page.

The check file named echelon_columns.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Getting fit uncertainties from an analytical Jacobian and comparing with curve_fit

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104442

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with scipy version 1.18.1 on made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum for a light and fast least-squares method that gets the covariance matrix (the table of fit uncertainties) from analytical derivatives and wanted to compare the result with the covariance matrix that the scipy function curve_fit returns.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test fitted the model a·exp(−b·x) + c to 200 noisy points.
The Jacobian J is the table of derivatives of the model with respect to the three parameters at every data point.

- The covariance computed as s² times the inverse of (J transposed times J) with an analytical J matched the covariance from curve_fit to about 1 part in 100000. The number s² is the sum of squared leftovers divided by (number of points minus number of parameters).
- The standard errors were 0.015067 and 0.016543 and 0.006517 from both routes.
- The covariance from the full analytical Hessian (which adds second-derivative terms weighted by the leftovers) differed from curve_fit by about 2 percent.
- Passing the analytical Jacobian into curve_fit with the argument jac made 200 fits take 0.038 seconds against 0.052 seconds with numerical derivatives.

## Best-guess answer

The function curve_fit already builds the covariance from the Jacobian at the solution so the hand formula s² · inverse(Jᵀ J) reproduces the curve_fit result when the same Jacobian is used.
The lightest change is to keep curve_fit and pass the analytical Jacobian with jac= because curve_fit then uses exact derivatives for both the fit and the covariance.
A hand-built route is scipy.optimize.least_squares with jac= followed by the hand formula.
The full Hessian gives a slightly different covariance and the difference shrinks when the leftovers are small.

The test file named fit_uncertainty.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Fixing KeyError: Couleur in a folium sector map

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/96052

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with folium version 0.20.0 on a tiny made-up map file and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The real map file of the asker was not available.

## The question

On 19 June 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum for the best method to build a folium map of all communes of one French department with four city sectors in four colours.
The map file has the properties nom and Secteur and Couleur and the style function and the tooltips failed with "KeyError: Couleur" and missing fields.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test file had two communes with all three properties and one commune with only a name.

- A style function that reads feature["properties"]["Couleur"] directly raised KeyError: Couleur which matches the report. One commune without the property is enough to stop the whole map.
- Filling in the missing properties for every commune before building the map worked: the map was built and all three colours and the tooltip text were present in the finished page.

## Best-guess answer

One possibility that fits the report is that the communes outside the four sectors have no Secteur and no Couleur in the map file.
The repair that worked in the test is a short loop before the map is built:

for f in data["features"]:
    p = f["properties"]
    p.setdefault("Secteur", "Hors secteur")
    p.setdefault("Couleur", "#cccccc")

folium.GeoJson(data,
    style_function=lambda f: {"fillColor": f["properties"]["Couleur"], "color": "black", "weight": 1, "fillOpacity": 0.6},
    tooltip=folium.GeoJsonTooltip(fields=["nom", "Secteur"], aliases=["Commune", "Secteur"])).add_to(m)

The loop gives every commune a sector label and a grey colour so the style function and the tooltip always find their fields.
The plain folium route needs no geopandas and no Fiona because folium reads the map file as an ordinary dictionary loaded with json.load.

# Forwarding input and output between a Python program and a child process without hanging

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/103413

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux with input and output connected through pipes and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. Behaviour in a real terminal window and on Windows was not tested.

## The question

On 29 August 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to pass the input of a program on to a child process and pass the output of the child back out at the same time.
The posted program used two background threads with shutil.copyfileobj and then waited for the child and the program hung.
The asker wanted the program to exit once the child finishes.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The child in the test answers every line in capital letters and stops when the line "quit" arrives.

- With the posted program the answer to the first line never arrived within 3 seconds and the program was still running 5 seconds after the "quit" line was sent.
- With the repaired program the answer HELLO arrived right away and the program exited 0.02 seconds after the child stopped with exit code 0.

## Why the posted program hangs (three causes)

1. shutil.copyfileobj reads in large blocks through a buffered reader and a buffered read waits until the whole block is full or the input ends so a single typed line can sit unread.
2. Writing into sys.stdout.buffer collects output in a buffer and nothing flushes the buffer so output can stay invisible.
3. Nothing closes the input of the child when the input of the program ends so a child that waits for the end of input waits forever.

## Best-guess answer

The repaired program worked in the test:

def pump_in():
    try:
        while chunk := os.read(sys.stdin.fileno(), 65536):
            proc.stdin.write(chunk)
    except (BrokenPipeError, OSError):
        pass
    finally:
        try: proc.stdin.close()
        except OSError: pass

def pump_out():
    while chunk := proc.stdout.read(65536):
        sys.stdout.buffer.write(chunk); sys.stdout.buffer.flush()

Thread(target=pump_in, daemon=True).start()
out = Thread(target=pump_out); out.start()
proc.wait()
out.join()
sys.exit(proc.returncode)

os.read returns as soon as any bytes are available and each piece of output is flushed at once and the input thread is a daemon thread so a read that is still waiting cannot keep the program alive after the child ends and joining the output thread makes sure every byte from the child is passed on before the exit.

The four test files sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts inside a folder named forward-test.

# The Galois group of the eigenvalue field of the 5-cycle graph as a permutation group

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/87751/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python libraries networkx and sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 9 February 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to turn the Galois group of a number field into a permutation group.
The posted program takes the eigenvalues of the 5-cycle graph (five dots joined in a ring) and builds a number field from the eigenvalues and calls K.galois_group() and then calls X.as_permutation_group() which fails.
Comments suggested PermutationGroup(X.gens()) and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The posted program never gives the name X to anything. The line K.galois_group() computes the group and throws the result away so the next line fails because X does not exist. Writing X = K.galois_group() is the first repair.
- The characteristic polynomial of the 5-cycle is (x − 2)·(x² + x − 1)² so the eigenvalues are 2 and (−1 + √5)/2 and (−1 − √5)/2.
- The eigenvalue 2 is a rational number so the field comes from x² + x − 1 alone and equals the rational numbers with √5 added (a field of degree 2).
- sympy returned the Galois group of x² + x − 1 as a permutation group with one generator that swaps the two roots (order 2).
- A direct check confirmed that replacing √5 by −√5 turns one eigenvalue into the other.

## Best-guess answer

The Galois group in the question is the group with two elements: the identity and the swap of the two irrational eigenvalues.
The repaired Sage lines worth trying are X = K.galois_group() followed by PermutationGroup(X.gens()) as the comment suggested and those lines were not tested for this page.
A reader without Sage can get the permutation group in Python with sympy:

p = sympy.Poly(x**2 + x - 1, x)
G, _ = p.galois_group()

# Measuring how far apart two graphs drawn in the plane are

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/88280/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the program and ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The question is open-ended so the page offers one workable approach and not the only correct approach.

## The question

On 19 March 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board (ask.sagemath.org question number 88280) for a method to measure the distance between two graphs.
Every node has two coordinates and a list of connected nodes and the graphs can be in several separate pieces and the node labels differ between the two graphs.
The asker wanted a first estimate based on the positions of corresponding nodes and mentioned the Laplacian as a possible tool.
The question had zero answers and zero comments when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The approach

A Python program (using the free libraries networkx and scipy) computes four numbers.

1. Mean partner distance: the program pairs every node of the first graph with a node of the second graph so that the total distance between partners is as small as possible and then reports the average distance between partners. The pairing solves the problem of differing labels because the pairing uses positions only.
2. Mismatched connections: after pairing the program counts connections that exist in one graph and not in the other graph.
3. Hausdorff distance: the largest distance from any node to the nearest node of the other graph.
4. Laplacian spectrum distance: a number computed from the connection pattern alone which ignores positions and labels.

## What the checks show

- The same graph with shuffled labels gave 0 for all four numbers.
- The same graph with every node nudged by about 0.2 gave a mean partner distance of 0.202 and 0 mismatched connections.
- The same positions with 2 connections rewired gave a mean partner distance of 0 and 4 mismatched connections and a Laplacian spectrum distance of 0.987.

The checks show that the position numbers react to moved nodes and the connection numbers react to rewired connections which means a pair of numbers (one of each kind) describes the difference better than a single number.
The pairing step needs both graphs to have the same number of nodes for a complete pairing and leaves extra nodes unpaired otherwise.

The program named graph_distance.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Counting graphs up to relabeling with the symmetric group (orbit counts by number of edges)

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83156/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the program and ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The question was short on detail so the page computes two readings of the question.

## The question

On 18 June 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to compute the set of orbits of the symmetric group S_n acting on collections of k pairs of vertices in order to count graphs that are the same up to renaming the vertices.
The asker could count the collections and was stuck on counting the orbits.
One commenter asked for code and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The method

The counting lemma of Burnside says that the number of orbits equals the average number of collections left unchanged by a rearrangement of the vertices.
Rearrangements with the same cycle lengths leave the same number of collections unchanged so the program visits one rearrangement per cycle type (one per partition of n) and weights the result by the number of rearrangements of that type.
For one rearrangement the program finds the cycles of the induced rearrangement of vertex pairs and a collection is left unchanged exactly when the collection is built from whole cycles.

## What the checks show

- Reading 1 (simple graphs: k different pairs of different vertices): the formula matched a brute-force count for n = 3 and n = 4.
- Reading 1 for n = 4 gives 1 and 1 and 2 and 3 and 2 and 1 and 1 graphs with 0 to 6 edges (total 11) and for n = 5 the total is 34 and for n = 6 the total is 156 and for n = 7 the total is 1044. All four totals equal the known numbers of graphs on 4 to 7 unlabeled vertices and every sequence reads the same forwards and backwards.
- Reading 2 (pairs may repeat and a pair may use the same vertex twice): the formula matched a brute-force count for n = 3 and n = 4 and gives 1 and 2 and 7 and 22 and 69 and 198 and 550 for n = 5 with k from 0 to 6.

## Best-guess answer

The orbit counts come from the Burnside average over cycle types and no list of orbits has to be built.
The Python program computes either reading through two switches (loops and repeats) and needs only a fraction of a second for n = 7.

The program named graph_orbits.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Centering histogram bars on whole numbers

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83318/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with matplotlib version 3.11.2 (the drawing library that the Sage histogram command uses according to a comment on the question) and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The Sage command itself was not tested.

## The question

On 4 July 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to make the bars of a histogram of whole numbers sit symmetrically around each value.
The call histogram([1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,2,2,2,2,4,4,3,4]) drew the bar for 1 shifted to the right and the bar for 4 shifted to the left and the asker had nudged the data by hand as a workaround.
A commenter pointed toward matplotlib and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- The default call cuts the range from 1 to 4 into 10 equal bins with edges 1.0 and 1.3 and 1.6 and so on. The value 1 falls into the bin from 1.0 to 1.3 (drawn to the right of 1) and the value 4 falls into the bin from 3.7 to 4.0 (drawn to the left of 4) which is exactly the shift in the question.
- With bin edges at the half numbers 0.5 and 1.5 and 2.5 and 3.5 and 4.5 the four bars were centered at exactly 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and the counts were 8 and 5 and 1 and 3 which matches the data.

## Best-guess answer

Giving the bin edges at half numbers fixes the picture without touching the data.
In matplotlib:

bins = np.arange(min(data) - 0.5, max(data) + 1.5, 1)
plt.hist(data, bins=bins, rwidth=0.9)

In Sage the matching call worth trying is histogram(data, bins=[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5]) because the Sage command passes the bins option on to matplotlib as far as the page author knows and that call was not tested for this page.

# Why the input() prompt of a child process shows up only after the answer is sent

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/87697

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The program of the asker was only partly readable so the test rebuilt the situation from the description.

## The question

On 9 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why the prompt text of input() in a child script does not appear on the captured output until after the parent program has already sent the answer.
The parent starts the child with subprocess.Popen and python -u and reads the output of the child line by line in a reader thread.
A plain print("123") before the input() call appeared normally.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The child prints 123 and then asks "Enter your name: " and then prints a greeting.

- With a reader that reads line by line the parent received only "123" before any answer was sent. After the answer was sent the parent received "Enter your name: hello Ada" as one single line.
- With a reader that takes whatever bytes have arrived the parent received "123" and "Enter your name: " before any answer was sent and the greeting afterwards.

## Best-guess answer

The child writes the prompt at the right moment. The prompt has no line break at its end and a line-by-line reader hands text over only after a line break arrives. The first line break after the prompt comes from the greeting so the prompt stays stuck inside the reader until then.
The repair that worked in the test is a reader that does not wait for line breaks:

def read_chunks():
    while chunk := os.read(p.stdout.fileno(), 4096):
        q.put(chunk.decode())

The Popen call for that reader uses bufsize=0 and leaves out text=True so the pipe hands over raw bytes right away.

The two test files sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts inside a folder named prompt-test.

# Is a four-coordinate formula Lawson's Klein bottle (the checks say torus)

## Link to the original question

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reference_desk/Mathematics

The copy of the page that was read turned out to be an old stored copy so the question (a section dated 11 December about the Klein bottle of Lawson) has probably moved into the archive of the help board and may already have an answer there.

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the Wikipedia Reference Desk for mathematics (in a section dated 11 December with the year not shown) whether the formula below describes Lawson's Klein bottle inside the three-dimensional sphere.
No reply appeared in the copy of the page read on 12 November 2026 and the copy may be an old stored copy.

The formula: w = cos θ cos φ and x = cos θ sin φ and y = sin θ cos φ and z = sin θ sin φ.
A Klein bottle is a closed surface with only one side and a torus is the surface of a ring doughnut which has two sides.

## What the checks show

Lawson's family of surfaces (written here from memory and not looked up today) uses two whole numbers m and k in the formula (cos mx cos y and sin mx cos y and cos kx sin y and sin kx sin y).

- The formula in the question equals the family member with m = 1 and k = 1 exactly (difference zero at 100000 random points) after renaming x as φ and y as θ.
- Every point of the formula in the question satisfies w times z = x times y which is the equation of a torus inside the sphere (the Clifford torus).
- The formula in the question gives the same point at (θ + π and φ + π) as at (θ and φ). That repeat keeps the handedness of the surface so the result is still a two-sided torus covered twice.
- The family member with m = 2 and k = 1 gives the same point at (x + π and −y) as at (x and y). That repeat flips the handedness of the surface (the minus sign in front of y) which is exactly what makes a one-sided Klein bottle.

## Best-guess answer

The formula in the question describes a torus and not a Klein bottle.
Lawson's Klein bottle is the family member with m = 2 and k = 1 which means the formula w = cos 2x cos y and x-coordinate = sin 2x cos y and third coordinate = cos x sin y and fourth coordinate = sin x sin y.
The naming of Lawson's family rests on memory so a reader who needs certainty could compare with Lawson's 1970 paper on minimal surfaces in the three-dimensional sphere.

The check file named lawson_check.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why a lambda inside a string annotation cannot find a global name after get_type_hints

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/103831

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 19 September 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why calling a lambda recovered from a string annotation raises "NameError: name FIND_ME is not defined".
The class in the post has two annotations (a regular function and a lambda that returns the module-level value FIND_ME) and the file starts with "from __future__ import annotations" which stores every annotation as text.
Calling typing.get_type_hints(Example) with default settings gave a working function and a broken lambda while passing globalns and localns explicitly made the lambda work.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The error reproduced on Python 3.13.18.
- The broken lambda does not have the module dictionary as its global namespace. The global namespace of the broken lambda is a dictionary holding the contents of the class which has no entry named FIND_ME.
- The source code of get_type_hints contains the line "base_globals, base_locals = base_locals, base_globals". For a class with no namespaces passed in the function swaps the two namespaces before evaluating the annotation text so the class contents are used as globals and the module dictionary is used as locals.
- A lambda remembers only the globals of the place where the lambda was created and never the locals. The lambda is created during that evaluation so the lambda remembers the class contents and loses the module dictionary.
- The regular function is only looked up by name during the evaluation and the lookup succeeds through the locals. The regular function was created earlier in the module so the function still has the module dictionary as globals.
- Passing both namespaces explicitly gave 42 and passing only globalns also gave 42 because the swap happens only when neither namespace is passed.

## Best-guess answer

The default behaviour differs from the commented-out lines in the post by exactly the swap: the defaults are the same two dictionaries in the opposite roles.
The repair that worked in the test is passing globalns=sys.modules[Example.__module__].__dict__ to get_type_hints.

The check file named lambda_hints.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Putting an LDAP address with host and attribute description into a certificate with the cryptography library

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/87403

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

## The question

On 7 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum whether the cryptography library can add the host part and the attribute description part of an LDAP address to the relative_name of a certificate revocation list location.
The asker quoted the certificate standard which wants an LDAP address such as ldap://ldap.example.com/cn=example%20CA,dc=example,dc=com?certificateRevocationList;binary.

The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

dp = x509.DistributionPoint(

    relative_name=None, reasons=None, crl_issuer=None)
builder = builder.add_extension(x509.CRLDistributionPoints([dp]), critical=False)

# A workaround for associated Legendre functions outside the interval from −1 to 1

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/88040/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library mpmath and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The checks ran in plain Python and not inside Sage.

## The question

On 2 March 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board whether the associated Legendre functions of the first and second kind (the versions used for x larger than 1) are missing from SageMath 10.8 while the Ferrers versions (the versions used between −1 and 1) exist and whether a workaround exists.
Two comments suggested looking at other libraries and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

The library mpmath has the functions legenp and legenq and both accept the setting type=3 which selects the versions for x outside the interval from −1 to 1. The library mpmath is one of the libraries that ships inside SageMath so the workaround needs no extra installation as far as the page author knows.

- The value of legenq(ν, μ, x, type=3) matched the hypergeometric formula for Q (formula 14.3.7 of the Digital Library of Mathematical Functions written from memory) to at least 30 digits at five test points including non-whole values ν = 2.5 and μ = 0.5.
- Q with ν = 0 at x = 2 equaled 0.5·log((x+1)/(x−1)) exactly and Q with ν = 1 at x = 2 equaled (x/2)·log((x+1)/(x−1)) − 1 to 31 digits.
- P with ν = 1 and μ = 1 at x = 2 equaled √(x²−1) and P with ν = 2 and μ = 2 at x = 2 equaled 3·(x²−1).
- The setting type=2 gave the Ferrers version: P with ν = 1 and μ = 1 at x = 0.3 equaled −√(1−x²).

## Best-guess answer

A workaround worth trying inside Sage is:

import mpmath
mpmath.legenq(nu, mu, x, type=3)
mpmath.legenp(nu, mu, x, type=3)

The results are numbers and not symbolic expressions so the workaround fits number checks of formulas and does not fit symbolic manipulation.
The page did not test formula 14.3.19 itself and did not check whether the functions are missing from Sage 10.8.

# Keeping fast spikes visible in a live matplotlib plot while drawing fewer points

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26255

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 without a screen and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The timings come from a machine without a display so the timings are rough and the page answers only the parts of the post that a test could settle.

## The question

On 29 July 2026 somebody on the matplotlib forum described a live display of sensor data arriving at about 2000 samples per second: a rolling line plot with a spectrogram below.
The asker reported a sharp drop in frame rate after adding the spectrogram and visible skipping after bursts and lost spikes when thinning the data and asked four things about figure layout and burst handling and live plotting versus logging and the choice of display backend.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- Thinning by keeping every 10th sample lost a one-sample spike of height 25 in the test.
- Thinning by keeping the smallest and the largest value of every screen column kept the spike. The test drew 1600 points in place of 8000 points and the largest drawn value was still 25.
- Redrawing the line took about 48 milliseconds with all 8000 points and about 23 milliseconds with the 1600 smallest-and-largest points.
- Redrawing the spectrogram picture took about 16 milliseconds while computing the spectrogram numbers took about 0.06 milliseconds so the drawing costs far more than the mathematics.

## Best-guess answer for the tested parts

The smallest-and-largest thinning answers the question about plotting every sample while staying fast because every spike survives and the number of drawn points depends on the width of the screen and not on the amount of data:

def minmax_decimate(y, columns):
    n = (y.size // columns) * columns
    blocks = y[:n].reshape(columns, -1)
    out = np.empty(columns * 2)
    out[0::2] = blocks.min(axis=1)
    out[1::2] = blocks.max(axis=1)
    return out

One possibility for the frame rate drop is the cost of redrawing the spectrogram picture on every frame so redrawing the spectrogram on every fifth or tenth frame while the line updates on every frame is worth testing.

## What stays open

The questions about two figures versus one figure and about live plotting versus logging and about the best display backend were not tested because the test machine had no display.

The test file named live_plot_speed.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why the PARI function qflllgram returned an identity matrix

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83810/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with PARI version 2.15.4 through the Python package cypari on small made-up lattices and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The checks did not use the number field data from the question and did not run inside Sage.

## The question

On 13 August 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board why calling qflllgram on a Gram matrix G (the table of dot products of the basis vectors of a lattice) returned an identity matrix while handing the same Gram matrix to the function qflll gave "the expected reduced basis".
The asker computes reduced bases of log-unit lattices of number fields.
One commenter asked for runnable code and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The function qflllgram does not return a reduced basis. The function returns a whole-number matrix T (a change of basis) and the reduced basis is the old basis multiplied by T.
- For a basis that was already short and nearly at right angles qflllgram returned the identity matrix. An identity matrix therefore means "the basis handed in is already reduced" and not "something went wrong".
- For the same lattice described by a skewed basis (vector lengths 1.005 and 7.428) qflllgram returned a matrix with the entries 1 and −7 and 0 and 1 and multiplying the skewed basis by that matrix gave short vectors again (lengths 1.005 and 1.158).
- The function qflll expects the basis vectors themselves as columns. Calling qflll on the basis returned the same matrix as calling qflllgram on the Gram matrix.
- Calling qflll on the Gram matrix returned a different matrix (entries 15 and −82 and −2 and 11) because qflll then treats the columns of the Gram matrix as if those columns were basis vectors which describes a different lattice.

## Best-guess answer

One possibility that fits the report is that the log-unit basis from PARI was already reduced so qflllgram correctly answered with the identity matrix and the output of qflll on the Gram matrix only looked like a result because qflll was reducing a different lattice.
The reduced basis comes from multiplying the matrix of basis vectors by the matrix that qflllgram returns and the reduced Gram matrix is T transposed times G times T.

The check file named lll_gram.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Solving a·log(r) + r = y for r (the answer needs the Lambert W function)

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/85789/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python libraries sympy and mpmath and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 3 November 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board whether Sage has a bug because the command solve(a*log(r)+r==y, r) returned r == -a*log(r) + y which still has r on the right side.
One commenter replied that the output probably means Sage could not find a solution and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The equation has a closed-form solution: r = a · W(e^(y/a) / a) where W is the Lambert W function (the function that undoes x·e^x).
- The Python library sympy returned exactly that formula for positive a and r and y.
- Number checks with 30 digits confirmed the formula: for a = 2 and y = 5 the formula gives r = 2.88260866130517 and putting that r back into a·log(r) + r − y gives a leftover smaller than 10^−30.
- For negative a the equation can have two real solutions or none. With a = −2 and y = 3 the two branches of W gave r = 0.253250909296112 and r = 6.84787750069176 and both passed the check. With a = −2 and y = −1 no real solution exists because the value inside W falls below −1/e.

## Best-guess answer

The Sage output is one possible sign that the solver gave up and not a wrong statement because the returned line is just the original equation rearranged.
The solution exists and reads r = a · W(e^(y/a) / a).
The derivation takes three steps: divide by a to get log(r) + r/a = y/a and take e to the power of both sides to get r·e^(r/a) = e^(y/a) and substitute u = r/a to get u·e^u = e^(y/a)/a which is the defining equation of W.
In Sage the function is available as lambert_w so the line a*lambert_w(exp(y/a)/a) is worth trying and that line was not tested for this page.

The check file named lambert_solve.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Where the screenwriting word "logline" comes from

## Link to the original question

https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Etymology_scriptorium/2024/February

The question sits in the section named logline on that page.

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) did the search in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has checked the sources yet which means the answer on this page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 29 February 2024 somebody asked on the Wiktionary word-origin board (the Etymology scriptorium) whether the film-script meaning of "logline" (a very short summary of a script) shares the origin of the sailing meaning (the rope tied to a wooden float that sailors used to measure the speed of a ship).
Nobody replied on the board.
The Wiktionary entry read on 12 November 2026 still gives one shared origin for both meanings with a first use in 1613. Source: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/logline

## What the records show

1. The Merriam-Webster dictionary gives the script meaning a separate origin: the word "log" plus the word "line" and originally the line in a television program log that summarizes the plot of a show. The same dictionary dates the first known use of the script meaning to 1982. Source: https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/logline

2. The listings section of the magazine TV Guide was itself called "the log" which was a text list of programs ordered by start time and channel with a short summary beside most programs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Guide_(magazine)

3. Many screenwriting websites say the word comes from log books that old Hollywood studio heads kept for the scripts the studio owned. None of the websites read for this page shows a document from the studio years that uses the word and the dictionary date of 1982 falls decades after the studio years.

## Best-guess answer

The script meaning does not come from the sailing rope because the script meaning names a line of text in a program log.
The two meanings are still distant relatives because the word "log" for a written record comes from the log book of a ship and the log book of a ship was named after the wooden float on the sailing rope.
A fitting correction for the Wiktionary entry could be two separate origin sections: the sailing meaning from 1613 and the script meaning from television program logs with a first known use in 1982.

## What is still open

No use of the script meaning earlier than 1982 was searched for inside scanned television trade magazines because the full-text search of those scans was out of reach.
The old Hollywood log book story could still be true if somebody finds a studio document that uses the word before television existed.

# Why a home-made Python match pattern gives "Invalid CFG, inconsistent stackdepth"

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/109464

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) read the Python source code and ran a small check in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has checked the work yet. The suggested fix was not tested because testing needs a rebuilt copy of Python with the asker's changes which means the fix is an unconfirmed best guess.

## The question

On 13 October 2026 somebody on the Python help forum (discuss.python.org topic number 109464) described a learning project that adds a new kind of pattern to the match statement inside the Python compiler (Python 3.14).
The new pattern calls a function and treats a true result as a match.
One pattern alone worked and two patterns joined with the "or" bar gave the error "ValueError: Invalid CFG, inconsistent stackdepth".
The asker wanted to know whether a function call leaves exactly one value on top of the stack and where to look for the cause.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the source code and the check show

1. A function call leaves exactly one new value on the stack. The check measured the stack change of the call instruction for a call with 1 argument as −2 which means the call removes the function slot and one extra slot and the argument (3 values) and puts back 1 result.

2. The Python 3.14 source file Python/codegen.c carries a comment above the pattern routines (lines 5670 to 5672) that says every pattern routine follows the convention of consuming the top of the stack (the value being matched) and jumping to the failure code when the pattern does not match.

3. The built-in value pattern follows the convention because the comparison instruction removes both the value being matched and the constant and leaves one true or false result. The bytecode of "case 1 | 0" shows the steps for each alternative: copy the value being matched (+1) then load the constant (+1) then compare (−1) then jump on false (−1). The stack is back to the starting height after each alternative.

4. The asker's routine pushes the result of the call and turns the result into true or false and jumps on false. Nothing in the routine removes the copy of the value being matched so the routine ends one value higher than the convention promises.

## Best-guess answer

One possibility for the cause is the missing removal of the value being matched because the "or" code makes a copy for every alternative and expects each alternative to use the copy up. Paths that should meet at the same stack height then meet at different heights and the compiler reports the inconsistent stack depth.

A fix worth testing is one extra line before the call that removes the copy when the function does not need the value:

ADDOP(c, LOC(p), POP_TOP);
VISIT(c, expr, p->v.MatchFunc.e);
ADDOP(c, LOC(p), TO_BOOL);
RETURN_IF_ERROR(jump_to_fail_pop(c, LOC(p), pc, POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE));

A pattern that should pass the matched value into the function can keep the copy and hand the copy to the call as an argument so the call uses the copy up.

One guess about why the constant version worked for the asker is that the compiler removes a jump whose condition is a known constant so the mismatched paths never meet. The guess was not tested.

The check file named match_stack.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Replacing a method in a Python test with a quick stand-in that uses self

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104184

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 6 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum whether a better or more common method exists for giving a mocked method access to self.
The posted test replaced a slow method with a mock and set a side effect function that takes self and the test failed with "missing 1 required positional argument: self".
The asker had found one repair (adding autospec=True) and asked about alternatives.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

Five tests passed.

- The posted version fails with a TypeError as reported because a plain mock placed on a class does not hand the object over as the first argument.
- Route 1 worked: patch.object(Pipeline, "very_expensive_method", new=quick_method). A plain function placed on the class becomes an ordinary method so self arrives without any extra work. Route 1 keeps no record of calls.
- Route 2 worked: patch.object(Pipeline, "very_expensive_method", autospec=True, side_effect=quick_method). Route 2 keeps the call record and the record includes the object as the first argument so m.assert_called_once_with(p) passes.
- Route 3 worked: patching the method on one single object with a side effect that already knows the object. Other objects of the class keep the real method.
- After each patch block ended the original method was back.

## Best-guess answer

The repair that the asker found (autospec=True) is a standard route and fits tests that also check how the method was called.
Route 1 with new= is the shortest route when the test only needs the quick behaviour and no call record.

# A mistake found in a published number list (OEIS A394252)

## Link to the original question

https://oeis.org/A394252

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) did the search and the computing in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the work yet which means every result on this page is unconfirmed except the one sum that any reader can check on a calculator.

## The question

The Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences holds an entry numbered A394252 at the address https://oeis.org/A394252 and the entry was submitted in March 2026.
The rule of the list is that the first term is 1 and each later term number n is the smallest whole number above the previous term that cannot be written as a sum of exactly n-1 earlier terms when repeats are allowed.
The comments inside the entry say that runs appear where each term is double the previous term and that nobody has a proof about how long those doubling runs get.

## Finding 1: the published term 31 breaks the rule of the list

The copy of the entry read on 12 November 2026 lists 13265690624 as term 31.
The number 13265690624 can be written as a sum of exactly 30 earlier terms because two copies of 829105664 plus twenty-eight copies of 414552832 add up to 13265690624.
Term 31 is supposed to be a number that 30 earlier terms cannot reach which means 13265690624 cannot be term 31.
The published term 32 (39657914368) is also wrong because term 32 was built on top of the wrong term 31.

## Finding 2: values for terms 31 to 38 from an exact program

- Term 31 is 19759378432
- Term 32 is 39518756864
- Term 33 is 79037513728
- Term 34 is 158075027456
- Term 35 is 316150054912
- Term 36 is 632300109824
- Term 37 is 1890267484160
- Term 38 is 3780534968320

The program that produced the eight values reproduced the first 30 published terms and matched a slow brute-force check through term 17 which means the eight values depend on the program being correct beyond term 30.

## Finding 3: a short proof of a limit on doubling runs

Suppose a doubling run starts at position s and has lasted L terms so far.
The next doubled number equals 2^L copies of the first term of the run.
Two equal copies can be merged into one bigger term of the same run and each merge lowers the count of terms by one.
Merging therefore lets the doubled number be written with any count of terms from 2 up to 2^L.
The doubled number sits at position s + L and so the doubled number fails as a term whenever s + L - 1 is between 2 and 2^L.
The doubling therefore must stop once s + L - 1 is at most 2^L.

The limit matches every run computed so far (run lengths 2 and 2 and 3 and 4 and 5 and 5 and 5 and 5 and 6).
The published run of 6 terms starting at position 26 violates the limit because 26 + 5 - 1 is 30 and 30 is less than 32.
The proof gives only an upper limit because nobody has proven yet that doubling always continues right up to the limit.

## What is still open

- Nobody has proven that a run always reaches the limit.
- Nobody has proven the pattern that the first term after a run equals three times the last term of the run minus the last term of the run before.
- The editors of the encyclopedia may have corrected the entry after 12 November 2026.
- Nothing has been sent to the encyclopedia.

The program files sit in the folder named boring-things at the top of this project inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Running parallel Python work with objects that pickle cannot handle

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/106518

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 with dill 0.4.1 and multiprocess 0.70.19 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the Python help forum (discuss.python.org topic number 106518) how to run parallel processing when a project holds objects that the standard pickle module cannot serialize and the library named dill can.
Serializing means turning an object into bytes so the object can travel to another process.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The test object was a small function created inside another function (a lambda) because standard pickle refuses that kind of object.

- Standard pickle failed on the test object and the plain ProcessPoolExecutor failed for the same reason.
- Route 1 worked: the main program turns the function and the argument into bytes with dill.dumps and the standard ProcessPoolExecutor carries the bytes and a small helper function in the worker rebuilds the function with dill.loads and calls the function. The four results came back as 5 and 6 and 7 and 8 as expected.
- Route 2 worked: the separate package named multiprocess is a copy of the standard multiprocessing module that uses dill inside so multiprocess.Pool(2).map accepted the test object directly and returned the same four results.

## Best-guess answer

Route 2 needs the smallest code change because only the import line changes (import multiprocess in place of import multiprocessing).
Route 1 keeps the standard library pool and needs one helper function:

def run_dill_payload(payload):
    func, arg = dill.loads(payload)
    return func(arg)

payloads = [dill.dumps((func, arg)) for arg in args]
results = list(executor.map(run_dill_payload, payloads))

Results that travel back from the worker still go through standard pickle in route 1 so a result that standard pickle cannot handle needs the same dill wrapping on the way back.

The test file named dill_parallel.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Speeding up point-inside-polygon lookups with one bulk call

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/88825

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library shapely version 2.2.0 on made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The real script and data of the asker were not used so the page tests one part of the problem only.

## The question

On 19 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to speed up a script that takes more than two weeks for one year of data.
The script checks more than a million drifting particles every hour for 30 days against 207 coral reef polygons with a loop that builds one point per particle and asks a spatial index and runs a "within" test.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test used 207 irregular made-up polygons and 200000 made-up particle positions for one time step.

- A loop with one point object and one index lookup per particle took about 1.6 seconds for 200000 particles (measured on 20000 particles and scaled up).
- One bulk call for all particles took 0.10 seconds which is about 16 times faster.
- Both methods agreed on which particles are inside a polygon.
- Scaled to one million particles and 720 hourly steps the loop needs about 1.6 hours and the bulk call needs about 6 minutes.

## Best-guess answer

The bulk route in shapely 2 replaces the inner loop with two calls:

tree = shapely.STRtree(polygons)                      # built once
pts = shapely.points(xs, ys)                          # all particle positions of one time step
pt_idx, poly_idx = tree.query(pts, predicate="within")

The result is two lists of matching numbers: particle number and polygon number for every particle that sits inside a polygon.
Even the loop in the test is far faster than two weeks so one possibility is that most of the run time of the real script sits somewhere other than the lookup (for example reading the data file hour by hour or building objects inside the loop) and timing each part of the real script is the step that would show where the two weeks go.

# Why an image drawn with imshow lands in the wrong place on a polar chart

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26078

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with a small made-up array and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 19 November 2025 somebody asked on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26078) why a large grid of depth values looked wrong on a polar chart (a round chart where position is given by a compass angle and a distance from the center).
Each column of the grid had a compass direction between 214 and 314 degrees and each row had a tilt angle above or below the horizon.
The posted program drew the grid with the command imshow and the asker reported a wrong angle range and clipping at the top and distance labels that did not match the data.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- With imshow the colored area covered compass angles from 180 to 360 degrees when the data belonged between 214 and 314 degrees. The command imshow draws a flat rectangular picture and does not bend the picture around the center of a polar chart.
- With imshow the distance axis ran from about 100 to 2127 because the posted program handed the smallest and largest depth values to imshow as the edges of the picture. Depth is the quantity shown by color so the depth values do not belong on the distance axis.
- With the command pcolormesh the colored area covered compass angles from 214 to 315 degrees which matches the data. The command pcolormesh receives the angle of every column and a distance for every row and bends each cell into the correct wedge.

## Best-guess answer

Replacing imshow with pcolormesh fixed the angle range in the test:

theta = np.radians(orientations)
radius = inclinations - inclinations.min()
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(theta, radius, depth[::rf, ::rf], cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
ax.set_rlim(0, radius.max())
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="depth (m)")

The lists theta and radius need the same thinning as the grid (orientations[::rf] and inclinations[::rf]) when the grid is thinned with rf.
Using the tilt angle as the distance from the center is an assumption made for this page because the post did not say which quantity belongs on the distance axis.

The test file named polar_image.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why clean-up callbacks in multiprocessing Pool workers get cut off

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104155

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux with the spawn start method and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 4 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why a clean-up callback registered with multiprocessing.util.Finalize finishes in a stand-alone Process and gets cut off half way in a worker of a multiprocessing.Pool.
In the posted program the callback starts when the pool block ends and the worker process is shut down before the callback can finish.
The asker warned that a lock held by such a worker might never be released and asked whether the behaviour is known and how to let the callback finish.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- A pool used with a "with" block: the callback did not finish (the event was never set) which matches the report.
- The source code of Pool.__exit__ calls terminate() so leaving the "with" block stops the workers abruptly.
- Calling pool.terminate() directly gave the same cut-off.
- Calling pool.close() followed by pool.join(): the callback finished.
- Calling close() and join() as the last two lines inside the "with" block: the callback finished.

## Best-guess answer

The cut-off comes from terminate() and the "with" block of a Pool calls terminate() at its end by design (the Python documentation states that leaving the block calls terminate as remembered).
The repair that worked in the test is to shut the pool down gently: call pool.close() and then pool.join() before the block ends because close() lets every worker finish its work and exit normally and a normal exit runs the registered callbacks to the end.
A library that cannot control how its users close their pools cannot rely on Finalize callbacks finishing in pool workers because any user who relies on the "with" block triggers the abrupt stop.

The test file named pool_finalize.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Which calls into C code reach sys.setprofile and which reach sys.monitoring

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/92391

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 with C types from the standard library in place of the hand-written extension from the post and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 May 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why special methods (such as __init__) defined in a C extension produce no events in sys.setprofile while ordinary C functions and Python-level __init__ methods do.
The asker wanted to know whether the behaviour is expected and whether another route exists for logging those calls.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test ran eight kinds of calls into C code under both tools.

- sys.setprofile reported c_call events only for array.append (an ordinary C method) and len (a built-in function).
- sys.setprofile reported nothing for creating objects of C types and nothing for item access and nothing for addition and nothing for d.__init__() or a.__len__() called by name.
- sys.monitoring (available since Python 3.12) reported CALL events for creating the two objects (with the type itself as the thing being called) and for array.append and len and also for OrderedDict.__init__ and array.__len__ called by name.
- sys.monitoring reported nothing for item access and nothing for addition.

## Best-guess answer

The missing events fit the design of the profiler hook: c_call events are tied to calls of built-in function and method objects. Creating an object of a C type runs the creation and init slots of the type directly inside the interpreter with no function object involved so no c_call event exists to report. The same applies to operators.
The route that worked in the test for logging object creation is sys.monitoring with the CALL event because the event fires for every call made by Python code and hands over the type being called. The init slot itself still stays invisible and the event for the type call stands in for the init slot.
Operators and item access on C types stayed invisible to both tools in the test.

The test file named profile_slots.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# What Python Protocol classes and ABC classes each enforce

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/97537

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 3 July 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why a Protocol class can carry a method with a real body that subclasses inherit and whether any reason remains to use ABC classes and what the catch is.
A Protocol describes the shape a class needs (structural typing) and an ABC is a base class with abstract methods that subclasses have to fill in.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

1. A class that inherits a protocol method with a body can be created and the body runs. Python allows protocol methods with bodies as default behaviour for classes that inherit the protocol on purpose.
2. A class that inherits a protocol and forgets the method can still be created and calling the method silently runs the empty placeholder and returns None. Nothing warns at run time.
3. An ABC subclass that forgets an abstract method cannot be created because Python raises a TypeError that names the missing method.
4. A protocol method marked with abstractmethod is enforced the same way for classes that inherit the protocol.
5. An isinstance check against a runtime_checkable protocol only looks for the method name: a class with a method of the wrong signature passed the check.
6. A class that never inherits anything counted as an instance of the protocol and did not count as an instance of the ABC.
7. An ABC can carry stored state and shared helper methods.
8. A protocol class itself cannot be created directly.

## Best-guess answer

The catch is in results 2 and 5: a plain Protocol enforces nothing at run time for subclasses that forget a method and the isinstance check is shallow so the protection of a Protocol comes mostly from a type checker run before the program starts.
An ABC still fits when missing methods should stop the program at object creation and when subclasses should share stored state or helper methods and when "is a member of this family" should mean "inherits from this base class on purpose".
A Protocol fits when unrelated classes (including classes from other libraries) should count without inheriting anything.
The two tools combine because abstractmethod works inside a Protocol (result 4).

The test file named protocol_vs_abc.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Linking two formulas for special Pythagorean quadruples (and why the solver choked)

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/85649/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 28 October 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to connect two descriptions of whole-number solutions of a² + b² + c² = d² that also satisfy d + a = c².
The first description uses four numbers u and v and s and t and the second description uses two numbers m and n.
The asker put eleven equations with N = 65 into the Sage solver and the solver failed and a later attempt reported "the dimension of the ideal is 7".
The question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The formulas in m and n satisfy a² + b² + c² = d² for every m and n (the difference expands to zero).
- The formulas in m and n satisfy d + a = c² for every m and n (the difference expands to zero).
- The extra equation a = 3·(3N − 3)/6 + 1 turns into N = (4m + 1)·(4n + 1). The number N is therefore tied to m and n by a simple product.
- For N = 65 the product rule leaves exactly four whole-number pairs: (m and n) = (0 and 16) or (1 and 3) or (3 and 1) or (16 and 0).
- Each pair gives one quadruple: (97 and −1054 and 34 and 1059) and (97 and 14 and 14 and 99) and (97 and 374 and 22 and 387) and (97 and 9506 and 98 and 9507). All four pass both equations.
- Each quadruple has exactly 4 whole-number choices of (u and v and s and t). For example (m and n) = (1 and 3) matches (u and v and s and t) = (−7 and 7 and 1 and 0).

## Best-guess answer

The link between the two descriptions is a short chain: split N into two factors of the form 4m + 1 and 4n + 1 and compute a and b and c and d from m and n and then find u and v and s and t from u² + v² = (d + a)/2 and s² + t² = (d − a)/2 with b and c picking out the matching signs.
One possibility for the solver failure is that two of the eleven equations are identities that add no information so the system has more freedom than a general solver expects and searching whole numbers directly (as the program does) avoids the problem.

The check file named quadruple_link.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why rdflib turns the prefix dct into dcterms

## Link to the original question

https://github.com/aigora-de/rdf-construct/issues/457

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on rdflib version 7.6.0 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the results on this page are unconfirmed.

## The question

An open GitHub issue with zero comments (aigora-de/rdf-construct issue number 457) has the title "Two prefixes for one namespace: rdflib keeps one, so a source's dct: comes back as dcterms".
Only the title was readable because the request to open the issue page was not approved in time so the answer on this page responds to the title and not to the full text of the issue.
The library rdflib is a Python library for linked data files and a prefix is a short nickname for a long web address inside such a file.

## What the tests show

- A Turtle file that declares the nicknames dct and dcterms for the same web address (http://purl.org/dc/terms/) comes back from rdflib with only one nickname because rdflib stores one nickname per web address.
- The nickname declared last in the file is the nickname that rdflib keeps. Declaring dct then dcterms kept dcterms and declaring dcterms then dct kept dct.
- Turning off the built-in nicknames of rdflib (the setting bind_namespaces="none") did not change which nickname was kept.
- Calling g.bind("dct", "http://purl.org/dc/terms/", override=True, replace=True) after reading the file made rdflib write dct in the output.

## Best-guess answer

A program that wants the nickname from the source file to survive can remember the wanted nickname and call bind with override=True and replace=True after reading the file.
Keeping both nicknames at once was not possible in any test because rdflib 7.6.0 stores one nickname per web address.

The test file named rdflib_prefix_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Getting custom-formatted text for warnings recorded with catch_warnings

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/83807

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 9 March 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why a custom warnings.formatwarning function leaves no trace in the list returned by warnings.catch_warnings(record=True).
The asker maintains a testing tool that has to record warnings and also has to test code that formats warnings and asked for alternatives that avoid private parts of the Python library.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

1. Without recording the custom formatter was called and the printed text carried the custom prefix.
2. With record=True the custom formatter was not called at all. The recorded entry is a WarningMessage object that keeps the raw parts: the message and the category and the file name and the line number.
3. Calling the public function warnings.formatwarning on the raw parts of a recorded entry afterwards produced the custom-formatted text.
4. A small custom recorder that replaces warnings.showwarning inside a catch_warnings block stored both the entry and the custom-formatted text at the moment of the warning and printed nothing.
5. After the block ended normal printing with the custom formatter was back.

## Best-guess answer

Recording skips formatting because formatting only happens on the way to printing and recording stores the raw parts in place of printing.
Two routes that use only public functions worked in the tests:

- Format later: text = warnings.formatwarning(w.message, w.category, w.filename, w.lineno, w.line) for each recorded entry w.
- Format at the moment of the warning: inside "with warnings.catch_warnings():" set warnings.showwarning to a function that appends both a warnings.WarningMessage(...) and warnings.formatwarning(...) to a list.

The second route matters when the custom formatter depends on the state of the program at the moment of the warning.

The test file named record_format.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.
