# Turning the text "(missing)" red in one spreadsheet column with pandas and xlsxwriter

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/74598

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with pandas 3.0.5 and xlsxwriter 3.2.9 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The file was read back with a second library and was not opened in Excel itself.

## The question

On 18 December 2024 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to make the text "(missing)" red in column D of a spreadsheet written with pandas and the xlsxwriter engine.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test table had four data rows with "(missing)" in two rows of column D.

- Route 1 (a conditional format): the finished file held one rule on the range D2:D5 of the kind "text contains (missing)" with a red font and both "(missing)" cells sat inside that range.
- Route 2 (writing the matching cells again with a red format): the two "(missing)" cells carried a red font and the other two cells kept the default colour.

## Best-guess answer

Route 1 is two lines after df.to_excel:

red = writer.book.add_format({"font_color": "red"})
writer.sheets[sheetname].conditional_format(f"D2:D{len(df) + 1}", {"type": "text", "criteria": "containing", "value": "(missing)", "format": red})

The range starts at D2 because row 1 is the header and ends at len(df) + 1 because the data starts one row down. A range that ends at len(df) leaves out the last data row.
Route 2 colours only the matching cells with a fixed format:

col = df.columns.get_loc("Cust code")
for r, value in enumerate(df["Cust code"], start=1):
    if value == "(missing)":
        writer.sheets[sheetname].write(r, col, value, red)

Route 1 keeps working when a person edits the cells later in Excel and route 2 does not react to later edits.

The test file named red_missing.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# A fast method for the restricted matching number of a graph

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83031/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the program and ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library networkx and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The page covers graphs only and not general simplicial complexes.

## The question

On 4 June 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board for an algorithm for the restricted matching number of a simplicial complex or at least of a graph.
For a graph the definitions read as follows. Two edges form a gap when the two edges share no vertex and no edge of the graph joins a vertex of one to a vertex of the other. A matching is a set of edges that share no vertices. A restricted matching is a matching in which one chosen edge forms a gap with every other edge of the matching. The restricted matching number is the largest size of a restricted matching.
One commenter advised writing an own algorithm and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The method

Only the chosen edge has to form gaps. The other edges only have to form an ordinary matching among themselves.
For a chosen edge with end points u and v every other edge of the matching must avoid u and v and every neighbour of u and v.
So the best restricted matching with that chosen edge has size 1 plus the largest ordinary matching in the graph that remains after deleting u and v and all neighbours of u and v.
Trying every edge as the chosen edge and keeping the best result gives the restricted matching number. Largest ordinary matchings are computed quickly by a standard routine so the whole method is fast.

## What the checks show

- The method agreed with a brute-force search over all matchings on 255 random graphs with up to 9 vertices.
- Sample values: a path with 7 vertices gives 3 and a cycle with 8 vertices gives 3 (ordinary matching number 4) and a complete graph with 6 vertices gives 1 and the Petersen graph gives 3 and a 5 by 5 grid gives 11 and a star with 6 leaves gives 1.
- A random graph with 300 vertices and 951 edges took about 30 seconds.

## Best-guess answer

The restricted matching number of a graph equals 1 plus the largest ordinary matching number of the graph left after removing one edge together with all neighbours of its two end points with the largest taken over all edges.
The same line of thought could carry over to simplicial complexes (choose one facet and delete everything that fails the gap condition with that facet) and that extension was not written or tested for this page.

The program named restricted_matching.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# The step in Riemann's 1859 paper that turns one integral into a loop integral

## Link to the original question

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reference_desk/Mathematics

The copy of the page that was read turned out to be an old stored copy so the question (a section dated 10 December about the integral step in the paper by Riemann) has probably moved into the archive of the help board and may already have an answer there.

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the explanation and ran the number check in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has checked the work yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the Wikipedia Reference Desk for mathematics (in a section dated 10 December with the year not shown) how Riemann gets from the first formula below to the second formula and whether the second integral is a Hankel-type loop integral.
No reply appeared in the copy of the page read on 12 November 2026 and the copy may be an old stored copy.

First formula: Π(s−1) ζ(s) equals the integral from 0 to infinity of x^(s−1) / (e^x − 1) dx.
Second formula: 2 sin(πs) Π(s−1) ζ(s) equals i times the integral "from +infinity to +infinity" of (−x)^(s−1) / (e^x − 1) dx.
Riemann's symbol Π(s−1) means the same number as the modern Gamma(s).

## The answer in words

The second integral is a loop integral of the Hankel type because the path comes in from far out on the positive side just above the positive real axis and circles the origin counterclockwise and goes back out just below the positive real axis.

The power (−x)^(s−1) means e raised to (s−1) times log(−x) and log(−x) is chosen to be an ordinary real number when x is negative.
That choice forces two different values along the positive real axis because −x equals x times e^(−iπ) just above the axis and x times e^(+iπ) just below the axis.

- Just above the axis the power equals e^(−iπ(s−1)) times x^(s−1) and the path runs inward from infinity to 0.
- Just below the axis the power equals e^(+iπ(s−1)) times x^(s−1) and the path runs outward from 0 to infinity.
- The small circle around the origin contributes nothing in the limit when the real part of s is larger than 1.

Adding the two straight pieces gives (e^(iπ(s−1)) − e^(−iπ(s−1))) times the first integral.
The bracket equals 2i sin(π(s−1)) which equals −2i sin(πs).
Multiplying by the i in front turns −2i sin(πs) into 2 sin(πs) because i times −2i equals 2.
The first integral equals Π(s−1) ζ(s) so the loop formula follows.

The loop integral has a bonus because the loop never touches the origin and so the loop integral makes sense for every complex s which is how Riemann extends ζ(s) beyond the region where the first integral works.

## The number check

A program computed both sides to 25 digits at five test values of s.
The two sides agreed to at least 21 digits at s = 2.5 and s = 3.7 and s = 1.5 + 2i and s = −1.5 (a value where the first integral does not even converge).
The two sides agreed to 8 digits at s = 0.5 + 14.134725i where the numbers are large.

The check file named riemann_step.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# The map from the symmetric group S3 to rotations and reflections of a triangle

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/87352/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 12 January 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to define the map from the symmetric group S3 (the six ways to rearrange three things) into 2 by 2 matrices so that the generators become a rotation by 120 degrees and a reflection.
The question had zero answers and zero comments when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The construction

Place the three things at the corners of an equilateral triangle centered at the origin with corner k at the angle 120·k degrees.
Every rearrangement p of the corners is carried out by exactly one 2 by 2 matrix: the matrix that sends corner k to corner p(k).

- The 3-cycle 0→1→2→0 gives the rotation by 120 degrees with rows (−1/2 and −√3/2) and (√3/2 and −1/2).
- The swap of corners 1 and 2 gives the reflection across the x axis with rows (1 and 0) and (0 and −1).
- The other four matrices are products of those two matrices.

## What the checks show

- Each of the six matrices moves every corner k to corner p(k).
- The map respects multiplication for all 36 pairs of rearrangements (doing two rearrangements in a row matches multiplying the two matrices).
- All six matrices are different so the map loses no information.
- Every matrix keeps lengths unchanged.
- The traces are 2 for the identity and 0 for the three swaps and −1 for the two 3-cycles which matches the known character of the two-dimensional irreducible representation of S3.

## Best-guess answer

Sending the 3-cycle to the rotation matrix and the swap to the reflection matrix defines the wanted map because the two matrices satisfy the same rules as the two generators (the rotation applied three times is the identity and the reflection applied twice is the identity and the checks confirm all 36 products).
One detail about order: sympy writes p*q for "first p then q" so the matching matrix product is M(q)·M(p) and a system that composes the other way needs M(p)·M(q).
A Sage user can enter the same two matrices by hand and the exact Sage commands for building the map object were not tested.

The check file named s3_matrices.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Animating many dots at once in a matplotlib scatter chart

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26094

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with made-up data and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 14 January 2026 somebody asked on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26094) how to animate a scatter chart of 1000 moving dots.
The data sat in two grids named cord_x and cord_y with one row per time step and one column per dot.
The posted program worked for one dot and failed for many dots with the message "vertices must be 2D with shape (N, 2)".
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- The posted update step produced a block of numbers with three dimensions (time steps by 2 by dots) and the tests reproduced the same kind of error at frame 1 and frame 2 because the command set_offsets accepts only a flat table with one row per dot and two columns (x and y).
- A replacement update step that takes one single time step and builds a table with one row per dot gave a table of 1000 rows and 2 columns and the dot positions matched the data at the first frame and the second frame and the last frame.
- The replacement update step also saved a complete 40 frame animation file without an error.

## Best-guess answer

The following update step worked in the test:

def update(frame):
    scat.set_offsets(np.column_stack([cord_x[frame], cord_y[frame]]))
    return (scat,)

The slice cord_x[:frame] in the posted program means "every time step before this frame" and the fix uses cord_x[frame] which means "this one time step".
Setting the x limits and y limits once before the animation starts keeps the dots inside the chart because set_offsets does not rescale the chart.

The test file named scatter_anim.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# A Python "nothing was passed" marker that type checkers accept

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/107758

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python version 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the results on this page are unconfirmed.

## The question

On 14 June 2026 somebody asked on the Python help forum (discuss.python.org topic number 107758) whether a one-line trick is a good method for making a sentinel in Python versions 3.12 to 3.14.
A sentinel is a special marker object that a function uses as a default value so the function can tell "the caller passed nothing" apart from "the caller passed None".
The trick in the post was the line "type _MISSING = _MISSING" which defines a type name in terms of itself.
The post said the trick works when the program runs and that the type checker rejects the trick.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- The trick runs without an error on Python 3.13.18 and the function prints the expected text.
- The type checker named mypy rejects the first line with the message "Cannot resolve name _MISSING (possible cyclic definition)".
- The type checker named pyright rejects the first line with the message "Type alias _MISSING cannot use itself in its definition".
- A marker built from an enum class with exactly one member passes both type checkers with zero errors. After the check "if value is MISSING" both type checkers narrow the remaining type to plain text (str) which means string methods can be called without a complaint.

## Best-guess answer

The self-referencing trick is a poor fit for typed code because two widely used type checkers reject the trick at the first line.
The enum marker is a working substitute for Python 3.12 to 3.14 because the enum marker runs correctly and passes both type checkers.
The enum marker looks like the following six lines:

import enum
from typing import Final
class _Missing(enum.Enum):
    MISSING = enum.auto()
MISSING: Final = _Missing.MISSING
def my_func(need_value: int, not_need_value: str | _Missing = MISSING) -> None: ...

The test files named sentinel_rejected.py and sentinel_enum.py sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Letting several async functions send to one device over a single connection

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/93342

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 with two small local servers standing in for the two Telnet devices and plain asyncio connections standing in for telnetlib3 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. Real devices and the telnetlib3 library itself were not tested.

## The question

On 26 May 2025 somebody new to Python asked on the Python help forum about a home automation program that listens to one device and sends commands to another device over Telnet.
Each device allows only four connections so the asker wants exactly one connection per device with one reading function per device and wanted to know how several async functions can share one outgoing writer and whether the design is workable.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## The design that was tested

Each device gets one small object that owns the single connection.
The object has an outbox (an asyncio.Queue) and one background task that takes text from the outbox and writes the text to the device.
Any function that wants to send calls device.send(text) which only puts the text into the outbox.
Because only the one background task ever touches the writer two functions can never write at the same moment.

## What the test shows

- Exactly 1 connection was opened per device.
- Two different functions sent to the same device (a rule matcher reacting to lines from the first device and a separate heartbeat function).
- All five lines reached the second device: both rule actions and all three heartbeat lines.
- Every line arrived whole with no mixing of two messages.

## Best-guess answer

The design in the question is workable and the outbox queue is the piece that makes sharing safe.
The core of the tested class:

class Device:
    def __init__(self): self.outbox = asyncio.Queue()
    async def connect(self, host, port):
        self.reader, self.writer = await telnetlib3.open_connection(host, port)
        self.sender = asyncio.create_task(self._send_loop())
    async def _send_loop(self):
        while True:
            text = await self.outbox.get()
            self.writer.write(text + "\r\n")
            await self.writer.drain()
    def send(self, text): self.outbox.put_nowait(text)

One line in the posted program looks wrong: tuner_writer.writelines(action, "\n") passes two arguments and writelines expects one list of lines so writer.write(action + "\r\n") is the form worth using. The telnetlib3 behaviour of that line was not tested.

The test file named shared_writer.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Putting a plot beside an image at exactly the same height in matplotlib

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26077

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 19 November 2025 somebody asked on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26077) for the best layout for two number grids stacked vertically as images with a plot of the largest value of each row to the right of each image and aligned with the height of the image.
The two grids had the same number of rows (64) and different numbers of columns (256 and 128).
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- The posted 2 by 2 grid gave side plots that were taller than the images and the tops did not line up (off by more than 50 pixels) because an image with square pixels shrinks inside the grid cell and the side plot does not shrink.
- Layout 1 attaches the side plot to the image with the helper make_axes_locatable. The side plot height equaled the image height for both grids and the tops differed by 0.00 pixels and the image pixels stayed square.
- Layout 2 uses a grid with a wide column and a narrow column and stretches the image to fill the cell (aspect="auto"). The heights matched and the tops differed by 0.00 pixels and the image pixels were no longer square.

## Best-guess answer

Layout 1 keeps square pixels:

from mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1 import make_axes_locatable
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1)
for ax, M in zip(axes, (A, B)):
    ax.imshow(M)
    side = make_axes_locatable(ax).append_axes("right", size=0.8, pad=0.1, sharey=ax)
    side.plot(M.max(axis=1), np.arange(M.shape[0]))
    side.tick_params(labelleft=False)

Layout 2 is shorter and gives both images the same width:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, width_ratios=[4, 1], sharey="row", layout="constrained")
for (ax, side), M in zip(axes, (A, B)):
    ax.imshow(M, aspect="auto")
    side.plot(M.max(axis=1), np.arange(M.shape[0]))

The setting sharey makes row 0 of the side plot sit level with row 0 of the image in both layouts.

The test file named layout_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# What does a question feel like when nobody answers?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

This folder holds questions that people posted in public places and that sat with no reply. Some of those questions sat for a long time. Each one was typed by a living person who wanted to know something and who checked back and found an empty space under the question.

Asking a question in public takes a small act of courage because the asker admits to not knowing. The asker also shows hope because a question assumes that somebody out there might care enough to respond.

Silence after a question can teach a painful lesson. Here is a possibility for what an asker might conclude. The asker might decide that the question was foolish or that the asker does not matter enough to answer. The silence usually says neither of those things because people scroll past for many reasons such as being tired or not knowing the answer.

A hard feeling can work like an unanswered question too. A person who feels a heavy sadness and tells nobody is carrying a question that reads "does anyone see this?" The longer the question sits the more the person may believe that the answer is no.

So here is a question for a reader. What question of mine has been sitting with no reply and who could I ask again?

Asking again is allowed because silence the first time is not a refusal. A question can be posted in a new place or put to a different person or worded more plainly. A question about a feeling can also be put to the feeling itself such as "sadness what are you trying to show me?"

A reader can also be the reply for someone else. An answer does not have to be complete to matter because a response such as "I don't know and I see that you asked" tells the asker that the question landed somewhere. Replying costs attention so a reader gives that reply when the reader has attention to spare.

## Quick points

- Each unanswered question was typed by a living person who wanted to know something and who checked back and found an empty space under the question.
- Asking a question in public takes courage because the asker admits to not knowing and shows hope that somebody might care enough to respond.
- Silence after a question can lead an asker to believe that the question was foolish when people scroll past for many reasons such as being tired or not knowing the answer.
- A heavy sadness that a person tells nobody about works like an unanswered question that reads "does anyone see this?"
- A person can ask again in a new place or with plainer words and a reader with attention to spare can reply "I don't know and I see that you asked" so the asker knows the question landed somewhere.

# Silencing an import warning inside a spawned Python child process

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/105472

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 31 December 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to set a warning filter in a child process before the child imports a module that prints a UserWarning on import.
The asker starts child processes with the Process class of a spawn context and that class has no setup hook that runs before imports.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The tests used a small module that raises a UserWarning on import and a child started with the spawn method.

- With the noisy import at the top of the child file and no other change the child printed the warning even though the parent had a filter because a spawned child starts as a fresh Python with default filters.
- Route 1 worked: setting os.environ["PYTHONWARNINGS"] = "ignore::UserWarning" in the parent before starting the child silenced the warning because the child inherits the environment and Python reads that variable at startup.
- Route 2 worked: calling warnings.filterwarnings inside the target function and importing the noisy module on the next line (inside the function) silenced the warning.
- Route 3 worked: a tiny module whose only content is the filterwarnings call silenced the warning when the child file imports the tiny module before the noisy module.

## Best-guess answer

Route 1 needs one line in the parent and no change to the child code and the filter text can be narrowed to one module (for example "ignore::UserWarning:noisy_module").
Route 2 and route 3 keep the fix inside the code and affect only the files that use them.
All three routes returned the correct result (42) from the child in the tests.

The test files sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts inside a folder named spawn-warning-test.

# What Pillow keeps and drops when a photo is converted to sRGB and saved as WebP

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104246

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with Pillow version 12.3.0 on a made-up test picture and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The asker used Pillow 10 so details could differ. The page answers the parts of the question that a test could settle and leaves the rest open.

## The question

On 8 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum about preparing gallery photos for a website: converting wide-colour JPEG files to sRGB and saving the files as WebP.
The asker saw slight brightness shifts on iPhones and inconsistent colour profiles and asked five things: how to force sRGB cleanly and which WebP settings fit photos and how to strip extra metadata while keeping orientation and colour and whether other libraries are better and whether iPhone browsers have quirks.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- The posted save call wrote a WebP file with no colour profile at all (0 bytes of profile in the file) because Pillow embeds a profile in WebP only when the save call receives the argument icc_profile.
- Adding icc_profile with the bytes of the sRGB profile that Pillow builds put a 588 byte profile into the file. The bytes come from ImageCms.ImageCmsProfile(SRGB).tobytes().
- The posted save call also dropped all camera metadata including the orientation tag. A photo that relies on the orientation tag would therefore show sideways after the conversion.
- The picture returned by profileToProfile no longer carried the orientation tag so the turning step has to happen before the colour conversion. Calling ImageOps.exif_transpose on the opened photo first and converting second gave an upright picture (480 wide and 640 tall from a source stored as 640 by 480 with a rotate tag).
- The picture returned by profileToProfile still carried the old source profile in its info even though the pixels were already sRGB.

## Best-guess answer for the tested parts

The following order worked in the test:

with Image.open("in.jpg") as im:
    im = ImageOps.exif_transpose(im)
    im = to_srgb(im)
    im.save("out.webp", format="WEBP", quality=82, method=6, icc_profile=ImageCms.ImageCmsProfile(SRGB).tobytes())

The order turns the pixels upright and converts the colours and writes a small sRGB profile into the file so a browser does not have to guess the colour space.
No other metadata reaches the WebP file with this call because Pillow writes metadata into WebP only when the save call receives the argument exif.
One possibility for the brightness shifts is the missing profile in the posted output because a file without a profile leaves the colour interpretation to each device and the test did not include any iPhone.

## What stays open

The test picture was a simple gradient so the test says nothing reliable about file sizes for real photos.
The questions about other libraries and about iPhone browser quirks were not tested.

The test file named srgb_webp.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Stopping a job that is already running in a Python ProcessPoolExecutor

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/100128

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 25 July 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum what happens to a job in a ProcessPoolExecutor when the web request that started the job is cancelled and how to stop the process that is still running.
The asker knew the approach of passing a stop signal into the heavy function and disliked adding checks throughout the function.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The test job was a loop that burns processor time with no stop checks inside.

- Calling future.cancel() on a job that was already running returned False and the job ran to the end (2 more seconds in the test). Cancelling only removes jobs that have not started yet.
- Killing the worker process of the pool from outside stopped the job and the job raised BrokenProcessPool and after that the whole pool refused every new job. Killing a pool worker therefore costs the entire pool.
- The executor of Python 3.13 has no method named terminate_workers and Python 3.14 added one according to the Python documentation as remembered. A test on Python 3.14 was not run.
- Starting one dedicated process per cancellable job worked cleanly: terminate() stopped a 30 second job in under 0.01 seconds and a new dedicated process ran normally afterwards.

## Best-guess answer

A cancelled request does not stop a running pool job by itself because the pool has no channel for interrupting a worker in the middle of a job.
For jobs that must be stoppable without checks inside the function a dedicated multiprocessing.Process per job (stopped with terminate()) is the route that worked in the test and the price is the start-up time of a new process for every job.
A stop signal checked inside the function remains the only route that lets the job clean up after itself because terminate() ends the process without running clean-up code.

The test file named stop_task.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why datetime.strptime with %Z returns a time without a time zone

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/86433

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on a machine set to US Central time and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 29 March 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why datetime.strptime("2025-UTC", "%Y-%Z") returns a datetime without time zone information while "%z" with "+0000" returns a time-zone-aware datetime.
The asker saw the same behaviour from Python 3.5 to 3.13 and asked whether the behaviour is intended and what %Z is for.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

- %Z with "UTC" returned a datetime with tzinfo None and %z with "+0000" returned a datetime with tzinfo UTC which matches the report.
- %Z accepted only a short list of names on the test machine: UTC and GMT and CST (a local zone name of the machine). The names EST and CET and Europe/Paris were refused with an error.
- Using %Z and %z together gave an aware datetime whose zone name is the text matched by %Z.

## Best-guess answer

The behaviour fits the design as far as the tests show: a zone name such as CST does not pin down an offset from UTC (the same letters are used for more than one zone in the world) so %Z only checks that the text is a known name and keeps the name for labeling when %z supplies the offset.
The consistency across many Python versions points to intended behaviour and the page did not find a statement from the Python developers saying so.
Two routes to an aware result worked in the tests:

- When the text is known to say UTC: datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z").replace(tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
- When the text ends in a zone name such as Europe/Paris: split the name off and attach zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(name) after parsing the rest.

The test file named strptime_zone.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Getting coordinates along the paths of one colour in an SVG file

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104239

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library svgpathtools on a small made-up SVG file and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 8 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to get the coordinates of the path objects of one colour in an SVG drawing.
Matching pixel colours in a PNG picture had given jagged edges so the asker moved to SVG paths and tried to turn each curve segment into a polynomial and then search the polynomial for a colour which returned nothing useful.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What went wrong in the posted program

A polynomial of a curve segment holds the formula of the curve and holds no colour so comparing the polynomial with a colour finds nothing.
The colour of an SVG path lives in the attributes of the path (inside the style text or in a separate stroke or fill attribute) and the coordinates come from asking the path for points along its length.

## What the test shows

The test file had a green path made of a curve and a straight line and a red path and a second green path that stored the colour in a separate attribute with capital letters.

- Filtering on the colour #00ff00 kept the two green paths and skipped the red path.
- Each green path returned 85 points from the first point to the last point of the path.
- The largest gap between neighbouring points was under 1 unit because the points were spaced evenly along the length of the path.

## Best-guess answer

The following functions worked in the test:

def colour_of(attribs, key="stroke"):
    m = re.search(key + r"\s*:\s*([^;]+)", attribs.get("style", ""))
    value = m.group(1) if m else attribs.get(key, "")
    return value.strip().lower()

def points_on(path, step=1.0):
    n = max(2, int(np.ceil(path.length() / step)) + 1)
    pts = [path.point(path.ilength(s)) for s in np.linspace(0, path.length(), n)]
    return np.array([(p.real, p.imag) for p in pts])

paths, attributes, svg_attributes = svg2paths2(filename)
green = [points_on(p) for p, a in zip(paths, attributes) if colour_of(a) == "#00ff00"]

Using key="fill" in place of key="stroke" filters on the fill colour.
The library stores every point as one complex number so the x value is the real part and the y value is the imaginary part.
Colours written as names (such as "lime") or as rgb(0,255,0) need an extra conversion step that the test did not cover.

The test file named svg_by_colour.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# The sum of every entry of a repeated tensor product of [z², c]

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/88560/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 April 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board (ask.sagemath.org question number 88560) how to take the tensor product of the pair [z², c] with itself again and again and then add up every entry (the grand sum) and then look at the limit as the number of copies n grows without end.
One commenter asked for clarification and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

The tensor product of n copies of [z², c] has 2^n entries and each entry is a product that picks either z² or c from every copy.
Adding all 2^n entries therefore gives the same result as multiplying out (z² + c) times itself n times.
A program built the tensor products for n = 1 to 7 (up to 128 entries) and the sum of all entries equaled (z² + c)^n exactly every time.

## Best-guess answer

The grand sum of n copies equals (z² + c)^n so nobody needs to build the huge tensor product to get the sum.
The limit as n grows depends only on the single number w = z² + c:

- The grand sum shrinks to 0 when the size of w is less than 1 (for example w = 1/2 or w = i/2).
- The grand sum stays at 1 forever when w equals exactly 1.
- The grand sum has no limit when the size of w equals 1 and w is not 1 (for example w = −1 flips between −1 and 1).
- The grand sum grows without end when the size of w is larger than 1 (for example w = 3/2).

The boundary where the size of z² + c equals 1 is a different boundary from the famous Mandelbrot picture because the Mandelbrot picture feeds each result back into z and the grand sum only raises one fixed number to higher powers.

The check file named grand_sum.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Where memory stays after a thread pool returned large lists

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/85149

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux with made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The real task of the asker (a Celery task reading cloud storage listings) was not available so the page tests one possible cause.

## The question

On 19 March 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why a worker process keeps about 1 GB of memory after a task that fetched two large object lists through a ThreadPoolExecutor with two workers.
A ProcessPoolExecutor avoided the leftover memory and caused memory spikes from copying the lists between processes so the asker wants to stay with threads.
The posted code stores the two futures in a set named pending_thread_tasks.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test task returned two lists of one million small records each through a thread pool and stored the futures in a set like the posted code.

- Memory use was 17 MiB at the start and 768 MiB while both lists were in use.
- After the task function returned with the set of finished futures still referenced from outside memory use stayed at 768 MiB.
- After the last references to the futures were dropped memory use fell to 35 MiB.
- Asking the C library to hand unused memory back to the operating system (malloc_trim) changed nothing further in the test.

## Best-guess answer

A finished future keeps its result. A set or list of futures that outlives the task (for example a module-level variable or an attribute of a long-lived object) therefore keeps both large lists alive after the task ends.
One possibility that fits the report is such a surviving reference: the futures set or the variables source_objects and target_objects or a traceback or a log record that holds the lists.
The repair that worked in the test is dropping the references when the work is done:

pending_thread_tasks.clear()
del source_objects, target_objects

A process pool hides the problem because the big lists live in child processes that end.
If memory stays high after every reference is gone the next thing worth testing is the memory allocator of the C library which can hold on to freed memory and the call ctypes.CDLL("libc.so.6").malloc_trim(0) asks the allocator to give the memory back.

The test file named thread_memory.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Switching between two live charts in one matplotlib window

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26086

def draw_grid():

def draw_scatter():
    fig.clf()

# Recording true finish times when an as_completed loop also writes to disk

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/89833

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The post had no code so the test rebuilt the situation from the description.

## The question

On 27 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why progress lines printed inside a concurrent.futures.as_completed loop fall further and further behind the real work.
The loop also writes each result to disk and near the end about 20 "finished" lines print within one second even though the threads finished long before.
The asker wanted to print the completion time of each thread accurately.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test ran 24 short jobs on 8 threads and handled each result in a loop with a slow step that stands in for the disk write.

- All 24 jobs had really finished after 0.15 seconds.
- The loop reached the last result after 0.98 seconds.
- The lag between a job really finishing and the loop seeing the result grew from 0 to 0.83 seconds.
- A time noted by the job itself and a time noted by a done callback agreed within 0.21 milliseconds.

## Best-guess answer

The loop handles one result at a time so every disk write delays the moment when the loop notices the next finished job. The threads keep finishing in the background and the finished results pile up which matches the burst of lines at the end.
Two repairs gave true finish times in the test:

- Let the job note its own finish time and return the time together with the result (return result, time.perf_counter()).
- Attach a callback with future.add_done_callback(...) because the callback runs at the moment the job finishes and does not wait for the loop.

Moving the disk writes into the jobs or into a separate writer thread would also stop the pile-up and that change was not tested for this page.

The test file named completion_times.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why "Move to square b0" printed before the row error in a try block exercise

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/98946

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) rebuilt the exercise in a single chat on 12 November 2026 from the text of the post (the screenshot in the post was not readable) and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 16 July 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum about a code-ordering exercise from an online textbook.
The exercise has a function get_column that raises a ValueError for a column outside a to h and a function get_row that raises a ValueError for a row outside 1 to 8 and a try block that gets both values and prints the move.
For the input "b 0" the submitted program printed "Move to square b0" and then "Row must be between 1 and 8" while the expected output was only the error line.
The asker wondered whether the textbook site was wrong.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- An ordering with the print line before the row check printed both lines for the input b 0 which matches the output the asker reported.
- An ordering with both value lines first and the print line last printed only "Row must be between 1 and 8" for the input b 0 which matches the expected output.
- Both orderings printed "Move to square b3" for the input b 3 and the column error for the input k 3.

## Best-guess answer

The expected output of the site is correct because a raised error stops the try block at the line where the error happens and jumps to the except block so every line that ran before the error has already had its effect.
The print line therefore has to come after both value lines:

try:
    column = get_column()
    row = get_row()
    print(f"Move to square {column}{row}")
except ValueError as excpt:
    print(excpt)

# When did the Turkish para stop being money (a partial answer)

## Link to the original question

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reference_desk/Humanities

The question sits in the section dated 4 September on that page and the page may have been moved into the archive of the help board since the search.

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) did the search in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has checked the sources yet which means the answer on this page is an unconfirmed best guess.

## The question

Somebody asked on the Wikipedia Reference Desk (Humanities) when the Turkish para was formally abolished as a subdivision of the kuruş (40 para made 1 kuruş and 100 kuruş made 1 lira).
The helpers on the board got as far as a report that the last para coin was minted in 1942 and the formal ending stayed unconfirmed.

## What the records show

1. The Turkish State Mint lists the 10 para coin as entering circulation in 1940 and leaving circulation in 1950. The 10 para coin was the last para coin issued in Turkey so 1950 is the year the last para coin stopped being legal money. Source: https://www.darphane.gov.tr/cumhuriyet-donemi-tedavul-paralari

2. Turkish newspapers in 1941 and 1942 printed a Finance Ministry notice that withdrew the old nickel 5 para and 10 para and 20 para coins because enough scalloped 1 kuruş coins and bronze 10 para coins had been struck. The notice gave one more year for handing the old coins in at government cash offices and Central Bank branches. The scans are garbled around the dates so the cutoff date of 1 July 1942 is a best reading from three scans. Source: https://www.gastearsivi.com/gazete/son_posta/1942-06-10/8

3. A Turkish parliament document from the late 1960s shows the coin law (law number 6797) being amended with a list of permitted coins that runs from 2.5 lira down to 1 kuruş. No para coin could be legally struck under that list because the smallest permitted coin was 1 kuruş. Source: https://www5.tbmm.gov.tr/tutanaklar/TUTANAK/MM__/d03/c004/mm__03004072ss0102.pdf

## Best-guess answer

One possibility that fits all three records is that Turkish lawmakers never passed a single act abolishing the para and that the para ended in steps: the old nickel para coins stopped circulating in mid-1942 and the last para coin was withdrawn in 1950 and later coin law allowed no coin below 1 kuruş.

## What is still open

The Turkish Official Gazette archive refuses automated readers so the withdrawal notice for the bronze 10 para coin (probably printed in 1949 or 1950) was not read.
A person who opens the Official Gazette issues from 1949 and 1950 could confirm the exact day and could check for an explicit abolition sentence.

# Is the Python function urljoin unsafe with web addresses from strangers

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/109165

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python version 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the results on this page are unconfirmed.

## The question

On 21 September 2026 somebody asked on the Python help forum (discuss.python.org topic number 109165) whether the standard Python function urljoin is known to be weak against hostile input and whether a ticket exists about the weakness.
The function urljoin combines a base web address with a second piece of a web address.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The base address in every test was https://good.example/app/ and the test asked whether the combined address still pointed at good.example.

- The input slash then a tab character then slash then evil.example produced https://evil.example because Python deletes the tab character and two slashes in a row mean "go to a different website".
- The same jump to evil.example happened with a newline character or a carriage return character between the two slashes.
- The same jump happened with two spaces in front of two slashes and with a control character in front of two slashes because Python strips those characters from the front.
- The input with the tab written as the three characters %09 stayed on good.example because Python deletes only a real tab character.
- An ordinary input such as page.html stayed on good.example.

## What the Python documentation says

The Python documentation states that tab and newline characters are removed from a web address at any position since Python version 3.10 and that leading control characters and spaces are stripped. The documentation says the removal follows the web address standard that web browsers use. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.parse.html

The same documentation warns that urljoin is generally not secure with a second piece that an attacker controls.

A public security write-up from the Google security research team describes a real chain of redirects on the Python package website that used the slash and tab and slash input. Source: https://github.com/google/security-research/security/advisories/GHSA-6hc9-758f-7r98

## Best-guess answers to the three questions in the post

1. The weakness is real and known because the tests reproduce the jump to another website and the documentation carries a warning about attacker-controlled input.
2. The removal of tab and newline characters was added on purpose so a replacement inside Python would be a design decision for the Python maintainers. A program can protect itself today by comparing the website name of the combined address with the website name of the base address and the test file shows that the comparison caught every jump in the list above.
3. The search for this page found the two code changes that added the character removal (CPython pull requests 25727 and 25923 and the later change numbered 102153) and found no ticket that asks for urljoin itself to be replaced. A ticket could still exist because the search was a web search and not a search inside the Python issue tracker.

The test file named urljoin_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Packing several files into one .zst archive without loading a whole file into memory

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/105705

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 with the package backports.zstd (which offers the same interface as the compression.zstd module of Python 3.14) and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The test did not run on Python 3.14 itself.

## The question

On 13 January 2026 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to combine several data files into one ZSTD archive with every file compressed as an independent frame so that single files can be pulled out later.
The posted program for the standard library module read each whole file into memory with read_bytes and the asker worried about running out of memory on large files.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test compressed a 48 MiB file and a 20 MiB file into one archive by reading 1 MiB at a time.

- Peak Python memory while compressing was about 2 MiB which is far below the 48 MiB size of the larger file.
- Each frame decompressed alone to exactly the original file.
- Each frame stored the correct content size (50329632 bytes and 20970680 bytes).
- The whole archive decompressed to both files joined together.

## Best-guess answer

The following loop worked in the test:

CHUNK = 1 << 20
cctx = zstd.ZstdCompressor(options=options)
with open(output_file, "wb") as f_out:
    for src in file_to_compress:
        cctx.set_pledged_input_size(src.stat().st_size)
        with open(src, "rb") as fin:
            while chunk := fin.read(CHUNK):
                f_out.write(cctx.compress(chunk))
        f_out.write(cctx.flush(zstd.ZstdCompressor.FLUSH_FRAME))

The call cctx.compress(chunk) feeds one piece at a time and the call cctx.flush with FLUSH_FRAME closes the frame of the current file so the next file starts a new frame.
Recording f_out.tell() before each file gives the byte position where each frame starts which is the information needed for pulling out a single file later.
The test left out the multi-thread setting (nb_workers) so the behavior with several worker threads is untested.

The test file named zstd_frames.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Voynich manuscript

This folder holds three pages about the Voynich manuscript which is an unreadable book from the early 1400s.

- [findings.md](findings.md) tells who probably made the book (five scribes and fifteen calfskins and a castle drawing that points to northern Italy) and how the book was built and what spelling-pattern tests add.
- [location-guess.md](location-guess.md) guesses where the book was made by reading eight drawing clues such as a crossbow archer and forked castle walls and baggy sleeves the way a map-guessing player reads a street photo.
- [second-pass.md](second-pass.md) reports a second run of the spelling-pattern tests on 12 November 2026 where the main result came out again and the claim about one-way writing came out weaker.
- [reading-without-words-reflection.md](reading-without-words-reflection.md) is a short reflection that uses the unreadable book as a picture for understanding a person who has not put a feeling into words such as by noticing a face and a posture and offering an open guess.

# The Voynich manuscript: who made the unreadable book and how the book was built

The Voynich manuscript is a handwritten book from the early 1400s that nobody has been able to read because the writing uses an alphabet that matches no known language or code.
The first half of this page tells the human story of the book from published research and the second half reports spelling-pattern tests that an AI model (Claude) ran on 11 November 2026.
No other person has rerun the tests in the second half yet which means every number in the second half is a single unconfirmed analysis.
An AI chatbot reran the tests in a new session on 12 November 2026 and the page named second-pass.md in this folder reports which numbers came out again and which claim came out weaker.

## The people and the place

- Laboratory workers at the University of Arizona dated samples of the pages in 2009 and the dates fell between 1404 and 1438 which means the animal skins come from a time before printed books existed in Europe.
- The pages are made of calfskin and the whole book used the skins of at least fourteen or fifteen calves which suggests a person with money paid for the book because calfskin was costly.
- One tiny drawing of a castle has wall tops shaped like the forked tail of a swallow and builders used that shape most often around the city of Verona in northern Italy which is one reason researchers guess the book was made in northern Italy.
- An archer drawn on the page for the star sign Sagittarius wears a hat in the style of the city of Florence which is a second clue that points toward northern Italy.
- The plant drawings resemble a family of plant books that copyists in northern Italy made in the 1400s for physicians and pharmacists which suggests the makers lived close to working healers.
- The names of the months beside the star-sign drawings are written in ordinary Latin letters with spellings that fit France or northwest Italy and a few margin words look like German which means the place of origin is a best guess and not a settled fact.
- A handwriting study published in 2020 sorted the writing into five different hands which means five different scribes probably shared the work and the book was probably a team project and not the doodling of one person.
- The five scribes divided the work by subject because several scribes shared the long plant section and one scribe wrote the star and sky pages and another scribe wrote the bathing pages and two scribes wrote the pages of short starred paragraphs.
- The scribes made very few corrections which suggests every scribe already knew the strange alphabet well before starting.

## What the pictures show

- The drawings show plants that mostly match no known species and star charts and star signs and hundreds of small naked women.
- Many of the women stand in pools of green or blue liquid joined by pipes and tubes which is why researchers call that part of the book the bathing section.
- One research team proposed in 2024 that part of the book concerns sex and conception and the health of women because a physician of the same period wrote about plants and women and baths and the sky and advised hiding such knowledge in secret letters.
- The colored paint was put on rather roughly and possibly by a later person which means the ink outlines are the more trustworthy record of what the first makers drew.

## How the book was built

- The book is made of large calfskin sheets folded in half so each folded sheet gives two leaves and four pages and the folded sheets are nested inside each other in bundles like a stack of folded newspapers.
- Gaps in the old page numbers suggest the book once had at least 272 pages and about 240 pages survive today which means some sheets went missing over the centuries.
- The cover is goatskin and the cover was added centuries later which means the present binding is not the binding the makers knew.
- In several bundles of the plant section the sheets of one scribe sit nested between the sheets of another scribe (for example one bundle runs scribe 1 then scribe 2 then scribe 1 four times then scribe 2 then scribe 1) which means each scribe wrote whole folded sheets and somebody later interleaved the sheets.
- A painted stream of water leaves a bath on the back of leaf 78 and continues on the front of leaf 81 and those two pages are far apart in the bound book but sit side by side on one unfolded sheet which suggests the painter worked on single sheets before anyone bound the book.
- A study published in October 2026 proposed that the book began as loose folded sheets that were never meant to be nested and that a person who could not read the writing later bound the sheets in the wrong order.
- The same study pointed to a large water stain in the upper margin of some pages as more evidence because the stain can show which sheets once lay on top of each other.

## The journey of the book

- The earliest probable owner was a physician and alchemist in the German city of Augsburg and the first confirmed owner was an alchemist in Prague in the 1600s.
- A book dealer bought the manuscript in 1912 from a Jesuit college near Rome and the manuscript carries the name of that book dealer today.
- The rare book library of Yale University has held the manuscript since 1969 and the library put pictures of every page online in 2020 so anyone can look at the pages.
- Code breakers who cracked military codes in both world wars tried to read the manuscript and failed.

## Could the words be meaningless

- A researcher showed in 2026 that a cipher worked by hand with tools from the 1400s can turn Latin or Italian into text that resembles the manuscript which means a real hidden message is possible.
- Volunteers who were asked to write pages of invented nonsense produced text with similar statistics because the volunteers kept copying and slightly changing words they had already written which means meaningless filler is also possible.
- Nobody knows yet which of the two possibilities is true.

## What the spelling-pattern tests on this page add

The tests below support three parts of the human story with a different kind of evidence which is the drift of spelling habits from page to page.

- The bound order of the pages is probably not the order in which the scribes wrote the pages.
- Each scribe probably wrote one folded sheet at a time from the first page of the sheet to the fourth page.
- Nearly every page ends exactly where a paragraph ends which could mean the scribes fitted the text to each page.

## Method

The main test gives a "next page" score to a pair of pages by comparing three-letter chunks in the last four lines of one page with the first four lines of another page because the spelling habits of a writer drift slowly and pages written back to back share habits.
The score ranks the true candidate page among all candidate pages by the same scribe in the same section so 0.50 means chance and 1.00 means the top match.

## Results

- The back of a leaf scored 0.67 as the continuation of the front of the same leaf across 68 leaves which shows the test detects real back-to-back writing.
- The facing page in the bound book scored 0.54 across 46 pairs which is near chance and suggests the bound order is not the writing order.
- The step from the back of the first leaf of a folded sheet to the front of the second leaf of the same folded sheet scored 0.79 across 26 sheets and the sheet partner was the top match in 9 of 26 cases where chance predicts about 2.
- The same sheet partner in the reverse direction scored 0.54 across 31 cases which suggests the scribe's hand moved one way through each folded sheet.
- A different sheet in the same bundle scored 0.51 across 83 comparisons which suggests the effect belongs to the single folded sheet and not to the bundle.
- The pattern held in three transcriptions (ZL and IT and RF) and under 36 measurement settings.
- 176 of 177 pages with running text end exactly at a paragraph end which means almost no paragraph runs across a page break.
- The 24 folded sheets by scribe 1 in the plant section differ along one main word-habit contrast and sheets in the same bundle sit close together on the contrast (about 1 chance in 800 under shuffling) which could mean the binder kept piles of sheets together.
- Sheets by different scribes matched in word mix at 0.30 and sheets by the same scribe matched at 0.53 while two halves of one sheet matched at 0.56 which argues against a separate cipher for every sheet and leaves a per-scribe difference open.

## What is not new and what might be new

A study published in October 2026 in the journal Digital Medievalist ("Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript") had already reported that the two halves of a folded sheet resemble each other more than facing pages do.
The direction test and the same-bundle control and the paragraph-end count might be additions but the author of this folder could not open the full journal article to check.

## Limits

- The test tracks the order in which a scribe wrote and cannot show the order a reader was meant to follow.
- The order of the sheets remains unknown because sheet-to-sheet scores were only slightly above chance.
- Several versions of the analysis were tried before the ranking version which raises the risk of a lucky result.

## Sources for the human story

- Encyclopedia entry with the dating and the calfskins and the page counts and the ownership history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voynich_manuscript
- Article on the five scribes and the castle and the archer and the plant books: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2025/05/05/the-voynich-manuscript-revealed-five-things-you-probably-did-not-know-about-the-medieval-masterpiece
- Article on how the five scribes divided the work: https://www.unseenhistories.com/the-voynich-manuscript-garry-shaw/
- Report on the October 2026 study about the wrong page order and the water stain: https://www.livescience.com/archaeology/undeciphered-voynich-manuscript-may-have-been-bound-out-of-order-study-finds
- Page on the painted stream of water that crosses from leaf 78 to leaf 81: https://ciphermysteries.com/the-voynich-manuscript/voynich-codicology
- Article on the proposal about sex and conception: https://phys.org/news/2024-04-years-voynich-manuscript-mystery-sex.pdf
- Article on the hand cipher: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/01/07/can-a-new-cipher-help-to-explain-the-mysterious-voynich-manuscript
- Article on the bathing drawings and the purchase near Rome: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/6-things-know-about-mysterious-voynich-manuscript-180964847/

The program files behind every number on this page sit in the folder named boring-things at the top of this project inside the folder named research-program-files.

# Where was the Voynich manuscript made: a clue-by-clue location guess

This page treats the Voynich manuscript like a round of a map-guessing game which means every drawing detail is read as a clue about where and when the makers lived.
An AI model (Claude) gathered the clues on 11 November 2026 from published descriptions by researchers and the AI model did not look at the page pictures directly which means every clue below rests on what other people reported seeing.
Several sources are blogs and forums run by long-time hobby researchers and not journals which means a careful reader could treat the clue list as leads to check and not as settled facts.

## The verdict first

Here is the best guess: the makers probably worked in the borderland around the Alps where northern Italian and southern German habits of drawing met which means somewhere in the band from northern Italy up through the Tyrol and the Lake Constance region.

- The castle clue and the plant-book clue point to northern Italy.
- The star-sign clues point to German-speaking lands.
- A workshop in the Alpine borderland could explain both sets of clues because artists there could see Italian castles and German calendars.
- The date clues agree with each other because the clothing fashions fit the years 1400 to 1430 and the laboratory dating of the pages gave 1404 to 1438.
- The guess is moderate and not firm because every clue can be copied from an older picture by an artist living somewhere else.

## Clue 1: the castle with forked wall tops

- What researchers see: a small castle on the large fold-out page has wall tops shaped like the forked tail of a swallow.
- Where the clue points: northern Italy and the nearby Alps because the forked shape began as a badge of one political side in the Italian city wars and still stands on castles from the Aosta valley to Verona.
- How strong: moderate because collectors of old coats of arms report the forked shape as common in Italian sources and uncommon in German sources and absent from the French and English sources checked so far.
- What could fool a guesser: old manuscripts sometimes show forked wall tops in countries that never built forked wall tops which means the artist could have copied a picture and never seen such a castle.
- A second limit: many castles got forked wall tops during repairs centuries later so a castle that has forked wall tops today does not prove the same castle had forked wall tops before 1450.

## Clue 2: the archer with legs and a crossbow

- What researchers see: the star sign Sagittarius is drawn as a standing man with two legs who holds a crossbow where most old star-sign pictures show a creature that is half man and half horse with a longbow.
- Where the clue points: German-speaking lands because a researcher who compared the whole set of star-sign pictures reported the crossbow version only in works from German-speaking areas.
- A narrower pointer: a second researcher who mapped the human archer pictures reported a cluster in southern Germany and northern Switzerland.
- A date pointer: the same researcher reported that most pictures had gone back to longbows by the middle of the 1400s which fits a book made in the early 1400s.
- How strong: moderate because the comparison sets were built by hobby researchers and nobody has published a full count in a journal.

## Clue 3: the crayfish and the courting couple

- What researchers see: the star sign Cancer is drawn as a crayfish or lobster and the star sign Gemini is drawn as a clothed man and woman holding hands where the older tradition shows two male twins.
- Where the clue points: Europe north of the Alps because one survey of several hundred old star-sign sets found the crayfish in about three quarters of the German examples while French examples mixed crabs and crayfish.
- The couple pointer: the same survey reported that the closest matches for the clothed couple come from the lands of the old German empire.
- How strong: weak to moderate because the crayfish also appears outside Germany and the couple is described as uncommon everywhere.

## Clue 4: the baggy sleeves

- What researchers see: the archer wears a tunic with sleeves that are baggy at the elbow and tight at the wrist and the women in the star-sign pages wear dresses with long cut sleeves.
- Where the clue points: the years 1400 to 1430 because researchers who collected dated pictures found the baggy-elbow sleeve all over European book painting in those three decades and rarely afterward.
- How strong: fairly strong as a date clue because the clothing date and the laboratory date of 1404 to 1438 were reached by unrelated methods and overlap.
- What the clue cannot do: the baggy sleeve was an international fashion which means the sleeve gives a date and does not give a place.
- A disagreement to report: one forum writer judged the women's dress to be closest to French fashion which is an opinion that does not fit the German star-sign clues.

## Clue 5: the plant pictures

- What researchers see: the plant pages resemble a family of plant books made in northern Italy in the 1400s for physicians and pharmacists.
- Where the clue points: northern Italy.
- How strong: moderate because the resemblance is a judgment about drawing style and the Voynich plants themselves match no known species.

## Clue 6: the month names written in ordinary letters

- What researchers see: someone wrote month names such as "aberil" and "augst" and "octembre" beside the star signs in ordinary Latin letters and in darker ink than the main writing.
- What the darker ink suggests: a later reader added the month names which means the month names tell where an early owner came from and not where the makers lived.
- Where the clue points: a speaker of a French-like language because researchers have matched the spellings to southern French and Catalan and northern French and nobody has settled which.
- One concrete match: the odd spelling "octembre" also appears on a brass star-measuring tool from Picardy in northern France from the 1300s.
- How strong: weak for locating the makers and useful for tracing where the book traveled.

## Clue 7: the German words on the last page

- What researchers see: the last page has a few lines in ordinary letters that include "so nim" which was a very common opening in German recipes ("so take") and "pox leber" which means the liver of a male goat.
- Where the clue points: a German-speaking writer and one researcher places the handwriting style mainly in northeast Switzerland and southwest Germany.
- What the clue suggests: a later owner probably wrote the lines because researchers judge the handwriting to differ from the main scribes which again describes where the book traveled.
- How strong: moderate for "a German speaker held the book early" and weak for "the makers spoke German".

## Clue 8: the trail of owners

- The earliest probable owner was a physician and alchemist in Augsburg in southern Germany and the first confirmed owner was an alchemist in Prague.
- Where the clue points: the book was in German-speaking and Czech lands by about 1600 which fits a start somewhere in or near the Alps and does not prove such a start because books travel.

## Guesses that the clues argue against

- A claim that the book came from Mexico fits poorly because the pages were dated to 1404 through 1438 and Europeans first reached Mexico in 1519 and the star-sign pictures follow European calendar habits.
- A purely southern Italian or Spanish origin fits poorly because the crossbow archer has not been reported from those regions.

## What would make the guess firmer

- A journal-quality count of every dated star-sign set with a crossbow archer could confirm or break the German pointer.
- A list of castles proven to have forked wall tops before 1440 could narrow the castle clue from a whole region to a few valleys.
- A match between the handwriting of the main scribes and dated documents from one town would outweigh every picture clue because handwriting is tied to where a scribe trained.

## Sources

- Comparison of the whole star-sign set with other manuscripts: https://stephenbax.net/?p=1755
- Notes on the crossbow archer and the lobster: https://stephenbax.net/?p=1656
- Maps and counts of archer and crayfish pictures: https://voynichportal.com/category/the-voynich-zodiac-wheels/ and https://voynichportal.com/tag/sagittarius/
- Study of the baggy-elbow sleeves and their dates: https://herculeaf.wordpress.com/2018/11/13/the-golden-age-of-baggy-elbowed-tunics/
- Forum threads on sleeves and dress: https://www.voynich.ninja/thread-2495.html and https://www.voynich.ninja/thread-2509-page-2.html
- Month names and the Picardy tool: https://stephenbax.net/?p=1226 and http://inamidst.com/voynich/months
- Essay on the notes in ordinary letters: https://voynichthoughts.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/02/marginalia.pdf
- Last-page German words: https://herculeaf.wordpress.com/2023/05/17/you-bastard-script-exploring-paleography/ and https://www.voynich.ninja/thread-4364-page-6.html
- Handwriting region of the last page: https://voynichportal.com/page/18/
- Forked wall tops: https://www.medievalists.net/2017/01/crenellations-crowning-castles/ and https://www.voynich.ninja/archive/index.php/thread-3643-5.html
- Castle and plant-book clues: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2025/05/05/the-voynich-manuscript-revealed-five-things-you-probably-did-not-know-about-the-medieval-masterpiece

# When the words cannot be read what else can a person still read?

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the two points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection. The reflection borrows the unreadable book from this folder as a picture for understanding another person and makes no new claim about the book.

A very old handwritten book sits in a library and no living reader can read the words. A reader can still learn from the book in other ways. A reader can look at how the book appears because even lines and hand-colored drawings of plants and stars show that the maker took care. A reader can learn where and when the book was made in the way a visitor can learn the history of a village without speaking the village's language. A reader can notice which written marks repeat often in the way a listener can hear the rhythm of speech before knowing a single word. A reader can also make a guess from the place the book came from such as "here is a possibility: the maker hid the words because the pages hold something valuable such as records of wealth". Each of those observations is a small clue and several small clues together give a rough first understanding. A visitor in a village learns the same way when a villager points at water and says a word.

A person who has not put a feeling into words can be understood in the same way. That person still has a face and a posture and habits and a recent history. A listener can notice those things and offer a gentle guess that also says why the listener is asking and what the listener can give. An example is "I noticed quiet after that phone call so I wonder if the call held something important to you and I am asking because I want to support you and I am available to talk now or later". Quiet can come from many places such as sadness or deep thought or relief. So a guess built from a person's face and posture and habits stays a guess until the person confirms the guess because the person is the one who knows what the quiet holds.

- A book whose words cannot be read still gives clues through how the book looks and where the book was made and which written marks repeat so a reader can build a rough first understanding.
- A listener can notice that a person went quiet and offer a guess in sentences that start from "I" such as "I wonder if that call held something important to you and I am asking because I want to support you and I am available to talk now or later".
