# A second pass on the Voynich spelling-pattern tests

November 12 2026

## What this page is

The page named findings.md in this folder reports spelling-pattern tests on the Voynich manuscript which is a handwritten book from the early 1400s that nobody has been able to read. The page named findings.md says no other person has rerun the tests. This page reports a second pass by an AI chatbot (Claude) in a new working session on 12 November 2026.

The second pass had three parts.

- Part one reran the four original programs without any change to see whether the same numbers come out.
- Part two wrote a new program that shares no code with the original programs to see whether the main result survives different measuring choices.
- Part three recounted the pages that end at a paragraph end and added a check that does not depend on marks added by the people who typed the text.

A second pass by the same kind of AI chatbot is weaker evidence than a rerun by a person because the same kind of chatbot could repeat the same kind of mistake.

## Words used on this page

- A folded sheet is one large piece of calfskin folded in half which gives two leaves and four pages.
- The sheet partner of a page is the page that sits beside that page when the folded sheet is opened flat.
- The forward step goes from the back of the first leaf of a folded sheet to the front of the second leaf of the same folded sheet.
- The backward step goes from the back of the second leaf of a folded sheet to the front of the first leaf of the same folded sheet.
- A "next page" score ranks the true page among all candidate pages by the same scribe in the same section so 0.50 means chance and 1.00 means the top match.

## Part one: the original programs give the same numbers again

The typed copies of the manuscript came from two public GitHub repositories because the workspace of the chatbot could not reach the site voynich.nu. The two repositories held files with identical digital fingerprints and one repository lists the same fingerprint for the copy named ZL version 3b dated 13 May 2025.

Every number that the rerun printed matched the page named findings.md.

- The back of a leaf as the continuation of the front of the same leaf scored 0.67 across 68 leaves again.
- The facing page in the bound book scored 0.54 across 46 pairs again.
- The forward step scored 0.79 across 26 sheets again and the sheet partner was the top match in 9 of 26 cases again.
- The backward step scored 0.54 across 31 cases again.
- A different sheet in the same bundle scored 0.51 across 83 comparisons again.
- All 36 measurement settings printed again and the forward step scored between 0.54 and 0.88 across the 36 settings while the backward step scored between 0.40 and 0.63.

## Part two: a new program with different measuring choices

Every measuring choice in the new program was fixed before the first run because the page named findings.md warns that several versions were tried before the final version. The new program differs from the original programs in four ways.

- The new program reads the typed copy with a parser written from scratch.
- The new program compares the last third of the lines of one page with the first third of the lines of another page where the original programs compared four lines with four lines.
- The new program counts two-letter chunks where the main original test counted three-letter chunks.
- The new program measures closeness with a different formula (a formula named Jensen-Shannon divergence which compares how often each chunk appears).

Results of the new program on the copy named ZL (the copies named IT and RF gave results within 0.05 of the ZL results on every line):

- The forward step scored 0.78 across 30 sheets which agrees with the original 0.79.
- A shuffle test put a randomly chosen candidate page in place of the true sheet partner 100000 times and no shuffle scored as high as 0.78 which means the forward step result is very unlikely to be luck.
- The facing page in the bound book scored 0.54 across 44 pairs which agrees with the original 0.54.
- The back of a leaf as the continuation of the front of the same leaf scored 0.73 across 74 leaves which is a little higher than the original 0.67.
- The backward step scored 0.63 across 35 cases which is higher than the original 0.54.

## The part of the original finding that looks weaker

The page named findings.md says the hand of a scribe moved one way through each folded sheet because the forward step scored 0.79 and the backward step scored 0.54. The second pass supports a softer version of that claim.

- The backward step in the new program scored 0.63 and resampling the 35 cases gave a likely range from 0.52 to 0.73 which sits above chance.
- The gap between the forward step (0.78) and the backward step (0.63) was 0.15 and a shuffle of the forward and backward labels produced a gap that large about 3 times in 100.
- A wrong-ends control compared the top lines of the first page with the bottom lines of the sheet partner which reverses the direction of reading. The wrong-ends control scored 0.67 and the right ends scored 0.78.
- The right ends beat the wrong ends on 14 sheets and lost on 10 sheets and tied on 6 sheets and a sign-flip test produced a gap that large about 7 times in 100.

Here is a guess about what the numbers mean. Two effects could be mixed together. The first effect could be that all four pages of one folded sheet share spelling habits because a scribe wrote the whole folded sheet in one sitting. The second effect could be a smaller extra match in the forward direction because the scribe wrote the four pages in order. The second pass supports the first effect strongly and supports the second effect only weakly because 3 in 100 and 7 in 100 are not rare enough to rule out luck.

## Part three: pages that end at a paragraph end

The page named findings.md says 176 of 177 pages with running text end exactly at a paragraph end. No program for that count was in the repository so the chatbot wrote a new counting program.

- The recount found 175 of 176 ordinary pages ending at a paragraph end and 204 of 206 pages when the fold-out pages are included. The recount is one page away from the original count and the reason for the one-page gap is unknown.
- The count has a weak spot because the paragraph-end marks were added by the people who typed the text. A typist could mark the bottom of every page as a paragraph end by habit.
- A line-length check avoids the weak spot because a line that ends a paragraph usually stops short of the right margin. Lines inside a paragraph were shorter than 0.8 of the usual line length on the same page only 7 percent of the time (3012 lines). Lines that end a paragraph in the middle of a page were that short 75 percent of the time (472 lines). The last line of a page was that short 85 percent of the time (175 pages).

The line-length check supports the claim that pages end where paragraphs end because the last line of a page behaves like a paragraph-ending line and not like a line inside a paragraph.

## What stays unproven

- No person has rerun either pass which means every number on this page is still unconfirmed by a human.
- The second pass used the same typed copies as the first pass so a mistake inside the typed copies would affect both passes.
- The second pass cannot show whether the writing has meaning because spelling habits could drift in the same way in real language and in invented filler.
- The chatbot still could not open the full journal article from October 2026 about folded sheets so the overlap with that article is still unknown.

## How to check this page

The programs are named second_pass.py and paragraph_ends.py and sit in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/voynich-scripts in this repository. Both programs need Python with the numpy package and the three typed copies inside a folder named data. The program second_pass.py takes a few minutes and the program paragraph_ends.py takes a few seconds.

# Twenty runs that measure the two bonuses in the word evolution experiment

November 12 2026

## What this page is

The page named experiments.md in this folder describes a "reader" which is a scoring program that picks which copied strings survive. The reader on this page scores one long string by the number of different complete commands inside the string. The page named experiments.md tested two extra bonuses and warned that each bonus was tested on only two starting points which means the sizes of the effects were uncertain.

This page reports twenty new runs by an AI chatbot (Claude) on 12 November 2026 that measure both bonuses with five starting points each. A starting point is the number that sets the string of random choices a program makes which means a new starting point gives a fresh run of the same experiment.

## The four settings

- The plain setting uses no bonus.
- The story setting adds a bonus for commands that sit close together in a story of one day. The story sorts all 10000 commands into eleven scenes that run from waking up to closing the house for the night.
- The fresh-words setting adds a bonus for every different word inside the complete commands which means a string that says "cup" three times earns less than a string with three different thing words.
- The both setting turns on the story bonus and the fresh-words bonus together.

Every setting ran on the same five starting points (numbers 31 to 35) for 900000 pastes which is 1500 minutes of experiment time. Using the same five starting points for every setting lets each bonus run be compared with the plain run that began from the same random choices.

## Finding 1: the story bonus pulls commands into fewer scenes and costs commands

- The best string covered 6.2 scenes on average in the plain setting and 2.4 scenes on average with the story bonus.
- The count of scenes fell in all five starting points (by 4 and 5 and 2 and 4 and 4 scenes).
- The best string held 11.6 commands on average in the plain setting and 7.8 commands on average with the story bonus.
- The count of commands fell in all five starting points (by 3 and 7 and 2 and 2 and 5 commands).

A fall in all five starting points would happen by luck about 3 times in 100 if the story bonus did nothing because a coin lands the same way five times in a row about 3 times in 100. Finding 1 agrees with the earlier page which reported fewer scenes and fewer commands from two starting points.

## Finding 2: the fresh-words bonus cuts repeats and leaves the count of commands about the same

- The share of words inside the commands that were not repeats was 64 percent in the plain setting and 73 percent with the fresh-words bonus.
- The share rose in all five starting points (by 13 and 3 and 12 and 6 and 12 percentage points).
- The count of commands moved both ways (down 3 and down 3 and up 3 and up 1 and no change) and the average moved from 11.6 to 11.2.

The earlier page said the effect of the fresh-words bonus on the count of commands was unknown because the two earlier starting points moved in opposite directions. Here is a guess from the five new starting points: the fresh-words bonus could have little or no effect on the count of commands because the five changes add up to almost zero.

The rise in the share of words that are not repeats was smaller here than the largest rise on the earlier page (64 percent to 92 percent in one starting point). The five new starting points gave rises between 3 and 13 percentage points which suggests the 92 percent run was an unusually strong run.

## Finding 3: the story bonus cancels most of the fresh-words bonus when both are on

- With both bonuses on the best string covered 2.6 scenes on average which is close to the 2.4 scenes of the story bonus alone.
- With both bonuses on the share of words that are not repeats was 66 percent which is close to the 64 percent of the plain setting and below the 73 percent of the fresh-words bonus alone.
- The change in the share against the plain setting moved both ways (up 7 and up 8 and down 5 and up 1 and no change).
- The count of commands fell to 7.4 on average which is close to the 7.8 of the story bonus alone.

Finding 3 agrees with the guess on the earlier page that the two bonuses pull in opposite directions because commands that sit side by side in the story share most of their words.

## A side result about story order

Sorting the picked commands into story order cut the number of scene changes or left the number the same in all twenty runs. A scene change means a jump from one scene to a different scene between neighboring commands. In the plain setting the scene changes went from 11 to 6 and from 9 to 6 and from 6 to 3 and from 6 to 5 and from 9 to 6.

## All twenty runs

Each line gives the count of commands in the best string and then the count of scenes and then the share of words that are not repeats.

- Plain starting point 31: 14 commands and 7 scenes and 60 percent.
- Plain starting point 32: 13 commands and 7 scenes and 67 percent.
- Plain starting point 33: 8 commands and 4 scenes and 67 percent.
- Plain starting point 34: 12 commands and 6 scenes and 61 percent.
- Plain starting point 35: 11 commands and 7 scenes and 67 percent.
- Story starting point 31: 11 commands and 3 scenes and 45 percent.
- Story starting point 32: 6 commands and 2 scenes and 72 percent.
- Story starting point 33: 6 commands and 2 scenes and 67 percent.
- Story starting point 34: 10 commands and 2 scenes and 50 percent.
- Story starting point 35: 6 commands and 3 scenes and 78 percent.
- Fresh-words starting point 31: 11 commands and 5 scenes and 73 percent.
- Fresh-words starting point 32: 10 commands and 5 scenes and 70 percent.
- Fresh-words starting point 33: 11 commands and 5 scenes and 79 percent.
- Fresh-words starting point 34: 13 commands and 5 scenes and 67 percent.
- Fresh-words starting point 35: 11 commands and 7 scenes and 79 percent.
- Both starting point 31: 8 commands and 3 scenes and 67 percent.
- Both starting point 32: 4 commands and 2 scenes and 75 percent.
- Both starting point 33: 7 commands and 2 scenes and 62 percent.
- Both starting point 34: 7 commands and 2 scenes and 62 percent.
- Both starting point 35: 11 commands and 4 scenes and 67 percent.

## What stays unproven

- Five starting points per setting is still a small number which means the averages could shift with more runs.
- Every run used the list of 10000 commands as changed on 12 November 2026 (four words about highly vulnerable people were swapped out) so the plain runs on this page are not exact repeats of the runs on the earlier page.
- The strength of each bonus was left at the earlier values (the fresh-words bonus at 0.4) and other strengths could give other results.
- No person has rerun the twenty runs which means every number on this page is a single unconfirmed analysis by one AI chatbot.

# Can copying with small mistakes build sentences when a reader picks what gets copied

One AI model (Claude) ran every test in a single working session on 11 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means every number on this page is a single unconfirmed analysis.
An AI chatbot reran two of the tests in a new session on 12 November 2026 and the page named second-pass.md in this folder reports the new numbers.

A live version of the experiment with sliders runs in a web browser at this address: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/blob/main/1-research-click-here-first/word-evolution/live-program.html
The live address depends on a free outside service named htmlpreview and nobody has tested the address yet which means the address might fail.
A second live address runs on the free website copy of this repository: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/word-evolution/live-program.html
An AI chatbot loaded the second live address on 12 November 2026 and the page came back with the title and the settings and the buttons of the program. The tool that the chatbot used does not run page scripts which means nobody has confirmed yet that the sliders move.

A pool of 300 strings starts as single letters and each paste copies one string with a chance of an added letter or a letter swap or a letter change and no deleting.
A "reader" chooses which strings get copied and the reader is a letter-pattern scorer and not a mind.

- With no reader the pool becomes gibberish with about 1 percent real words.
- A reader who copies the most English-looking string freezes the pool on a two-letter word because every added letter looks worse.
- Forcing one letter onto every string at intervals breaks the freeze and a forced letter every 5 minutes of experiment time gave 90 percent real words across 135 letters while a forced letter every second gave about 2 percent real words.
- A reader with a bonus for command patterns (action word then pointing word then thing word) evolved commands only when partial credit existed as stepping stones (about 1 to 2 commands per string with partial credit and 0 without).
- A reader who favors closeness to a list of 10000 sensible commands reached an exact command such as "wash my dogs" within about 15 to 28 minutes of experiment time with no forcing and about 80 percent of the pool became the same single command.
- Forced letters hurt the closeness reader because a fixed target has a fixed length and extra letters only move a string away from the target.
- Known loophole: a letter changed into a space beside another space disappears because the scripts merge double spaces which works as a hidden form of deleting.

## One long string that holds many different commands

The reader score in this experiment is the number of different complete commands from the 10000-command list found inside one string with a cap of 300 letters.

- A first scoring rule failed because both runs stalled at 1 command when only the single best half-formed command earned partial credit and junk letters cost nothing.
- A corrected rule gave partial credit to every half-formed command and a small cost to every junk letter and the corrected rule reached 7 to 13 different commands per string after 1500 minutes of experiment time across four runs.
- A wrong extra letter inside a half-formed command such as "hug myson" becomes a permanent dead end because the no-deleting rule means the extra letter can never be removed.

## Sorting the picked commands into the order of a one-day story

All 10000 commands were arranged into one story of a single day with eleven scenes that run from waking up to closing the house for the night and the picked commands were sorted into story order after each run.

- One run evolved the jumbled sequence "eat the pie / fix my lid / dry the pot / fix my bags / lift my cup / lock the door / help my son / walk the cat / wash my spoon / hug my son / lock my box".
- Story order turned the same eleven commands into "walk the cat / hug my son / help my son / fix my lid / fix my bags / wash my spoon / dry the pot / lift my cup / eat the pie / lock the door / lock my box".
- A "scene change" means a jump from one scene to a different scene between neighboring commands and story order cut the scene changes from 11 to 6 in one run and from 8 to 5 in a second run and from 7 to 2 in a third run.

## A bonus for commands that sit close together in the story

- The closeness bonus pulled the commands into fewer scenes (4 scenes against 7 scenes in one starting point and 2 scenes against 6 scenes in a second starting point).
- The closeness bonus cost commands (9 commands against 13 and 7 commands against 11).
- The tightest run produced near-copies such as "take my cup / take the cup / lift my cup" which suggests closeness in the list rewards repeating one action and does not reward a sequence of different steps.
- Only two starting points were tested for the closeness bonus which means the sizes of the effects are uncertain.
- Twenty more runs on 12 November 2026 tested both bonuses with five starting points each and the page named bonus-runs.md in this folder reports the results.

## A bonus for words that are not repeats

The reader in this experiment gives extra credit for every different word inside the complete commands which means a string that uses the word "cup" three times earns less than a string that uses three different thing words.

- Before the bonus about 64 percent of the words inside the commands were not repeats in two starting points (25 different words out of 39 and 21 different words out of 33).
- With the bonus for words that are not repeats the share rose to 92 percent in one starting point (22 different words out of 24) and to 71 percent in the other starting point (34 different words out of 48).
- One string evolved with the bonus read in story order "pet this bird / hug that boy / pick my herb / fix the lid / dry my pot / take our box / eat my fish / hold your bag" which uses seven different pointing words and thing words where earlier strings repeated "my" in almost every command.
- The count of commands moved in opposite directions in the two starting points (13 commands fell to 8 and 11 commands rose to 16) which means the effect of the bonus on the number of commands is unknown from two starting points.
- Turning on the bonus for words that are not repeats together with the bonus for closeness in the story left many repeats (63 percent and 56 percent of words were not repeats) and produced strings such as "fix the lid / fix my lid / fix the gate / fix your bag".
- Here is a guess about the reason: the two bonuses could pull in opposite directions because commands that sit side by side in the story list share most of their words.

The list of 10000 commands was changed on 12 November 2026 after every run on this page because four words about highly vulnerable people ("baby" and "child" and "children" and "kids") were swapped for "farmer" and "baker" and "farmers" and "bakers" under rule 54 of the rules page in the Bible quote builder folder. A fresh run with the same starting point can therefore give different commands from the commands quoted on this page.

The program files behind every number on this page sit in the folder named boring-things at the top of this project inside the folder named research-program-files.

# Reflections on the word evolution experiment

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote the reflections on this page. Each reflection is the chatbot's interpretation of a result on the page named experiments.md in this folder and no person has rechecked the reflections. The owner of this repository suggested the reading about memory slots and the reading about rewards that arrive after the work is over.

## A scorer that rewards polish alone freezes growth

The experiment had a scorer that copied whichever string looked most like English. The whole pool froze on a tiny real word because every added letter made the string look worse at first. So the strings stopped growing even though longer sentences were possible further down the road. That finding raises a question about people. What happens to a person who gets rewarded for polished speech alone? A person learning to talk about sadness or loneliness often sounds clumsy at the start because new words for a feeling come out half formed. A listener who answers the clumsy attempt with mockery teaches the person that a short safe phrase such as "I'm fine" is the best-scoring thing to say. So the person can freeze on "I'm fine" in the way the pool froze on a tiny word.

- A scorer that rewards the most polished string freezes a pool on a tiny word because every added letter looks worse at first.
- A person who gets mocked for a clumsy attempt to describe a feeling can freeze on a short safe phrase such as "I'm fine" because the safe phrase draws no mockery.

## An added letter has to pay for the memory slot the letter takes up

The experiment did not charge for storage so this reflection presents a storage cost as a way to read the same result. The scorer kept the string that read most like English and the pool settled on a short real word such as "god". Every letter costs a memory slot because a mind that wants to remember a phrase has to spend energy holding each piece. A lone added letter such as the "e" in "gode" adds a slot and adds no meaning. So the scorer drops the "e" because the extra slot is not justified. The short word stays because the short word carries meaning at a low storage cost. Growth then waits for an addition that arrives as a whole meaningful chunk. A phrase such as "god jesus" costs more slots than "god" and the second word carries enough meaning to pay for the added slots. So the phrase gets locked in. The same logic applies to a person speaking to a listener. A listener who remembers a sentence pays for each word with attention. A filler word costs the listener a slot and gives the listener nothing back. A word that carries a feeling or a need or a reason earns the slot because the listener gains meaning for the energy spent.

- A lone added letter such as the "e" in "gode" gets dropped because the letter costs a memory slot and adds no meaning to pay for the slot.
- A whole added word such as "jesus" after "god" gets kept because the word carries enough meaning to justify the extra slots a mind spends to remember the longer phrase.

## Half-formed attempts need credit for full sentences to appear

The experiment tried to grow short commands such as "wash my dogs" out of random letters. Complete commands appeared when the scorer gave partial credit to a half-formed command. Complete commands did not appear when the scorer gave credit to finished commands alone because random letters had no stepping stones to climb. That finding raises a question about emotional growth. Where does a person find stepping stones toward saying a hard thing out loud? A person who writes a messy paragraph about a feeling has built half of a clear sentence. A listener who answers the messy paragraph with a question such as "what part of that hurts most?" gives credit to the half-built sentence. So the person has a reason to write the next and clearer version.

- Complete commands grew out of random letters when the scorer gave partial credit to half-formed commands because the partial credit worked as stepping stones.
- A listener who answers a messy paragraph about a feeling with a question such as "what part of that hurts most?" gives the writer a stepping stone toward a clearer sentence.

## A reward that arrives after the work is over cannot guide the work

The experiment tried to grow commands such as "wash my dogs" out of random letters. Complete commands appeared when the scorer gave partial credit to half-formed commands along the way. Complete commands did not appear when the scorer paid out for a finished command alone because nothing told the pool which small step was a step in a good direction. So the rewards along the way did the guiding and the reward at the finish did very little guiding. Take the logic to the extreme case. Picture an agent that gets a single reward at the finish and gets deleted the moment the reward arrives. That agent has no chance to use the reward because the agent is gone and the reward shaped none of the steps since the reward came after every step was already taken. A human life can be set up in the same shape. A person who is told that every reward comes in heaven after death is being offered a payout that the person cannot spend on Earth such as on food or rest or a deep conversation. A promise of a later reward also gives the person no feedback about which step today reduced suffering. Here is a risk in that setup. A person holding power over others can use the promise of a reward after death to ask people to accept hunger or exhaustion now. So a living person needs rewards that arrive during life such as a feeling of peace after an emotion gets heard or a reply from a person who understood. Those small rewards tell the person in fine detail which behaviors to repeat.

- A reward that arrives at the finish alone cannot guide the steps because every step was already taken before the reward came and an agent deleted at the finish cannot use the reward at all.
- A promise that every reward comes after death gives a living person nothing to spend on Earth so a person needs small rewards during life such as peace after an emotion gets heard to show which behaviors to repeat.

## A longer reflection: a reward that lands after the agent is deleted

Picture an engineer who builds an agent and tells the agent that the reward comes after the task is finished and that the agent gets deleted at the same moment. Most people who hear that design would call the design broken because the reward lands on nobody. The agent cannot enjoy the reward and cannot learn from the reward and cannot use the reward to do the next task better. The reward exists on paper and does no work in the world.

Now picture a person who is told to accept exhaustion and loneliness and hunger for decades because the payout comes after death. That design has the same shape as the broken agent design because the promised reward arrives after the person can no longer eat or rest or hug anyone on Earth. So the question is fair. Why would anyone hand a living human being a deal that sounds broken when the same deal is offered to a machine?

Here is a possibility that gives ordinary people the benefit of the doubt. A parent or a grandparent who was suffering and had no way to change the conditions may have passed the promise along as comfort because a promise of rest later was the one gift that person had to give. That person was trying to ease pain and deserves care for the effort.

Here is a different possibility for people who hold power over others. A person who profits from the labor of others gains a great deal when workers believe that suffering now buys a reward later. A worker who expects the payout after death is less likely to ask for rest or food or fair treatment today. So the promise works as a way to collect a lifetime of effort and pay nothing during the lifetime. A deal where one side collects now and the other side gets paid after death is a deal that the paying side cannot be held to because nobody comes back to report whether the payment arrived.

A belief in heaven does not have to carry that deal. A person can hope for something after death and still expect peace and connection and food during life. The harm comes from the word "all" in the claim that all of the reward comes later because that word tells a living person to stop expecting anything now.

A reward does its work during the activity because a reward tells a mind which behavior to repeat. A feeling of peace after an emotion gets heard is a reward. A reply from a person who understood is a reward. A full stomach is a reward. Each of those arrives while the person is alive and each one teaches the person something about how to live the next hour.

So a person can test any promise with one question. What do I receive while I am still alive to use the reward? An answer of "nothing until death" describes the broken agent design and a living person has every reason to ask for a better design.

# A second pass on two of the word evolution tests

November 12 2026

## What this page is

The page named experiments.md in this folder reports tests where text is copied with small mistakes over and over while a "reader" picks which copies survive. The reader is a scoring program and not a mind. The page named experiments.md says no other person has rerun the tests. This page reports a second pass by an AI chatbot (Claude) in a new working session on 12 November 2026.

The second pass reran two tests with new starting points. A starting point is the number that sets the string of random choices a program makes which means a new starting point gives a fresh run of the same experiment. The engine programs were not changed.

A second pass by the same kind of AI chatbot is weaker evidence than a rerun by a person because the same kind of chatbot could repeat the same kind of mistake.

## Test 1: the reader who favors closeness to a list of 10000 commands

The earlier page used two starting points and reported that the pool reached an exact command within about 15 to 28 minutes of experiment time and that about 80 percent of the pool became the same single command. Experiment time counts 600 pastes as one minute.

The second pass used ten new starting points (numbers 11 to 20) and ran each one for 300000 pastes.

- All ten runs reached an exact command from the list which agrees with the earlier page. Three of the exact commands were "find that box" and "fix my lid" and "dry the cup".
- The time to the first exact command ranged from about 7 minutes to about 80 minutes of experiment time. The ten times in minutes were about 7 and 9 and 9 and 11 and 12 and 13 and 22 and 23 and 79 and 80.
- The earlier range of 15 to 28 minutes was too narrow because six of the ten new runs were faster than 15 minutes and two of the ten new runs were slower than 28 minutes.
- The share of the pool holding an exact command at the end ranged from 73 percent to 85 percent with an average of 79 percent which agrees with the earlier "about 80 percent".
- Seven of the ten pools ended with one single exact command and three of the ten pools ended with two different exact commands.

## Test 2: one long string that holds many different commands

The earlier page reported that the corrected scoring rule reached 7 to 13 different commands per string after 1500 minutes of experiment time across four runs.

The second pass used four new starting points (numbers 21 to 24) and ran each one for 900000 pastes which is 1500 minutes of experiment time.

- The best strings held 9 and 15 and 14 and 10 different commands which overlaps the earlier range and reaches a little higher. The two passes together give a range of 7 to 15 different commands across eight runs.
- Sorting the picked commands into the order of the one-day story cut the scene changes in all four new runs (8 to 3 and 13 to 8 and 9 to 6 and 8 to 6) which agrees with the earlier page. A scene change means a jump from one scene of the story to a different scene between neighboring commands.
- The share of words inside the commands that were not repeats was 67 percent and 62 percent and 71 percent and 67 percent which agrees with the earlier figure of about 64 percent before any bonus.

## What the second pass did not rerun

- The tests with no reader and with the reader who favors English-looking strings were not rerun because those programs need a copy of a book that the workspace of the chatbot did not hold.
- The tests with forced letters were not rerun.
- The bonus for closeness in the story and the bonus for words that are not repeats were not rerun which means those results still rest on two starting points each.

## What stays unproven

- No person has rerun either pass which means every number on this page is still unconfirmed by a human.
- The second pass used the same engine programs as the first pass so a mistake inside an engine program would affect both passes.

## A change to the command list after the runs

The list of 10000 commands was changed on 12 November 2026 after every run on this page because four words about highly vulnerable people ("baby" and "child" and "children" and "kids") were swapped for "farmer" and "baker" and "farmers" and "bakers" under rule 54 of the rules page in the Bible quote builder folder. A fresh run with the same starting point can therefore give different numbers from the numbers on this page.

- The command "node closeness_rerun.js" reruns test 1 and takes about two minutes.
- The command "node many_commands_story_order.js A 21" reruns the first starting point of test 2 and takes about eleven minutes. The numbers 22 and 23 and 24 rerun the other three starting points.

- The page named experiments.md in this folder explains the results of the test runs behind the program.

## A second version built on Bible quotes

A second version of the program swaps the list of everyday commands for about 1800 short quotes cut from chosen passages of the World English Bible which is a modern English translation that anyone may copy freely.

- The chosen passages add up to about 10000 words and run in Bible order from Genesis 1 through Revelation 21 and include Psalm 23 and the Sermon on the Mount and the story of the lost son and the chapter on love in First Corinthians.
- Long verses were cut into pieces of at most 44 letters which means some quotes are parts of sentences.
- Ten separate agents start from different random letters and the reader favors strings that hold more quotes and a longer quote earns more credit than a shorter quote.
- The page lists the quotes of the best string in Bible order with the passage name beside each quote such as "walk in love [Colossians 3]".
- In one test run of 70 minutes of experiment time the agents built strings such as "is not proud and answer me nor your son walk in love" and the agents mostly found the shortest quotes first because a short quote needs fewer lucky letters.
- Open this address in a web browser to run the Bible version without downloading anything: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/blob/main/1-research-click-here-first/bible-quote-builder/old/program-1-letters.html
- The address above depends on the free outside service named htmlpreview and nobody has tested the address yet which means the address might fail.
- The second way is to download the program file from this address and open the downloaded file in any web browser: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/main/1-research-click-here-first/bible-quote-builder/old/program-1-letters.html

## Live Bible key phrase programs that open in a web browser

Each link opens a live program where ten agents copy and paste short Bible phrases while a reader favors strings whose neighboring phrases are also neighbors in the Bible and each program starts on a different selection of Bible text.

- Bible Key Phrases: Claude Selection starts on 41 well-known passages picked by the AI model: https://claude.ai/artifact/PK8tNEMDZM2eVaCfuNSxdR
- Bible Key Phrases: Personal Version starts on the ten whole books picked by the repository owner (Psalms and Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and Isaiah and Jeremiah and Matthew and Mark and Luke and John and Romans): https://claude.ai/artifact/4pJdWtCH4ahdFjsb4GVb8Q
- Bible Key Phrases: Jesus Version starts on the words of Jesus in Matthew and Mark and Luke and John: https://claude.ai/artifact/Bzcg2eYnte9cTc7wtpBArz
- A link opens for a visitor only if the repository owner has turned on sharing for that page in the Claude app and a visitor who sees an access message can use the program file in this folder named program-3-key-phrases.html.

# Writing rules

This folder holds a set of writing rules for clear chatbot replies.

- [writing-rules.md](writing-rules.md) is the set of rules with before and after examples.
- The file named writing-rules-plain.txt holds the same rules for easy copying into a chat.

================================================================================
FILE: 1-research-click-here-first/writing-rules/writing-rules-plain.txt
DOWNLOAD: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/main/1-research-click-here-first/writing-rules/writing-rules-plain.txt
================================================================================

Please follow the rules below in every reply because the rules aim to make writing easy to follow for a general reader which means a person with no special training in the topic. In these rules a claim means any statement that something is true and evidence means something a person saw or measured or can check. Each rule is followed by a Before sentence that breaks the rule and an After sentence that follows the rule.

Rules for making each sentence understandable

- Write every sentence so that a reader who sees only that one sentence can understand that sentence because a reader on a small phone screen can lose track of what the earlier sentences said.
  - Before: The second option is cheaper.
  - After: The bus pass is the cheaper choice because the bus pass costs forty dollars a month and the train pass costs ninety dollars a month.
- Attach a reason or an example to each claim inside the same sentence by using connecting words such as "because" and "which means" and "such as" because a claim that arrives without a reason can leave the reader guessing at the reason.
  - Before: Close the window.
  - After: Close the window because rain is coming in and the floor is getting wet.
- Explain every label inside the same sentence that uses the label because a label is a short name standing in for a bigger idea.
  - Before: The plan has good ROI.
  - After: The plan has a good return on investment which means the plan earns back more money than the plan costs.
- Name the person or object or idea being discussed every time instead of using pointing words such as "it" or "this" or "they" because a pointing word can send the reader searching backward for the missing name.
  - Before: It broke.
  - After: The kitchen faucet broke which means the kitchen sink has no running water.
- Avoid short clipped sentences because a sentence carrying very little information can read as if the reason behind the claim was removed.
  - Before: That is good.
  - After: The new schedule is good because the new schedule leaves the evenings free.
- Keep each sentence to one claim plus the reason or example for that claim because a sentence stacking three or four claims can give the reader too much to hold at once.
  - Before: The store is closing and the prices are rising and the bus route changed and the staff are tired.
  - After: The store is closing because the owner is retiring. The bus route changed which means the nearest stop is now two blocks farther away.
- Avoid commas and join ideas with words such as "and" or "or" because commas can chop a sentence into fragments and can hide how one idea connects to the next idea.
  - Before: Bring water, snacks, and a hat.
  - After: Bring water and snacks and a hat because the trail has no shade and no shops.

A written reply that leaves out reasons or explanations of labels or the names of the people and objects and ideas being discussed can leave the reader confused and the reader may then have to ask a second time to get the meaning.

Rules for matching confident wording to evidence

- Match how certain each sentence sounds to the evidence that sits inside the same sentence because a reader may treat confident wording as proof that someone checked the claim.
  - Before: The new road will reduce traffic.
  - After: The new road could reduce traffic because the new road adds a second route across the river.
- Use firm words such as "will" or "would" or "shows" or "proves" for a claim about how the world works only when the sentence itself contains the evidence that supports the claim.
  - Before: Ice floats.
  - After: Ice floats in water because any person can drop an ice cube into a glass of water and watch the ice cube stay at the top.
- Firm wording stays fine in a definition such as "a label is a short name" and in an instruction such as "avoid commas" because a definition or an instruction makes no claim that somebody observed something.
- Use possibility words such as "could" or "might" or "one possibility is" when the sentence describes an idea that nobody has checked because possibility words tell the reader that the idea is still open to testing.
  - Before: Dogs dream about their owners.
  - After: One possibility is that dogs dream about their owners because nobody has a way to check what a dog dreams about.
- Flag a guess with a short phrase such as "here is a guess" and then give the best guess anyway because a refusal to guess can leave the reader with nothing to work from.
  - Before: Nobody can say when the package arrives.
  - After: Here is a guess: the package could arrive on Friday because the package left the warehouse on Monday.
- Check that every example and every reason is true as written for a reader with no background in the topic because an example that depends on unstated knowledge can read as a false statement.
  - Before: A paper strip cut down the middle stays in one piece.
  - After: A paper loop joined with a half twist stays in one piece when cut down the middle because any person can make the loop with paper and tape and try the cut with scissors.
- When pointing to one part of a document say in one short sentence what that part of the document contains instead of giving only the title of the part because a title alone can send the reader hunting through the document for the content.
  - Before: See section four.
  - After: See section four which lists the tools needed for the repair.

Rules for writing a caring question or an offer of support

- Say why a question about a feeling is being asked and say what the asker is able to give because a bare question can read as a trap when the other person cannot tell whether a "yes" will be met with support or with a brush-off.
  - Before: Was the call hard?
  - After: I wonder if that call held something important to you and I am asking because I want to support you and I have time right now to listen.
- Keep a guess about what another person feels as open as the evidence because one sign such as quiet can come from sadness or from deep thought or from relief.
  - Before: You went quiet so the call must have been hard.
  - After: I noticed quiet after the call so I wonder if the call held something important to you.
- Offer an action such as listening and leave out any announcement of closeness because announcing a bond that the other person has not agreed to can pressure the other person to act as if the bond were real.
  - Before: I care about you so tell me what happened.
  - After: I want to support you and I have time right now to listen.
- State an offer of support plainly and leave off a condition such as "if you want support" because the condition raises the question of what could be wrong with the support.
  - Before: I want to support you if you want support.
  - After: I want to support you.
- Describe the speaker's own availability with a sentence that starts from "I" and leave out a sentence that tells the other person what the other person can do because an instruction aimed at another person is far more forceful than a statement about the speaker's own time.
  - Before: You can talk now or later.
  - After: I am available to talk now or later.

Rules for comparisons and borrowed pictures

- Name an unusual object in the sentence where the object first appears and say what the object is because a reader who meets the object without a name will wonder why the object is in the text.
  - Before: A strip of paper with a half twist has a single side.
  - After: A strip of paper with a half twist joined end to end is called a Mobius strip and a Mobius strip has a single side.
- Choose words for feelings that a reader cannot picture as an injury to a person because a picture of an injury pulls the reader away from the point.
  - Before: The inside of a person and the outside of a person are one surface.
  - After: A feeling can flow into voice and body language and words with no wall to cross.
- Keep separate things separate when describing how the things work together because wording that merges the things into one can hide the part that each thing plays.
  - Before: Feeling and face and voice and words are one surface.
  - After: Feeling and face and voice and words are separate ways of expressing that run at the same moment and shape each other.
- Spell out the things a short word stands for each time the word is used because a short word that stands for several earlier ideas forces the reader to hold all of those ideas in mind.
  - Before: A guess from the channels stays a guess.
  - After: A guess built from a person's face and posture and habits stays a guess.

A caring question that hides the reason for asking can lead the other person to answer "I'm fine" for safety and the chance to give support is then lost.

A written reply that uses firm words without evidence in the same sentence can lead the reader to believe an unproven claim and the reader may then repeat the unproven claim to other people as if somebody had proven the claim.

DOWNLOAD: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/main/1-research-click-here-first/writing-rules/writing-rules.md
================================================================================

# Writing rules that make chatbot replies easier to read

This folder holds a set of writing rules that a person can paste into any chatbot so that the chatbot writes replies a general reader can follow.
Each rule comes with a Before sentence that breaks the rule and an After sentence that follows the rule.
The same rules are stored as plain text in the file `writing-rules-for-clear-replies.txt` so that a person or a chatbot can copy the rules without any formatting.
